This is because C. jejuni infection can trigger the production of specific anti-ganglioside antibodies through molecular mimicry, leading to more extensive nerve damage and a more severe clinical course.

Age > 40 years
Age > 40 years is incorrect because older age is actually associated with a poorer prognosis in GBS. Patients over 40 years of age typically experience more severe disease, longer recovery times, and are more likely to have residual deficits.

Female sex
Female sex is incorrect because sex has not been consistently shown to be a significant prognostic factor in GBS. While GBS is slightly more common in males, gender does not reliably predict disease severity or outcome.

High anti-GM1 antibody titre
High anti-GM1 antibody titre is incorrect because elevated anti-GM1 antibodies are associated with more severe disease and poorer outcomes. These antibodies are particularly associated with axonal forms of GBS, which generally have a worse prognosis than demyelinating forms.

Low peak expiratory flow rate
Low peak expiratory flow rate is incorrect because respiratory compromise, indicated by a low peak expiratory flow rate, is a marker of disease severity and is associated with worse outcomes. Patients requiring ventilatory support have longer recovery times and are more likely to have residual deficits.

stem: Which one of the following conditions is least recognised as a cause of a seventh nerve palsy?
explanation:
Systemic lupus erythematosus
The correct answer is Systemic lupus erythematosus. Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is an autoimmune disease that can affect multiple organ systems, but it is not commonly recognised as a cause of seventh nerve palsy. While neurologic manifestations are common in SLE, they more typically include cognitive dysfunction, seizures, and psychosis. Peripheral neuropathies such as seventh nerve palsy are relatively rare in SLE.

Acoustic neuroma
Acoustic neuroma, on the other hand, is a well-recognised cause of seventh nerve palsy. Acoustic neuromas (also known as vestibular schwannomas) are benign tumours arising from the Schwann cells of the eighth cranial nerve. They can compress the adjacent facial nerve (seventh cranial nerve), leading to facial weakness or paralysis.

Herpes zoster
Similarly, Herpes zoster infection can lead to seventh nerve palsy. When this occurs in association with a vesicular rash in the ear canal, it is known as Ramsay Hunt syndrome. The virus infects the geniculate ganglion of the facial nerve, causing inflammation and subsequent palsy.

HIV
HIV has also been associated with seventh nerve palsy. HIV-associated facial nerve palsy can occur due to direct viral invasion or secondary to opportunistic infections or malignancies in patients with advanced disease.

Diabetes mellitus
Finally, Diabetes mellitus is a common cause of mononeuropathies including facial neuropathy. Hyperglycaemia leads to metabolic and vascular changes that result in damage to peripheral nerves. Diabetic mononeuropathy often presents with sudden onset unilateral facial weakness similar to Bell's palsy.

stem: A 31-year-old man attends his appointment with an oncologist after being referred by his family physician. The man reported feeling nauseous and having a persistent headache for the past month. The pain was not relieved by the regular over-the-counter painkiller. The patient confirms that he has a significant family history of cancer and this is why he has been referred to see the oncologist. After chromosome analysis which revealed an abnormality related to the chromosome 3p, the patient is explained that his condition will put him at higher risk of developing several tumors, which could be both benign and malignant. The oncologist tells the patient that this condition can be passed on to future generations and that the patient's children have a fifty-percent chance of developing the condition, given his spouse does not carry the mutation as well. The patient is happy to know that he will not need a screening flexible sigmoidoscopy. Which of the following diseases is the patient at the highest risk of developing due to his underlying condition?
explanation:
Clear-cell renal carcinoma
Von Hippel-Lindau syndrome is associated with the development of clear-cell renal cell carcinoma. This patient presented with a persistent headache and feeling nauseous, in the setting of a positive family history of cancer. This has prompted the family physician to make a referral to an oncologist for further investigations. An abnormality related to the chromosome 3p, which carries the VHL gene, indicates that this man might be suffering from Von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) syndrome. This is an autosomal dominant condition which increases the risk of developing several cancers. Clear-cell renal carcinoma is one of the tumors which patients with VHL syndrome are at an increased risk of suffering from, although the most common tumors are hemangiomas.

Lung carcinoma
Lung carcinoma is one of the major causes of death worldwide. The disease is mainly due to smoking but can also occur in non-smokers due to environmental pollutants. Symptoms include persistent cough, hemoptysis, and loss of weight. Chest X-ray is an important first-line investigation in patients suspected of having lung cancer.

Prostate carcinoma
Prostate carcinoma is one of the most common cancers in men. Patients usually present with lower urinary tract symptoms such as frequency, poor flow, or nocturia amongst others. While these symptoms are often due to benign prostatic hypertrophy, it is important to investigate these patients to rule out a prostate malignancy.

Breast carcinoma
Breast carcinoma is one of the most common cancers in women. It can be non-invasive or invasive. Invasive ductal carcinoma is the most common of all breast cancers. Treatment ranges from wide-margin excision to mastectomy, and may also include radiotherapy and chemotherapy.

Osteogenic sarcoma
Osteogenic sarcoma, also known as osteosarcoma, is one of the most prevalent bone tumors of malignant origin. The disease usually occurs in those under 20 years and above 65 years of age. Anatomically, it develops in the metaphyses of the long bones, typically around the knee. A characteristic X-ray appearance is that of the Codman triangle.

stem: A 34-year-old woman presents to the neurology clinic with a 3-month history of intermittent double vision, worse in the evenings. She also reports difficulty chewing food during meals. Examination reveals bilateral ptosis that worsens after sustained upward gaze for 60 seconds. Pupillary reflexes are normal. Blood tests show normal thyroid function and vitamin B12 levels. Which investigation would be most appropriate to confirm the suspected diagnosis?
explanation:
Acetylcholine receptor antibody testing
Testing for acetylcholine receptor antibodies is a key step in investigating patients with suspected myasthenia gravis. Acetylcholine receptor antibody testing is the most appropriate initial investigation to confirm the diagnosis of myasthenia gravis in this patient. The clinical presentation of fatigable muscle weakness affecting extraocular muscles (diplopia), bulbar muscles (difficulty chewing), and demonstrable ptosis worsening with sustained activity is highly suggestive of myasthenia gravis. Acetylcholine receptor antibodies are positive in approximately 85-90% of patients with generalised myasthenia gravis, making this the first-line serological test. It is noninvasive, widely available, and has good sensitivity for confirming the diagnosis. A positive result would support the clinical diagnosis and guide subsequent management decisions, including consideration of immunosuppression and screening for thymoma. The test is particularly useful as it has high specificity, meaning a positive result strongly confirms the diagnosis. While the sensitivity is not 100%, the high positivity rate makes it the most appropriate initial confirmatory test.

Single fibre electromyography
Single fibre electromyography has the highest sensitivity (92-100%) for diagnosing myasthenia gravis and would eventually confirm the diagnosis if antibody testing were negative. However, it is a more invasive, technically demanding, and less widely available investigation. In clinical practice, serological testing is performed first as it is simpler and less burdensome for the patient. Single fibre EMG is typically reserved for cases where there is strong clinical suspicion but negative antibody tests, or when the diagnosis remains uncertain after initial investigations.

CT thorax
CT thorax is an important investigation in confirmed myasthenia gravis to screen for thymoma, which is present in approximately 15% of cases, or thymic hyperplasia. However, it does not confirm the diagnosis of myasthenia gravis itself. This investigation would typically be performed after the diagnosis has been established through clinical assessment and serological or neurophysiological testing. Ordering a CT thorax before confirming the diagnosis would be premature and not the most logical next step in the diagnostic pathway.

Muscle-specific tyrosine kinase antibody testing
Muscle-specific tyrosine kinase antibody testing is useful in patients with suspected myasthenia gravis who are seronegative for acetylcholine receptor antibodies. Approximately 40% of acetylcholine receptor antibody-negative patients will be positive for MuSK antibodies. However, given that acetylcholine receptor antibodies are positive in the majority of cases, it would be inappropriate to test for MuSK antibodies first. The logical approach is to test for acetylcholine receptor antibodies initially, and only proceed to MuSK antibody testing if the first test is negative but clinical suspicion remains high.

Creatine kinase
Creatine kinase is typically normal in myasthenia gravis and is therefore not useful for confirming the diagnosis. Elevated CK levels would suggest a primary muscle disorder such as polymyositis or muscular dystrophy rather than a disorder of neuromuscular transmission. While it might be measured as part of a broader investigation of muscle weakness, it would not help establish the diagnosis of myasthenia gravis and is not the most appropriate test in this clinical context where the pattern of fatigable weakness strongly suggests a neuromuscular junction disorder.

stem: A 28-year-old woman with suspected multiple sclerosis has been reviewed in the outpatient neurology clinic with new diplopia when looking the right. On examination of the patient's eye movements, the left eye does not adduct on rightward gaze and the right eye exhibits nystagmus. All other eye movements are normal. The pupils are equal and reactive to light. The neurologist arranges an MRI scan of the brain. Where is the lesion likely to be seen on MRI imaging?
options: Left paramedian area of the midbrain and pons
Left ventromedial periaqueductal grey matter at the level of the superior colliculus
Right paramedian area of the midbrain and pons
Right ventromedial periaqueductal grey matter at the level of the superior colliculus
explanation:
Left paramedian area of the midbrain and pons
The medial longitudinal fasciculus is located in the paramedian area of the midbrain and pons. The patient here has presented with a typical history and examination of internuclear ophthalmoplegia. Internuclear ophthalmoplegia occurs due to lesions in the medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF), which is located in the paramedian area of the midbrain and the pons. Multiple sclerosis is an autoimmune disorder of demyelination, hence highly myelinated tracts such as the MLF are often affected. In order to generate conjugate eye movements, a signal is sent from the paramedian pontine reticular formation (PPRF) to the pontine abducens nucleus. A signal is then sent from the abducens nucleus to the ipsilateral lateral rectus muscle via the abducens nerve and to the contralateral oculomotor nucleus to control the contralateral medial rectus muscle. Fibres from the abducens nucleus cross the midline of the brainstem and form a highly myelinated tract, the MLF, which travels up the contralateral side of the brainstem, through the paramedian area of the midbrain and pons to the oculomotor nucleus. The contralateral medial rectus muscle is then innervated from the oculomotor nucleus in the midbrain. The eye which fails to adduct is ipsilateral to the lesion in the MLF as the oculomotor nucleus does not receive a signal from the contralateral abducens nucleus to adduct. This results in a failure of conjugate gaze and diplopia. The horizontal nystagmus of the right eye above is explained by Hering's law of equal innervation, whereby the 'weak, medial rectus muscle prompts the cortex to increase innervation to the oculomotor nucleus. This prompts an equally increased, and in this case, excessive innervation to the contralateral abducens nucleus, resulting in horizontal nystagmus of the right eye.

Right abducens nerve
A lesion of the right abducens nerve is incorrect. The right abducens nerve is functioning in the scenario above as the patient can look to the right. The fact that the right eye exhibits nystagmus is related to Hering's law as mentioned above.

Left ventromedial periaqueductal grey matter at the level of the superior colliculus
The ventromedial periaqueductal grey matter at the level of the superior colliculus is home to the nucleus of the oculomotor nerve. The nerve nuclei of the oculomotor nerve innervate ipsilaterally, emerging from the medial aspect of the cerebral peduncles. Hence a lesion of the left oculomotor nucleus would affect the left eye and lesion of the right oculomotor nucleus would affect the right eye. Lesions of the oculomotor nuclei would result in a more profound ophthalmoplegia with the eye often resting in the 'down and out' position, due to unopposed lateral rectus and superior oblique contraction.

Right ventromedial periaqueductal grey matter at the level of the superior colliculus
The ventromedial periaqueductal grey matter at the level of the superior colliculus is home to the nucleus of the oculomotor nerve. The nerve nuclei of the oculomotor nerve innervate ipsilaterally, emerging from the medial aspect of the cerebral peduncles. Hence a lesion of the left oculomotor nucleus would affect the left eye and lesion of the right oculomotor nucleus would affect the right eye. Lesions of the oculomotor nuclei would result in a more profound ophthalmoplegia with the eye often resting in the 'down and out' position, due to unopposed lateral rectus and superior oblique contraction.

stem: You review a 62-year-old man three days after he had been admitted with an acute coronary syndrome. His past medical history includes myasthenia gravis for which he takes long-term prednisolone. Since admission his symptoms of myasthenia have become markedly worse. In particular you notice bilateral ptosis and slurring of speech. Which of the following recently started medications is most likely to be responsible?
explanation:
Bisoprolol
Beta-blockers such as bisoprolol are common precipitants of myasthenic crises.

stem: A 40-year-old woman presents with increasing muscle weakness. She reports the weakness mainly affects her shoulders, hips and upper arms. On questioning, she feels her symptoms are worse after a period of inactivity such as sitting and on repeat movement/exercise her weakness actually improves. She confirms she has associated symptoms of a dry mouth and sometimes has difficulty passing urine. On examination, she has reduced power of the shoulders and upper arms with reduced reflexes throughout. The rest of her examination including peripheral nerve and cranial nerve exam is normal. What is directly affected in this patient's most likely condition?
explanation:
Voltage-gated calcium channels
Lambert-Eaton syndrome - antibodies against the voltage-gated Ca2+ channels. This patient has presented with features in keeping with Lambert-Eaton syndrome, a myasthenic syndrome associated with muscle weakness, particularly affecting the limb-girdle region, which generally improves with repetitive contractions. Further features of the condition include hyporeflexia and autonomic disruption such as dry mouth, impotence and difficulty micturating. Lambert-Eaton syndrome is an autoimmune condition due to antibodies directly affecting the presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels in the peripheral nervous system.

Chloride channels
Chloride channels are involved in several regulatory functions within the body including the transport of epithelial fluid in the lung, pancreas and other organs. The main condition associated with chloride channel disruption is the genetic disease cystic fibrosis causing symptoms of mucus thickening and pancreatic insufficiency from birth.

Myelin sheaths
The myelin sheaths are affected in several demyelination neurological conditions including multiple sclerosis, transverse myelitis and Guillain-Barré syndrome. In these conditions the myelin surrounding the nerve cell axons is affected, reducing the electrical impulses that are passed along the nervous system. The symptoms seen in these conditions are not improved with repeat use/contractions.

Nicotinic acetylcholine receptors
Blockage of the nicotinic acetylcholine receptors is the pathophysiology of the neuromuscular disease myasthenia gravis (MG). MG is a similar autoimmune condition to Lambert-Eaton syndrome causing progressive weakness however MG is normally associated with ocular issues including ophthalmoplegia and ptosis. Also, in contrast to Lambert-Eaton syndrome, repeated muscle contraction and activity in MG results in muscle fatigue and a worsening weakness, not an improvement.

Voltage-gated sodium channels
Voltage-gated sodium channels disruption is the pathophysiology in several conditions, in particular neurological syndromes resulting in increased seizure activity such as erythromelalgia and generalised epilepsy with febrile seizures plus (GEFS+) and electrolyte imbalance syndromes such as hyperkalemic and hypokalemic periodic paralysis. The sodium channels are not affected and play no role in Lambert-Eaton syndrome.

stem: A 28-year-old woman presents to the GP with a 3-month history of increased fatigue, which has been particularly worse over the last 2 weeks. She feels increasingly lethargic throughout the day and is experiencing muscle cramps. Cardiovascular, respiratory, gastrointestinal and neurological examinations were all within normal limits. There is no past medical history of note. The patient only reports a previous episode of visual disturbance 6 months ago, where they were unable to see clearly out of the left eye and red colours were not as pronounced. This symptom resolved spontaneously within 2 weeks. Blood were taken and the results showed: Hb 105g/L (115-160 g/L) WCC 5.6 x109/L (4.0-11.0 x109/L) Na+ 140mmol/L (135-145mmoL/) K+ 3.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.0mmol/L) Urea 3.7 mmol/L (2.0-7mmol/L) Creatinine 80 umol/L (55-120umol/L) Vitamin B12 413ng/L (200-900 ng/L) Folate 3.1 nmol/L (3.0 nmol/L) ESR 24 mm/hr (0-29mm/hr) What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Multiple sclerosis
Lethargy is a very common early symptom of multiple sclerosis. Important risk factors for multiple sclerosis include female sex, ages between 20-40 and family history. Multiple sclerosis can present with monocular visual disturbances and peculiar sensory phenomena. Typically, the lesions associated with MS will be separated in anatomical location and time; giving a relapsing and remitting course of symptoms. However, lethargy, as well as other non-specific symptoms such as leg cramping, increased urinary frequency and bowel dysfunction, can commonly be seen in early presentations of multiple sclerosis.

Anaemia
Whilst the patient does have mild anaemia, the previous symptoms of visual disturbance would not be seen and are more suggestive of multiple sclerosis.

Fibromyalgia
Fibromyalgia may present with muscle aches and fatigue, however, the previous neurological disturbances would not be seen.

Giant cell arteritis
Giant cell arteritis can present with muscle aches and fatigue. Visual loss can also be seen. Nevertheless, the presentation is typically in those over 50 years of age alongside other features in the history such as headaches, jaw claudication and scalp tenderness. Red desaturation is less commonly seen and is more in keeping with multiple sclerosis. Typically, visual loss in giant cell arteritis does not recover if left untreated.

Myasthenia gravis
Myasthenia would be more commonly seen with fatiguability following exertion. Visual disturbances are more commonly binocular with other symptoms such as diplopia and ptosis.

stem: Which one of the following haematological disorders is most associated with gingival hyperplasia?
explanation:
Acute myeloid leukaemia
Gingival hyperplasia, the overgrowth of gum tissue, is a common finding in patients with acute myeloid leukaemia (AML). It can be seen in up to 20% of patients with AML and is particularly associated with monocytic subtypes M4 and M5. This is thought to be due to infiltration of the gingival tissues by leukemic cells. The condition often regresses following successful treatment of the underlying leukaemia.

Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia
Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia is not typically associated with gingival hyperplasia. This type of leukaemia usually presents with lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, and systemic symptoms such as fatigue, weight loss and fever. Oral manifestations are rare but when they do occur, they usually involve oral ulcers or opportunistic infections rather than gingival hyperplasia.

Myelofibrosis
Myelofibrosis is a chronic disorder characterised by bone marrow fibrosis leading to extramedullary haematopoiesis - production of blood cells outside the bone marrow such as in the spleen or liver. Common symptoms include anaemia, fatigue, splenomegaly and bone pain. Gingival hyperplasia is not a feature of this condition.

Polycythaemia rubra vera
Polycythaemia rubra vera is a myeloproliferative disorder characterised by an increased number of red blood cells. It may present with headaches, pruritus after bathing in warm water, erythromelalgia (burning pain in hands or feet), and thrombotic events. There are no specific oral manifestations associated with polycythaemia rubra vera.

Haemophilia A
Haemophilia A, while it does affect the blood system like all these conditions, primarily causes problems due to deficiency or dysfunction of clotting factor VIII leading to increased bleeding tendency rather than causing gingival hyperplasia. Dental procedures may lead to prolonged bleeding in these patients but they do not have an increased risk for gingival hyperplasia compared to the general population.

stem: A 72-year-old man presents to the Medical Assessment Unit with a 3-week history of intermittent confusion and mild right-sided weakness. His wife reports he has become increasingly forgetful and unsteady on his feet. There is no clear history of trauma. On examination, he has subtle right-sided pronator drift and mild cognitive impairment (MMSE 23/30). A CT head is performed. What is the most likely radiological finding?
options: Bilateral hyperdense collections in the frontal regions
Hypodense crescent-shaped collection over the left cerebral convexity
Hyperdense lesion in the left parietal lobe with surrounding oedema
Diffuse cortical atrophy with widened sulci
explanation:
Hypodense crescent-shaped collection over the left cerebral convexity
On CT imaging, a chronic subdural haematoma will appear as a hypodense (dark), crescentic collection around the convexity of the brain. Hypodense crescent-shaped collection over the left cerebral convexity is the correct answer. This patient's presentation is highly suggestive of a chronic subdural haematoma (CSDH). The gradual onset of confusion, progressive neurological deficit (right-sided weakness), and cognitive impairment over weeks are classic features. The right-sided weakness indicates a left-sided lesion (contralateral to the deficit). On CT imaging, a CSDH typically appears as a hypodense (dark), crescent-shaped collection that follows the convexity of the brain. The hypodensity develops as the haematoma ages over weeks, with protein breakdown and increased fluid content. CSDHs are common in elderly patients due to age-related brain atrophy creating tension on bridging veins, which can tear with even minor (and sometimes unnoticed) trauma.

Bilateral hyperdense collections in the frontal regions
Bilateral hyperdense collections in the frontal regions would be more consistent with acute subdural haematomas, which appear hyperdense (bright) on CT due to the presence of fresh blood. Acute subdurals typically present with a more rapid onset of symptoms following a clear history of trauma, rather than the gradual progression seen in this case. Additionally, bilateral frontal collections would likely produce different neurological deficits than the unilateral right-sided weakness described.

Hyperdense lesion in the left parietal lobe with surrounding oedema
Hyperdense lesion in the left parietal lobe with surrounding oedema describes the appearance of an intracerebral haemorrhage or tumour. This is an intra-axial (within brain tissue) rather than extra-axial lesion. While this could cause right-sided weakness, the acute onset and rapid progression would be more typical for an intracerebral haemorrhage, and the surrounding oedema pattern is more characteristic of a tumour or subacute haemorrhage, neither of which fit the clinical timeline.

Enlarged ventricles with periventricular lucency
Enlarged ventricles with periventricular lucency describes findings consistent with normal pressure hydrocephalus or obstructive hydrocephalus. While normal pressure hydrocephalus can present with cognitive impairment and gait disturbance (part of the classic triad along with urinary incontinence), it typically doesn't cause focal weakness and would affect both sides equally.

Diffuse cortical atrophy with widened sulci
Diffuse cortical atrophy with widened sulci is a finding associated with neurodegenerative conditions such as Alzheimer's disease or other dementias. While this could explain the cognitive impairment, it would not account for the focal right-sided weakness or the relatively rapid progression of symptoms over just three weeks.

stem: You want to prescribe an antiemetic to a 19-year-old female who is having a migraine attack. Which one of the following medications is most likely to precipitate extrapyramidal side-effects?
explanation:
Metoclopramide
The correct answer is Metoclopramide. Metoclopramide is a dopamine antagonist and it works by blocking dopamine receptors in the chemoreceptor trigger zone of the central nervous system. This action prevents nausea and vomiting triggered by most stimuli. However, its antagonistic effect on dopamine can also lead to extrapyramidal side effects such as acute dystonic reactions, akathisia, and parkinsonism. These side effects are more common in young people and females.

Meptazinol
Meptazinol is an incorrect choice because it's not an antiemetic but rather an opioid analgesic used for the relief of moderate to severe pain. It works primarily by binding to mu-opioid receptors in the central nervous system, which does not typically cause extrapyramidal side effects.

Ondansetron
Ondansetron, another incorrect choice, is a selective serotonin 5-HT3 receptor antagonist which blocks these receptors both peripherally on vagal nerve terminals and centrally in the chemoreceptor trigger zone. It's commonly used as an antiemetic to treat nausea and vomiting caused by cancer chemotherapy, radiation therapy, and surgery but rarely causes extrapyramidal side effects.

Domperidone
Domperidone is also a wrong answer. Domperidone is a peripheral dopamine D2 and D3 antagonist that increases gastric motility and lower oesophageal sphincter tone. While domperidone has been associated with an increased risk of cardiac arrhythmias at high doses or in patients with predisposing factors, it does not readily cross the blood-brain barrier so it's less likely to cause extrapyramidal side effects compared to metoclopramide.

Cyclizine
Lastly, Cyclizine isn't the best choice either. Cyclizine is a histamine H1 antagonist used commonly for motion sickness and postoperative nausea and vomiting (PONV). It works by inhibiting histaminergic pathways in the vestibular system within the brain thus preventing motion-induced emesis. Extrapyramidal reactions are not typically seen with cyclizine use.

stem: A 23-year-old woman attends a follow-up neurology appointment for focal seizures. Six months previously she was started on levetiracetam which has been titrated to the maximum dose. Despite this, seizures are uncontrolled and she opts to try an alternative medication. She has plans to start a family in the next few years but currently uses barrier contraception. She is otherwise fit and well. What is the most appropriate alternative medication?
explanation:
Lamotrigine
Focal seizures not responding to first-line drug - try lamotrigine or levetiracetam (i.e. the first-line drug not already tried) and if neither help then carbamazepine. NICE guidelines state that lamotrigine or levetiracetam are considered first-line monotherapy for focal seizures. If one of these is ineffective, the other should be considered. Therefore, lamotrigine should be used in this case. Lamotrigine and levetiracetam are considered the safest anti-epileptics in pregnancy. Data suggests lamotrigine also has a lower risk of major congenital malformations.

Carbamazepine
Carbamazepine is a second-line option for focal seizures. Therefore, it should not yet be used. It is also important to note that carbamazepine is associated with a dose-dependent increased risk of congenital malformations and therefore this would be a reason to avoid this medication at this point if possible due to the patient's plans to start a family.

Ethosuximide
Ethosuximide is not indicated for focal seizures either as monotherapy or add-on treatment. It is the first-line option for absence seizures for both men and women.

Oxcarbazepine
Oxcarbazepine is an alternative second-line option for focal seizures. It is therefore not appropriate to try this at this stage.

Sodium valproate
Sodium valproate is only indicated as an add-on for focal seizures. It is not recommended for women and girls able to have children due to the significant risk of major congenital malformations.

stem: A 39-year-old female who presents with a 3-month history of acute attacks of loss of vision and weakness in the lower limbs is diagnosed with neuromyelitis optica. When making a diagnosis of neuromyelitis optica, which of the following is a possible distinguishing feature from multiple sclerosis?
options: Brain CT not meeting criteria for Multiple sclerosis at disease onset
explanation:
NMO-IgG seropositive
Neuromyelitis optica which is also known as Devic's disease is an autoimmune disorder in which immune system cells and antibodies attack the optic nerves and the spinal cord. The pathophysiology is still however completely unclear. The diagnosis of neuromyelitis optica is determined as follows: Absolute criteria: Optic neuritis Acute myelitis

Supportive criteria: Brain MRI not meeting criteria for MS at disease onset

Spinal cord MRI with contiguous T2-weighted signal abnormality extending over three or more vertebral segments NMO-IgG seropositive status (The NMO-IgG test checks the existence of antibodies against the aquaporin 4 antigen.)

Compared to multiple sclerosis, the acute episodes are not understood to be triggered by the immune system's T cells, but rather by antibodies called NMO-IgG.

Memory loss
Multiple sclerosis (MS) can present with memory loss, optic neuritis, acute myelitis but is not NMO-IgG seropositive.

Brain CT not meeting criteria for Multiple sclerosis at disease onset
Brain MRI not meeting criteria for Multiple sclerosis at disease onset is a distinguishing factor from neuromyelitis optica but not Brain CT.

stem: A 65-year-old man is referred to the neurology outpatient clinic due to a resting tremor of his right hand. A diagnosis of Parkinson's disease is made. He is otherwise well and is not currently disabled by his symptoms. What is the most appropriate treatment?
options: New generation dopamine receptor agonist e.g. ropinirole
Conventional dopamine receptor agonist e.g. bromocriptine
explanation:
New generation dopamine receptor agonist e.g. ropinirole
Following the NICE 2017 guidelines, it is now recommended to use a dopamine receptor agonist for motor symptoms that are not affecting a patient's quality of life.

Conventional dopamine receptor agonist e.g. bromocriptine
Following the NICE 2017 guidelines, it is now recommended to use a dopamine receptor agonist for motor symptoms that are not affecting a patient's quality of life.

stem: A 24-year-old man presents to the emergency department complaining of two weeks of tingling in his feet and difficulty walking. He has no medical history. He frequently inhales nitrous oxide with his friends. His diet is normal. On examination, there is impaired proprioception and vibration sense extending to the ankles. The plantar responses are extensor. The ankle reflexes are absent and the knee reflexes are brisk. Blood tests: Vitamin B12 level 700pg/ml (200-900) What is the likely diagnosis?
options: Subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord
explanation:
Subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord
Subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord is correct. The patient uses nitrous oxide on a regular basis. This can cause a functional B12 deficiency (the B12 levels will be normal) and can give rise to subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord like in true B12 deficiency. In this setting, it is important to check a methylmalonic acid (MMA) level. In the setting of functional B12 deficiency, this will be high. This is characterized by dorsal column abnormalities (impaired vibration and proprioception sense), absent ankle jerks, extensor plantar responses, and brisk knee reflexes.

Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis
Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis is incorrect. This tends to cause a pure motor weakness with a combination of upper and lower motor neuron signs. Dorsal column involvement is not typical.

Guillain-Barre syndrome
Guillain-Barre syndrome is incorrect. This causes a lower motor neuron distribution of weakness +/- sensory loss. Extensor plantar responses are not a feature and therefore this is unlikely.

Pellagra
Pellagra is incorrect. This is caused by niacin deficiency, which causes the syndrome of pellagra characterized by dementia and dermatitis and diarrhea, and ultimately, death. You may get extensor plantar responses and absent ankle jerks in this condition. However, it is very unlikely to develop in someone described as having a 'normal' diet. It is more likely to occur in food-limited populations.

Syphilis infection
Syphilis infection is incorrect. This is a cause of absent ankle jerks and extensor plantar responses. However, there is no history of exposure and we are told he has a common reason to have a functional B12 deficiency and therefore this is a less likely diagnosis in this context.

stem: A 19-year-old university student presents to the neurology clinic following two episodes of sudden, brief muscle jerks affecting both arms whilst studying. The episodes occurred 3 weeks apart, both in the morning shortly after waking. She describes her arms suddenly 'jumping' causing her to drop her coffee cup. There is no loss of consciousness or confusion afterwards. Her neurological examination is normal. What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?
explanation:
Levetiracetam
Levetiracetam is the correct answer as it is the first-line treatment for myoclonic seizures according to current UK guidelines. This patient presents with classic myoclonic seizures - sudden, brief, shock-like muscle contractions affecting both arms without impairment of consciousness. The timing shortly after waking is typical, as myoclonic seizures often occur in the morning or when tired. Levetiracetam is particularly effective for myoclonic seizures and is preferred over other antiepileptic drugs for this seizure type. It has a favourable side effect profile and no significant drug interactions, making it suitable for a young university student. The drug works by binding to synaptic vesicle protein SV2A and has proven efficacy in juvenile myoclonic epilepsy, which commonly presents in teenagers and young adults.

Carbamazepine
Carbamazepine is not appropriate for myoclonic seizures and may actually worsen them. It is primarily used for focal seizures and can paradoxically increase the frequency of myoclonic jerks and absence seizures. This makes it contraindicated in generalised epilepsy syndromes that include myoclonic seizures.

Ethosuximide
Ethosuximide is the first-line treatment specifically for absence seizures (petit mal), not myoclonic seizures. While both are generalised seizure types, they have different mechanisms and treatment approaches. This patient's description of sudden muscle jerks without loss of consciousness is not consistent with absence seizures.

Lamotrigine
Lamotrigine is second-line for myoclonic seizures and first-line for tonic-clonic and focal seizures. While it can be effective for myoclonic seizures, levetiracetam is preferred as first-line therapy due to superior efficacy in this seizure type.

Sodium valproate
Sodium valproate was previously considered first-line for myoclonic seizures, but recent MHRA guidance strongly restricts its use in people under 55 years due to teratogenic risks and potential effects on neurodevelopment, making it inappropriate for this 19-year-old patient.

stem: A 56-year-old-male on haemodialysis via a right internal jugular tunnelled line presented with a 2-week history of fevers, night sweats and weight loss. Blood and line cultures grew Staphylococcus aureus and a transesophageal echocardiogram confirmed a vegetation. His tunnelled line was removed and he dialysed via a temporary femoral line. After 2 weeks of IV flucloxacillin, he began to get night sweats, fevers and a persistent headache. He became confused and hypoactive, needing full nursing care now. What is the most likely cause for his symptoms?
explanation:
Brain abscess
Headache, fever and focal neurology and suggestive of a brain abscess. This is a case of a brain abscess formation as a complication of infective endocarditis secondary to tunnelled line sepsis. Patients who dialyse via a tunnelled line are at significantly increased risk of infections vs patients who dialyse via a fistula. In this case, the tunnelled line was the likely medium by which the mitral valve became infected. Patents need to be watched closely for signs of an embolic phenomenon when diagnosed with endocarditis. The common embolic phenomenon is renal involvement (blood + protein on a urine dip and an acute kidney injury), hepatic or splenic infarcts (may show up as pain in the right or left upper quadrant or deranged liver function tests), ocular involvement (reduced vision causing retinal deposits or ocular artery occlusions) or central nervous system involvement (septic emboli to the brain causing stroke-like symptoms). If the septic deposits seed and aren't fully treated, they can go on to develop a brain abscess. This will typically show up as headaches, fevers and some focal neurology on examination. It will occur in the context of infection getting worse while on appropriate initial antibiotics.

Myocardial abscess
Myocardial abscess formation should be closely looked out for. It will often manifest as a heart block on an ECG due to its proximity to the AV node. The PR interval should be watched closely as a new 1st-degree heart block could be the first sign of this.

Meningitis
Meningitis is a distinct possibility here. If there were signs of meningism or the CT was negative for an abscess, then a lumbar puncture should be attempted to look for CSF involvement.

Stroke
Strokes in this context could either be septic emboli getting stuck in vessels, or a hemorrhagic transformation of previous emboli.

Temporary line sepsis
In a patient with fevers and any plastic line in situ, line sepsis should always be considered. Femoral lines are notorious for higher risk of infection. The line site should be checked daily for erythema or exudate.

stem: Which type of motor neuron disease carries the worst prognosis?
explanation:
Progressive bulbar palsy
Progressive bulbar palsy is the correct answer as it carries the worst prognosis among the motor neuron disease variants. Progressive bulbar palsy primarily affects the lower cranial nerves (IX, X, XII), leading to dysarthria, dysphagia, and tongue fasciculations. The involvement of bulbar muscles controlling swallowing and respiration significantly increases the risk of aspiration pneumonia and respiratory failure. Patients with progressive bulbar palsy typically have a median survival of approximately 2-3 years from symptom onset, which is shorter than other motor neuron disease variants. The rapid progression of bulbar symptoms often leads to earlier respiratory compromise and nutritional difficulties, contributing to the poor prognosis.

Relapsing-remitting
Relapsing-remitting is incorrect because this is not a recognised pattern in motor neuron disease. Motor neuron diseases are characteristically progressive neurodegenerative conditions. The term 'relapsing-remitting' is typically associated with multiple sclerosis, which is an autoimmune demyelinating disease affecting the central nervous system, not a motor neuron disease. Motor neuron diseases may show periods of apparent stabilisation, but true remission of symptoms does not occur.

Progressive muscular atrophy
Progressive muscular atrophy is incorrect as the answer to this specific question. While progressive muscular atrophy is indeed a variant of motor neuron disease, it primarily affects the lower motor neurons, leading to muscle weakness, atrophy, and fasciculations without upper motor neuron signs. The prognosis for progressive muscular atrophy is generally better than progressive bulbar palsy, with median survival typically ranging from 5-10 years after symptom onset.

Spinocerebellar ataxia
Spinocerebellar ataxia is incorrect because it is not a motor neuron disease. Spinocerebellar ataxia comprises a group of hereditary ataxias characterised by progressive cerebellar degeneration and dysfunction of the spinocerebellar tracts. These conditions primarily affect coordination, balance, and speech rather than causing the characteristic upper and lower motor neuron signs seen in motor neuron diseases. The prognosis varies widely depending on the specific genetic subtype.

Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis
Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis is incorrect as the answer to this specific question about worst prognosis. Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is the most common form of motor neuron disease, affecting both upper and lower motor neurons. While ALS has a poor prognosis with median survival of 3-5 years from symptom onset, progressive bulbar palsy (which is actually a variant of ALS with predominant bulbar involvement) typically progresses more rapidly and carries a worse prognosis due to the early involvement of respiratory and swallowing functions.

stem: A 68-year-old man presents to the emergency department 3 hours after sudden onset right-sided weakness and dysphasia. CT head excludes haemorrhage. CT angiography demonstrates occlusion of the left middle cerebral artery (M1 segment). His blood pressure is 168/94 mmHg. He has a National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale (NIHSS) score of 16 and pre-stroke modified Rankin scale of 1. What is the most appropriate acute management?
options: Blood pressure lowering then intravenous thrombolysis
explanation:
Intravenous thrombolysis and mechanical thrombectomy
Intravenous thrombolysis and mechanical thrombectomy is the correct answer. This patient has a large artery acute ischaemic stroke with confirmed occlusion of the proximal anterior circulation (left M1 segment of the middle cerebral artery). He presents within 6 hours of symptom onset, has a good pre-stroke functional status (modified Rankin scale 1), and significant neurological deficit (NIHSS 16, which is >5). According to NICE and the 2023 National Clinical Guideline for Stroke, he should be offered both intravenous thrombolysis (as he is within 4.5 hours) and mechanical thrombectomy (as he has a proximal anterior circulation occlusion within 6 hours). The combination of both treatments provides the best chance of recanalisation and functional recovery. His blood pressure of 168/94 mmHg does not require lowering before thrombolysis as it is below the threshold of 185/110 mmHg. Time is critical in acute stroke management, and both treatments should be initiated as soon as possible without unnecessary delay.

Intravenous thrombolysis alone
Intravenous thrombolysis alone would be suboptimal management. While this patient meets criteria for thrombolysis (within 4.5 hours, haemorrhage excluded, blood pressure acceptable), he also has a confirmed proximal anterior circulation occlusion on CT angiography. Large vessel occlusions have poor recanalisation rates with thrombolysis alone. The evidence from multiple randomised controlled trials demonstrates superior outcomes when mechanical thrombectomy is added to thrombolysis for proximal large vessel occlusions. Offering thrombolysis alone would deny this patient the proven benefits of thrombectomy.

Mechanical thrombectomy alone
Mechanical thrombectomy alone is not recommended in this scenario. While the patient clearly meets criteria for thrombectomy (proximal anterior circulation occlusion, within 6 hours, good functional status, significant deficit), he also meets criteria for thrombolysis as he presents within 4.5 hours of symptom onset. Current guidelines recommend offering both treatments together when the patient is eligible for both, as the combination provides better outcomes than either treatment alone. There is no contraindication to thrombolysis in this case.

Aspirin and clopidogrel
Aspirin and clopidogrel would be inappropriate as acute management. While antiplatelet therapy is important in acute ischaemic stroke, aspirin 300mg should only be given after thrombolysis has been considered and either administered or excluded. In this case, the patient is clearly eligible for reperfusion therapies (thrombolysis and thrombectomy), which take priority. Dual antiplatelet therapy with aspirin and clopidogrel is used in specific circumstances for secondary prevention but is not the acute management for a patient eligible for reperfusion therapy. Giving antiplatelets before considering thrombolysis would be a significant error.

Blood pressure lowering then intravenous thrombolysis
Blood pressure lowering then intravenous thrombolysis is unnecessary and would cause harmful delay. The patient's blood pressure is 168/94 mmHg, which is below the threshold of 185/110 mmHg required before thrombolysis. The guidelines specifically state that blood pressure should be lowered to below 185/110 mmHg before thrombolysis, but this patient's blood pressure is already within acceptable limits. Attempting to lower it further would waste precious time in a time-critical intervention and is not indicated. Additionally, this option fails to recognise that the patient also requires mechanical thrombectomy given the large vessel occlusion.

stem: A 41-year-old female presented to the neurology clinic with a 3-month history of urinary frequency and incontinence. She has a background medical history of multiple sclerosis, hypertension and hypercholesterolaemia. What is the next step in her management?
options: Kidneys, ureters, and urinary bladder (KUB) ultrasound
explanation:
Kidneys, ureters, and urinary bladder (KUB) ultrasound
Multiple sclerosis patient with bladder dysfunction - get an ultrasound first to assess bladder emptying. Kidneys, ureters, and urinary bladder (KUB) ultrasound is the correct answer. This patient has a neurogenic bladder secondary to multiple sclerosis. She requires a KUB ultrasound to establish if she has a significant post-voiding residual volume as this will influence her treatment options. NICE guidelines for 'urinary incontinence in neurological disease' recommend the use of bladder ultrasound during initial clinical assessment.

Doxazosin
Doxazosin is an incorrect answer. Alpha-blockers, such as doxazosin, are typically used in the management of voiding dysfunction secondary to benign prostatic hyperplasia. They can be used as an adjunct therapy and infrequently as a monotherapy for the treatment of neurogenic bladder in multiple sclerosis. They are not considered a first-line treatment and a KUB ultrasound is certainly indicated before their introduction to establish if there is a significant post-voiding residual volume.

Intermittent self-catheterisation
Intermittent self-catheterisation is an incorrect answer. If this patient has a significant post-voiding residual volume then intermittent self-catheterisation will be of benefit. However, a KUB ultrasound is required first to establish the presence of a post-voiding residual volume. There is little benefit from intermittent self-catheterisation if there is no volume of urine to drain.

Oxybutynin
Oxybutynin is an incorrect answer. Anticholinergics may worsen symptoms in some patients. A KUB ultrasound should be performed before their introduction. If there is no significant post-voiding residual volume then anticholinergics may improve urinary frequency. However, if there is a significant post-voiding residual volume then anticholinergics may lead to urinary retention.

Pelvic floor muscle exercises
Pelvic floor muscle exercises are an incorrect answer. Pelvic floor muscle exercises may be useful as an adjunct to other treatments in the management of a neurogenic bladder secondary to multiple sclerosis. However, the first step in this patient's management is further investigation with a KUB ultrasound to help identify the mechanism underlying the bladder dysfunction.

stem: A 76-year-old man is admitted with a right hemiparesis. He first noticed weakness on his right side around six hours ago. A CT scan shows an ischaemic stroke and aspirin 300mg is commenced. In terms of further management in the acute phase, which one of the following values should not be corrected?
explanation:
BP 210/110
Hypertension should not be treated in the initial period following an ischaemic stroke (unless prior to thrombolysis) Elevated blood pressure should not be treated in the acute phase following a stroke unless complications develop.

stem: An 81-year-old woman was admitted eight days ago to the hospital with right-sided weakness. After a normal CT head, she was managed with high-dose aspirin for a suspected stroke which was subsequently confirmed on MRI. She is now medically optimised for discharge. The therapy team are involved in planning her discharge. She previously lived alone, with a daughter who helped with the shopping. What is the most appropriate tool for estimating her ability to return home?
options: National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale (NIHSS)
Program of Research to Integrate the Services for the Maintenance of Autonomy 7 (PRISMA-7)
explanation:
Barthel index
The Barthel index is a scale that measures disability or dependence in activities of daily living in stroke patients. There are many scoring criteria within medicine. Often deciding which one is most appropriate depends on the nature of the scale, with certain scales being specific to some conditions. If a specific scale exists then they are often more helpful than more generic scoring criteria. For stroke, assessing the degree of ongoing disability is most commonly measured using the Barthel index. This assesses 10 tasks and is scored according to the amount of time or assistance required by the patient for each given task. This index is used to assess the functional status of a patient post-stroke and to monitor their improvement with ongoing rehabilitation to regain independence after the event. Therefore, it is the most appropriate scale for this patient.

Berg balance scale
The Berg balance scale makes a measure of a person's static and dynamic balance abilities. Although this is useful information for assessing a patient's functional ability, it is not as encompassing as the Barthel index which also takes into account areas such as feeding, bathing, dressing, and continence.

Clinical frailty score
The clinical frailty score can be used to assist in making care decisions. Its use is based on patient mobility, function, and cognition from two weeks prior to presentation. Therefore, it is not the most appropriate score to use in this patient for discharge planning.

National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale (NIHSS)
The National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale (NIHSS) is used to quantify the degree of impairment caused by a stroke. It is helpful in prognostication, particularly in areas such as mortality. The NIHSS looks at neurological deficits, whereas the Barthel index is designed to look at functional ability, and is more helpful for discharge planning.

Program of Research to Integrate the Services for the Maintenance of Autonomy 7 (PRISMA-7)
The Program of Research to Integrate the Services for the Maintenance of Autonomy 7 (PRISMA-7) consists of a brief, seven-item yes/no questionnaire designed as a quick frailty screening tool. Therefore it is not the most suitable tool for discharge planning for this post-stroke patient.

stem: Which one of the following is least associated with myotonic dystrophy?
explanation:
Aortic regurgitation
The correct answer is Aortic regurgitation. Myotonic dystrophy is a type of muscular dystrophy that affects muscles and other body systems. It presents with muscle stiffness (myotonia) and muscle weakness, but it also has systemic manifestations including cataracts, endocrine changes, and cardiac abnormalities. However, the cardiac abnormalities associated with myotonic dystrophy are typically arrhythmias and conduction defects rather than valvular heart diseases such as aortic regurgitation.

Dysphagia
Dysphagia is indeed associated with myotonic dystrophy. This condition affects several types of muscle tissue, including those in the gastrointestinal tract which can lead to dysphagia or difficulty swallowing.

Diabetes mellitus
Diabetes mellitus is another condition linked to myotonic dystrophy. The disease can affect the function of the pancreas leading to insulin resistance and eventually diabetes mellitus.

Testicular atrophy
Testicular atrophy is also seen in males with myotonic dystrophy due to disruption in hormonal regulation.

Learning difficulties
Learning difficulties are often present in congenital forms of myotonic dystrophy. Cognitive impairment may range from attention deficits to intellectual disability depending on the severity of the disease.

stem: A 33-year-old male is admitted with a subacute headache, confusion, and nausea. On closer questioning, you note that this gentleman appears irritable, confused, and is hearing voices. Prior to this, his wife reports he has had a recent viral upper respiratory tract infection. He is otherwise fit and well and takes no regular medications. On examination, you note that he is neglecting to use his right arm. He is otherwise, neurologically intact. A subsequent CT head reveals no space occupying lesion, infarct or bleed. Later, an MRI is performed which reveals bilateral asymmetric and poorly marginated hyperintense T2-weighted and FLAIR lesions within the subcortical white matter. A lumbar puncture reveals no oligoclonal bands in the CSF. What is the likely underlying diagnosis?
explanation:
Acute disseminated encephalomyelitis
The answer is acute disseminated encephalomyelitis which is a neurological condition which occurs typically a few weeks following a viral illness or vaccination. It can present with motor weakness, encephalopathy, seizures and coma. It is found on T2-weighted MRI imaging which reveals poorly-defined hyperintensities in the subcortical white matter. These lesions can develop throughout the course of the illness and hence serial MRIs may be required.

Alzheimer's disease
Alzheimer's disease and herpes encephalitis would not present with these MRI findings.

Multiple sclerosis
Multiple sclerosis is a differential diagnosis but is not necessarily definitively linked with a preceding illness.

Meningitis
The absence of prominent meningism features makes meningitis less likely.

Herpes simplex encephalitis
Alzheimer's disease and herpes encephalitis would not present with these MRI findings.

stem: A 58-year-old lady presents to clinic with a 6-month history of limb weakness and falls. She has hypercholesterolaemia and takes simvastatin. On examination, there is wasting of the intrinsic hand muscles and left biceps with fasciculations in the left biceps and shoulder girdle. There is a generalised weakness with brisk left biceps and bilateral knee reflexes and a right extensor plantar response. The sensation is normal throughout. Examination of the cranial nerves was normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Multifocal motor neuropathy with conduction block
explanation:
Motor neurone disease
The clinical description is a subacute progressive weakness with a mixture of lower and upper motor neurone signs without sensory involvement. The diagnosis is motor neurone disease. You would suspect motor neurone disease in any patient with a mixture of lower and upper motor neurone signs without sensory involvement. Some pathologies can cause lower and upper motor neurone signs in different parts of the body (e.g. syringomyelia). The fact that these paradoxical signs co-exist in the same myotome clinches the diagnosis.

Compressive cervical myelopathy
A cervical myelopathy would not cause lower motor neurone signs.

Multifocal motor neuropathy with conduction block
Multifocal motor neuropathy with conduction block would not cause upper motor neurone signs.

Myopathy
Myopathy would not cause upper motor neurone signs.

Myasthenia gravis
Myasthenia gravis would not cause upper motor neurone signs.

stem: A 63-year-old female presents with a four-month history of progressive weakness in the lower limbs associated with numbness. She also complains of feeling tired and lightheaded lately. She has had recent investigation for this and showed macrocytic anaemia with vitamin B12 deficiency. She is currently awaiting to commence on B12 replacement. Otherwise, she is normally fit and well and is not on any regular medication. Neurological examination of the lower limb shows the following: Left Right Power Sensation to coarse touch, pain, temperature and pressure normal normal Sensation to fine touch and vibration reduced reduced Proprioception reduced reduced Ankle reflex absent absent Babinski response upgoing upgoing Which of the following area of the spinal cord is most likely affected in this patient?
explanation:
Dorsal and lateral columns
In subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord, the dorsal columns and lateral corticospinal tracts are affected. The correct answer is 'dorsal and lateral column'. This patient has reduced power in the lower limbs with reduced sensation to fine touch, loss of proprioception and vibratory sensation. These symptoms and signs are suggestive of subacute combined degeneration of the cord likely secondary to vitamin B12 deficiency. It most commonly affects the dorsal columns, and less commonly, the lateral columns. Involvement of the dorsal columns manifests clinically as issues with proprioception and vibration sense. Whilst the lateral columns primarily contain the corticospinal tracts which are the principal motor pathway.

Anterior and dorsal columns
The anterior and dorsal columns are not the primary areas affected in subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord. The dorsal columns are affected, but the anterior columns, which primarily contain the spinothalamic tracts responsible for pain, temperature, coarse touch, and pressure sensations, are not typically involved in this condition.

Anterior and lateral columns
The anterior and lateral columns are not the primary areas affected in subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord. The lateral columns are affected, but the anterior columns, which primarily contain the spinothalamic tracts responsible for pain, temperature, coarse touch, and pressure sensations, are not typically involved in this condition.

Lateral horn
The lateral horn of the spinal cord contains the neuronal cell bodies of the sympathetic nervous system. Disruption of the lateral horns at the levels of T1-T2 can lead to the classic triad of partial ptosis, anhidrosis, and miosis seen in Horner syndrome. This is not the area affected in subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord.

Ventral horn
The ventral horns of the spinal cord contain motor neurones for skeletal muscles. Associated pathology includes amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease, and progressive muscular atrophy. This is not the area affected in subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord.

stem: A 43-year-old woman is referred to the ambulatory care unit with rightsided facial pain, headache and double vision. Symptoms had gradually worsened over the last 2 weeks. She had been well before this. On examination, ptosis of the right eye is noted. She is also found to have a dilated, unresponsive right pupil. Eye movements of the right eye are also limited - the eye is fixed in a down-and-out position. There is no fatiguability of the ptosis or the eye movements. Neurological examination of the upper and lower limbs is unremarkable. What is the most likely cause of this presentation?
options: Guillain Barre syndrome - Miller Fisher variant
explanation:
Posterior communicating artery aneurysm
Posterior communicating artery aneurysm is correct. This patient is presenting with a third nerve palsy. A 'surgical' (i.e. with pupillary involvement) third nerve palsy suggests a compressive aetiology. This involves compression of the whole nerve and is characterised by a triad of ptosis, pupillary dilatation, and an ophthalmoplegia that leaves the eye in a down-and-out position (due to the unopposed action of the lateral rectus and superior oblique muscles). The third nerve palsy with pupil involvement and an associated headache strongly suggests a posterior communicating artery aneurysm as the cause.

Cavernous sinus thrombosis
Cavernous sinus thrombosis is incorrect. A cavernous sinus thrombosis, due to the anatomical proximity to cranial nerves 3, 4, 6 and the ophthalmic branch of 5, usually causes impairment in a mixture of these cranial nerves rather than an isolated 3rd nerve palsy.

Diabetic neuropathy
Diabetic neuropathy is incorrect. Patients with vascular risk factors such as diabetes, hypertension, and hypercholesterolemia can experience peripheral nerve vascular microinfarctions. Diabetic neuropathy affecting the oculomotor nerve would cause a 'medical' (with pupil sparing) third nerve palsy. This would be characterised by ptosis and ophthalmoplegia but would not result in pupillary dilatation. This is because the parasympathetic fibres within the third nerve are found superficially, where the blood supply is primarily from vasa nevorum. In contrast, the somatic muscle fibres supplying levator palpebrae superioris and the extraocular muscles are deep within the third nerve and supplied by intraneural arteries, which are more vulnerable to ischaemic damage.

Guillain Barre syndrome - Miller Fisher variant
Guillain Barre syndrome - Miller Fisher variant is incorrect. Miller Fisher variant can cause a complex ophthalmoplegia that may look like a 3rd nerve palsy, but the ophthalmoplegia is usually bilateral. Miller Fisher variant is also associated with ataxia, areflexia and commonly a prodromal illness - none of which are described in this patient.

Myasthenia gravis
Myasthenia gravis is incorrect. Myasthenia gravis could indeed produce complex ophthalmoplegia and ptosis, but the key differentiating factor is that in myasthenia gravis, these changes would become more pronounced with repetitive movement, a phenomenon known as fatiguability. The symptoms are also usually bilateral, albeit may be asymmetrical.

stem: A 62-year-old man is referred to the neurology clinic with a 5-year history of a tremor affecting both hands. It is most noticeable when he is holding a cup or writing. He reports that a glass of wine significantly improves his symptoms, and his father had a similar condition. On examination, a fine, high-frequency tremor is present when his arms are outstretched. There is no tremor at rest and the rest of the neurological examination is normal. What is the most appropriate initial pharmacological treatment?
explanation:
Propranolol
Propranolol is the treatment of choice for essential tremor. This patient's presentation is classical for essential tremor. Key features include the postural nature of the tremor (present on action and when holding a posture against gravity), bilateral involvement, a positive family history (suggesting an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern), and a characteristic improvement with small amounts of alcohol. The absence of a rest tremor or other features like bradykinesia or rigidity makes Parkinson's disease unlikely. According to UK guidelines (NICE), a non-selective beta-blocker such as propranolol is the recommended first-line pharmacological treatment for essential tremor if medical therapy is required. Its exact mechanism in tremor suppression is not fully understood but is thought to be mediated via peripheral beta-2 adrenoceptors.

Levodopa
Levodopa is the primary treatment for Parkinson's disease. This patient's tremor is postural, whereas the classic Parkinsonian tremor is a low-frequency, 'pill-rolling' tremor that is most prominent at rest and improves with voluntary movement. Furthermore, the patient has no other signs of Parkinsonism, such as bradykinesia, rigidity, or postural instability. Therefore, a diagnosis of Parkinson's disease is not supported by the clinical findings, and treatment with levodopa would be inappropriate.

Primidone
Primidone is an anticonvulsant medication that is also an effective treatment for essential tremor. It is considered a first-line agent alongside propranolol. However, propranolol is often trialled first, particularly in patients without contraindications like asthma or heart block, due to primidone's potential for acute adverse effects (e.g., sedation, nausea, ataxia) upon initiation. Therefore, while a valid treatment, it is generally considered an alternative first-line or second-line option rather than the most appropriate initial choice for this patient.

Procyclidine
Procyclidine is an anticholinergic medication. Its primary use in movement disorders is for treating drug-induced parkinsonism and, occasionally, the tremor in younger patients with Parkinson's disease. It is not recommended for the treatment of essential tremor. Additionally, anticholinergic drugs carry a significant side-effect burden, including confusion, dry mouth, and urinary retention, which is particularly problematic in older adults like the 62-year-old man in this scenario.

Ropinirole
Ropinirole is a dopamine agonist used in the management of Parkinson's disease and restless legs syndrome. As with levodopa, it targets the dopaminergic system, which is not the primary pathology in essential tremor. The clinical features in the vignette are not suggestive of Parkinson's disease, making ropinirole an incorrect choice. It would not be effective for essential tremor and would expose the patient to unnecessary side effects.

stem: A 24-year-old female presents to her general practitioner with three days of tingling in her left arm and double vision. She had been feeling fatigued for the six months prior to this clinic visit. There no significant past medical history and she is on no medications. She smokes five cigarettes per day and drinks approximately one bottle of wine per week and works as a journalist. Neurological examination revealed reduced sensation in her left upper limb. Upon testing her eye movements, it was noted that on left lateral gaze, her right eye failed to adduct and her left eye demonstrated nystagmus. Given the likely diagnosis, where is the anatomical location of the lesion causing the eye signs on examination?
explanation:
Medial longitudinal fasciculus
Internuclear ophthalmoplegia is due to a lesion in the medial longitudinal fasciculus. This myelinated structure is located in the brainstem and is responsible for conjugate eye movements. This patient presents with tingling and double vision, and examination findings suggestive of internuclear ophthalmoplegia (INO). This is consistent with a diagnosis of multiple sclerosis. INO is a disorder of conjugate lateral gaze. When an attempt is made to look contralaterally from the affected side, the affected eye fails to adduct and the contralateral eye demonstrates nystagmus. The side of medial longitudinal fasciculus that is affected is that of the eye that fails to adduct.

Mamillary bodies
Mamillary bodies is not the right answer. The ophthalmoplegia associated with Wernicke's encephalopathy can sometimes mimic internuclear ophthalmoplegia. However, there is no history of alcohol excess and the description is classic for internuclear ophthalmoplegia, typically associated with multiple sclerosis.

Neuromuscular junction
Neuromuscular junction is incorrect. Ocular myasthenia can sometimes mimic an INO but this is not the likely diagnosis based on the history.

Optic nerve
Optic nerve is incorrect. A lesion of the optic nerve would cause monocular visual loss.

Optic tract
Optic tract is incorrect. A lesion of the optic tract would cause homonymous hemianopia.

stem: A 32-year-old man is brought in following a seizure. His family reports he has been severally unwell the past few days with a fever and vomiting. He was started on antibiotics by his GP last week for suspected bacterial sinusitis following a prolonged period of symptoms including thick nasal mucus and facial discomfort. However, his family confirms he did not complete the antibiotic course. A CT head with contrast is performed and demonstrates a ring-enhancing lesion with evidence of inflammation of the sinuses. What antibiotic regime should be commenced?
explanation:
IV ceftriaxone and metronidazole
Brain abscess: IV 3rd-generation cephalosporin + metronidazole. This patient has presented with a brain abscess, secondary to spread from an initial sinus infection. Diagnosis is often confirmed via a contrast CT head showing a ring-enhancing lesion that results from the formation of a capsule surrounding the build-up of inflammation and concomitant dead brain tissue. A lumbar puncture is contraindicated due to the risk of potential cerebral herniation. If identified broad-spectrum antibiotics should be commenced immediately. A 3rd generation cephalosporin with additional cover for potential anaerobic and microaerophilic is the recommended regimen such as IV ceftriaxone and metronidazole. Dexamethasone should also be considered in patients with evidence of intracranial pressure.

IV ceftriaxone and ampicillin
IV ceftriaxone and ampicillin is mainly used for the management of suspected meningitis in young children, those over 50 years or patients who are immunocompromised. The addition of ampicillin, to the standard 3rd generation cephalosporin, is recommended to cover for potential Listeria monocytogenes infection more common in these patient groups. This patient has presented with a brain abscess, not just meningitis, and is not a member of this high-risk patient group.

IV ceftriaxone and co-trimoxazole
IV ceftriaxone and co-trimoxazole are not commonly used in combination. Co-trimoxazole, which is made up of sulfamethoxazole and trimethoprim, can cover a range of bacterial, fungal and protozoan infections however it is mainly used as a prophylactic drug to prevent infections such as pneumocystis pneumonia and toxoplasmosis in patients with HIV/AIDS or other immunosuppressive conditions.

IV ceftriaxone and gentamicin
IV ceftriaxone and gentamicin can be used in combination to treat certain infections such as infective endocarditis or neutropenic sepsis however they are not commonly used for cerebral infections e.g. brain abscess or meningitis.

IV ceftriaxone and vancomycin
IV ceftriaxone and vancomycin should only be considered for brain abscess treatment in countries where cephalosporin resistance is high (e.g. the US) or there is specific reason to suspect specific resistant infections (e.g. in patient with known methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus MRSA).

stem: A 45-year-old female with a history of epilepsy is reviewed in the neurology clinic. Which one of the following features is most likely to be attributable to sodium valproate therapy?
explanation:
Tremor
Sodium valproate may cause tremor. In the BNF tremor is listed as a 'less frequent' side effect.

Hirsutism
Alopecia is much more common than hirsutism in patients treated with sodium valproate. In the BNF hirsutism is listed as a 'very rare' side effect.

stem: A 28-year-old lady presents with a two-day history of headaches, nausea and vomiting, and blurred vision. She is long-sighted and has worn glasses since childhood. She has a background of severe migraines and was recently started on a prophylactic medication by her GP. On examination, both eyes are red with mid-dilated unreactive pupils bilaterally. Which medication is the most likely cause of this presentation?
explanation:
Topiramate
Topiramate can precipitate acute angle closure glaucoma. Topiramate is used as a first-line agent in the prophylaxis of migraine. It is an important cause of drug-induced acute angle closure glaucoma, typically occurring within one month of treatment. Topiramate-induced acute angle closure glaucoma is usually treated with cycloplegia and topical steroids alone rather than laser peripheral iridotomy.

Aspirin
High-dose aspirin can be used in the acute treatment of migraine. A single dose of 900mg can be taken as soon as the migraine symptoms develop. However, aspirin is not known to cause acute angle closure glaucoma.

Propranolol
Propranolol can be used as a first-line prophylactic treatment for people with episodic or chronic migraine but it is not known to be associated with acute angle closure glaucoma. Adrenergic drugs, in contrast, can precipitate an attack.

Sodium valproate
Sodium valproate is licensed for migraine prophylaxis though paradoxically itself commonly causes headaches. However, it is not known to cause acute angle closure glaucoma.

Sumatriptan
Sumatriptan can be used in the acute treatment of migraine. It can commonly cause nausea and vomiting, but not angle closure glaucoma.

stem: A 15-year-old girl is referred to the neurology clinic with a 3-month history of brief episodes of 'zoning out'. Her mother reports that during these episodes, the patient stares blankly, is unresponsive, and occasionally has eyelid fluttering. Each episode lasts about 10-15 seconds, after which she continues her activities with no recollection of the event. These episodes occur multiple times daily and have affected her school performance. Her past medical history is unremarkable. An EEG shows 3 Hz spike-and-wave discharges during hyperventilation. What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?
explanation:
Ethosuximide
Ethosuximide is the correct first-line treatment for this patient with typical absence seizures. The clinical presentation of brief episodes of unresponsiveness with eyelid fluttering, lasting 10-15 seconds with immediate recovery, is characteristic of absence seizures. This is further confirmed by the EEG finding of 3 Hz spike-and-wave discharges during hyperventilation, which is the classic EEG pattern in absence epilepsy. According to NICE guidelines, ethosuximide is recommended as the first-line treatment for absence seizures due to its high efficacy and favorable side effect profile in this specific seizure type. Ethosuximide works by inhibiting T-type calcium channels in thalamic neurons, which are implicated in the generation of absence seizures. It has been shown to provide seizure freedom in approximately 70-80% of patients with absence epilepsy and is particularly effective in children and adolescents with this seizure type.

Carbamazepine
Carbamazepine is not appropriate for absence seizures and may actually exacerbate them. While carbamazepine is effective for focal seizures and generalized tonic-clonic seizures, it can worsen absence seizures by increasing the frequency of spike-wave discharges. This paradoxical effect makes carbamazepine contraindicated in patients with absence epilepsy, and using it in this patient could lead to worsening of her seizure control and potentially precipitate absence status epilepticus.

Lamotrigine
Lamotrigine is considered a second-line treatment for absence seizures according to NICE guidelines. While it can be effective for absence seizures, it is not as efficacious as ethosuximide for this specific seizure type. Lamotrigine has a broader spectrum of action and is useful in patients with multiple seizure types. However, it requires slow titration due to the risk of serious skin reactions, particularly in children and adolescents, making it less ideal as a first-line option when a more specific and rapidly effective treatment like ethosuximide is available.

Levetiracetam
Levetiracetam is also considered a second-line treatment for absence seizures. While it has a broad spectrum of action against various seizure types, including absence seizures, studies have shown that it is less effective than ethosuximide for pure absence epilepsy. Levetiracetam may be considered if the patient has concurrent seizure types or if first-line treatments are ineffective or not tolerated. However, it is not the optimal first choice for a patient presenting with typical absence seizures alone.

Sodium valproate
Sodium valproate, although historically used for absence seizures with good efficacy, is no longer recommended as a first-line treatment in females of childbearing potential due to significant teratogenic risks. The MHRA and NICE have strengthened their advice against sodium valproate use in females younger than 55 years unless specific conditions are met. Given that this patient is a 15-year-old girl who will soon enter her reproductive years, sodium valproate should be avoided if possible, especially when equally effective alternatives with better safety profiles, such as ethosuximide, are available.

stem: A 65-year-old presents to his GP with swollen and tender gums that bleed easily when brushing. He reports that his symptoms have been progressively worsening over the past few months. His medical history includes hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, and type 2 diabetes and mentions that one of his medications was adjusted shortly before the onset of his symptoms. On examination, there is significant gum swelling and overgrowth, particularly around the upper and lower anterior teeth, with no signs of infection or ulceration.
