An updated set of observations are taken: Heart rate 156 beats per minute Blood pressure 102/65 mmHg Oxygen saturations 98% on 3L/min nasal specs Respiratory rate 24/min A bedside ECG is performed which reveals polymorphic ventricular tachycardia. Which of the following postoperative medications is the likely cause of her deterioration?
explanation:
Ondansetron
5-HT3 antagonists such as ondansetron can predispose to prolonged QT interval and increased risk of polymorphic VT. This patient has developed polymorphic ventricular tachycardia (VT) postoperatively, most likely due to the administration of ondansetron. Ondansetron is a 5-HT3 antagonist, a medication commonly used for postoperative nausea and vomiting. It can be associated with prolongation of the QTc interval which can deteriorate into polymorphic VT or torsades de pointes. It is generally treated with a magnesium sulphate infusion.

Morphine
Morphine is not generally associated with polymorphic VT, but is more associated with respiratory depression in high doses.

Metoclopramide
Metoclopramide is a dopamine antagonist also used as an anti-emetic. It is not linked with polymorphic VT, but has been linked with Parkinson like symptoms and movement disorders, particularly in young females.

Diclofenac
Diclofenac is an example of a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory medication. Its use tends to be linked with renal dysfunction, but is not linked with VT.

Cyclizine
Cyclizine is an antihistamine, also useful in treating nausea. Its use is linked with the development of some tachyarrhythmias, but is not linked to prolongation of the QT interval/ polymorphic VT.

stem: A 35-year-old man is referred to a neurology clinic. His partner has noticed that he is having repeated episodes of loss of awareness during the day. These episodes last for a few seconds and are associated with fluttering of the eyelids. There is no memory of the episode upon recovery. The examination is unremarkable at the time of review. Given the likely diagnosis, what medication should be avoided?
explanation:
Carbamazepine
Carbamazepine is contraindicated in absence seizures. The description of these episodes is typical of an absence seizure. Carbamazepine may exacerbate absence seizures rather than improve them.

Ethosuximide
Ethosuximide is incorrect. This is the first-line anti-epileptic drug that is used in the management of absence seizures. It blocks T-type calcium channels.

Lamotrigine
Lamotrigine is incorrect. This is a second-line option for the management of absence seizures. It is a sodium channel blocker. It is a preferred 2nd line option, particularly in women, where sodium valproate is less appropriate.

Levetiracetam
Levetiracetam is incorrect. This is another 2nd line option for the treatment of absence seizures in women. Although the mechanism by which it works in epilepsy is largely unknown it is postulated that it binds to synaptic vesicle glycoprotein 2 and inhibits presynaptic calcium channels.

Sodium valproate
Sodium valproate is incorrect. This is a 2nd line treatment for the management of absence seizures. This is typically reserved for use in men due to its potential for teratogenicity in women.

stem: A 10-year-old is referred to neurology due to episodes her GP feels are epileptiform. Her mother reports that she appears to just 'stop', sometimes even in mid conversation, for several seconds at random times during the day. During these episodes she can be unresponsive to questioning and has no recollection of them. Which of these drugs is contraindicated in this condition?
explanation:
Carbamazepine
Carbamazepine is contraindicated in absence seizures. Carbamazepine is contraindicated and can worsen absence seizures (along with phenytoin, vigabatrin and gabapentin).

Ethosuximide
Ethosuximide is the gold standard treatment and valproate, lamotrigine and clonazepam can all be useful.

Sodium valproate
Ethosuximide is the gold standard treatment and valproate, lamotrigine and clonazepam can all be useful.

Lamotrigine
Ethosuximide is the gold standard treatment and valproate, lamotrigine and clonazepam can all be useful.

Clonazepam
Ethosuximide is the gold standard treatment and valproate, lamotrigine and clonazepam can all be useful.

stem: A 66-year-old woman is investigated for ascites and found to have ovarian cancer. She presents due to 'unsteadiness'. On examination there is evidence of nystagmus and past-pointing. Which one of the following antibodies is most likely to be present?
explanation:
Anti-Yo
This lady has developed cerebellar syndrome secondary to anti-Yo antibodies.

stem: A 58-year-old is brought in by ambulance with acute left-sided weakness affecting his face, arm and lower limb. He reports these symptoms came on suddenly 2 hours ago whilst cleaning his garage. He has a past medical history of type two diabetes for which he takes metformin. He works as a solicitor and is usually fit and well. On examination, heart rate is 80 beats/min, blood pressure 160/80mmHg, oxygen saturations 98% on air, respiratory rate 18/min, temperature 36.5ºC, and blood glucose level 6.5. His pulse is regular, heart sounds normal, chest clear, and abdomen soft non tender. Examination of the neurological system reveals reduced power 2/5 in the left upper limb, and power 3/5 in the left lower limb. Power is 5/5 in the right upper and lower limbs. Sensation is intact throughout. There is a left-sided facial droop with forehead sparing. Examination of the visual fields reveals a homonymous hemianopia. The patient is taken urgently for a CT head, which reveals no intracranial haemorrhage. CT angiography is performed which demonstrates an occlusion of the right proximal middle cerebral artery. What is the correct definitive management of this patient?
explanation:
Thrombolysis and thrombectomy
A combination of thrombolysis AND thrombectomy is recommend for patients with an acute ischaemic stroke who present within 4.5 hours. This patient has presented with an acute ischaemic stroke of the anterior cerebral circulation, as manifested by a unilateral hemiparesis and homonymous hemianopia. The CT angiogram confirms this diagnosis by demonstrating an occlusion of the proximal middle cerebral artery. NICE updated their stroke guidelines in 2019 to include thrombectomy. The guidelines state that thrombectomy should be offered as soon as possible and within 6 hours of symptom onset, together with intravenous thrombolysis (if within 4.5 hours), to people who have: Acute ischaemic stroke and confirmed occlusion of the proximal anterior circulation demonstrated by computed tomographic angiography (CTA) or magnetic resonance angiography (MRA). We are told that the symptoms came on 2 hours ago, therefore the patient is within the thrombolysis window of 4.5 hours. As the patient has presented within the time window, the correct answer is thrombolysis and thrombectomy.

Anti-hypertensives
Blood pressure should not be lowered in the acute phase of a stroke unless there are complications such as hypertensive encephalopathy or to facilitate thrombolysis.

Thrombolysis
Thrombolysis alone is not the most appropriate management. The patient is within the time window for both thrombolysis and thrombectomy.

Aspirin 300mg and fondaparinux
Aspirin 300mg should be given, but alone this is not the most appropriate management.

Aspirin 300mg only
Aspirin 300mg should be given, but alone this is not the most appropriate management.

stem: A 35-year-old woman presents with a one-week history of blurred vision in her right eye and pain with eye movement. One year prior, she experienced sudden weakness and stiffness in her left leg, which resolved over three days. She also reports a transient decrease in colour perception six months ago. Examination reveals a relative afferent pupillary defect and optic disc swelling on the right side. Which MRI sequence is most appropriate for identifying the characteristic lesions associated with this condition?
explanation:
MRI FLAIR sequence
The MRI FLAIR sequence is the correct answer. Multiple sclerosis (MS) is defined by recurrent neurological symptoms. The patient presents with blurred vision in her right eye, associated with pain on movement, and has experienced weakness and stiffness in the limbs that resolved over three days a year previously, as well as a transient reduction in colour perception six months ago. These clinical features are indicative of MS and align with its relapsing-remitting nature, where patients undergo exacerbations followed by periods of remission. MRI FLAIR sequences are particularly adept at identifying hyperintense lesions on T2-weighted images, which are characteristic of MS; they effectively reveal lesions within periventricular areas and can detect the pathognomonic Dawson fingers that extend perpendicular to the corpus callosum. This imaging modality is proficient at detecting disseminated lesions across both time and space, which are crucial criteria for diagnosing MS.

MRI diffusion-weighted sequence
The MRI diffusion-weighted sequence is primarily utilised for detecting acute ischaemic strokes by highlighting areas of restricted diffusion. However, it is not the optimal choice for visualising chronic lesions typical of MS since it focuses on changes in water molecule diffusion within brain tissue – a feature not commonly associated with MS lesions.

MRI STIR sequence
The MRI STIR sequence is widely used in soft tissue imaging and is particularly useful for detecting oedema and inflammation in various conditions. It plays a significant role in evaluating thyroid eye disease due to its sensitivity to oedema and ability to assess soft tissue involvement. Nevertheless, other MRI sequences offer superior visualisation of demyelinating plaques found in MS.

MRI susceptibility-weighted sequence
The MRI susceptibility-weighted sequence is invaluable for identifying microhaemorrhages or iron deposits within cerebral tissues in conditions such as haemochromatosis. It also has applications in cases involving cerebral microhaemorrhages and vascular anomalies but falls short in depicting key features of MS like periventricular plaques and Dawson fingers.

MRI T1-weighted sequence
The MRI T1-weighted sequence provides high-resolution images that delineate anatomical structures clearly and can be essential when assessing brain anatomy and atrophy. However, it has limited sensitivity for high-signal lesions prevalent in MS; these lesions are more conspicuously identified on T2-weighted or FLAIR sequences. Although T1-weighted sequences can show contrast-enhancing lesions signifying active inflammation, they are less sensitive when it comes to detecting chronic non-enhancing lesions.

stem: Which one of the following is not a recognised adverse effect of phenytoin use?
explanation:
Gynaecomastia
Gynaecomastia is not a recognised adverse effect of phenytoin use, making this the correct answer. Phenytoin is an anticonvulsant medication commonly used in the management of epilepsy and other seizure disorders. While it has numerous side effects, gynaecomastia (the development of breast tissue in males) is not typically associated with phenytoin therapy. Gynaecomastia is more commonly associated with other medications such as spironolactone, cimetidine, certain antipsychotics, and hormonal agents.

Slurred speech
Slurred speech is an incorrect answer as it is a well-documented adverse effect of phenytoin, particularly when serum levels are elevated. This manifestation is part of the spectrum of cerebellar toxicity that can occur with phenytoin use. Slurred speech may be one of the earlier signs of phenytoin toxicity and can signal the need for dose adjustment or serum level monitoring.

Nystagmus
Nystagmus is an incorrect answer because it is a classic adverse effect of phenytoin therapy. Nystagmus, characterised by involuntary rhythmic eye movements, typically occurs at therapeutic or slightly elevated serum phenytoin levels. It is often one of the first clinical signs of approaching phenytoin toxicity and can be observed during neurological examination.

Diplopia
Diplopia is an incorrect answer as it is a recognised side effect of phenytoin. Double vision can occur as phenytoin levels increase and represents another manifestation of the drug's effect on the central nervous system. Diplopia often appears after nystagmus but before more severe neurological symptoms develop.

Ataxia
Ataxia is an incorrect answer because it is a common adverse effect of phenytoin, particularly at higher serum concentrations. Ataxia manifests as impaired coordination and balance, and represents a more advanced sign of phenytoin toxicity. The progression of phenytoin's neurological side effects typically follows a pattern: nystagmus appears first, followed by diplopia, then ataxia, and finally mental status changes and seizures at very high levels.

stem: A 24-year-old woman presents for advice. Over the past few months she has been having increasing problems with migraine around the time of menstruation. Her current migraine started around 6 hours ago and has not responded to a combination of paracetamol and aspirin. What is the most appropriate next step to relieve her headache?
explanation:
Sumatriptan
The correct answer is Sumatriptan. Sumatriptan is a 5-HT1 receptor agonist, commonly known as a 'triptan', which is used in the acute treatment of migraine. It works by constricting the blood vessels in the brain to relieve headaches, pain, and other migraine symptoms. According to the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guidelines, triptans are recommended as second-line treatment when simple analgesics such as paracetamol and non-steroidal antiinflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) have failed.

Codeine
Codeine is an opioid analgesic that can be used for pain relief but it's not generally recommended as first-line therapy for migraines due to its potential for addiction and side effects such as constipation and drowsiness. Furthermore, codeine can lead to medication-overuse headaches if taken regularly.

Ergotamine
Ergotamine was once a mainstay of migraine treatment but has largely been replaced by triptans because they have fewer side effects and are more effective. Ergotamines can cause nausea, vomiting, and peripheral vasoconstriction leading to cold extremities or even gangrene in severe cases.

Venlafaxine
Venlafaxine is a serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor (SNRI) used primarily in the treatment of depression, generalised anxiety disorder, panic disorder and social phobia. While it may have some efficacy in preventing migraines, it would not be used acutely to relieve a migraine that has already started.

Norethisterone
Norethisterone, a synthetic form of progesterone, is often used to delay menstruation or treat conditions like endometriosis or heavy menstrual bleeding. While hormonal changes can trigger migraines in some women, norethisterone would not act quickly enough to relieve an ongoing migraine attack.

stem: A 55-year-old man is diagnosed with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. Which one of the following drugs has been shown to confer a survival benefit?
explanation:
Riluzole
Riluzole is a glutamate antagonist which has been shown to slow the progression of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and confer a survival benefit. The NICE guideline NG42 recommends offering riluzole to people with ALS to slow disease progression. It works by decreasing the release of glutamate, thereby reducing neuronal excitotoxicity, which is thought to play a role in the pathogenesis of ALS.

Rituximab
Rituximab is a monoclonal antibody used primarily in the treatment of B-cell malignancies such as nonHodgkin's lymphoma and chronic lymphocytic leukaemia. It can also be used in some autoimmune conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis and vasculitis, but there is no evidence that it confers any benefit in ALS.

Interferon-beta
Interferon-beta is primarily used in the management of multiple sclerosis (MS), not ALS. It helps reduce inflammation and prevent nerve damage in MS but does not have any proven benefit in slowing down or halting the progression of ALS.

Cyclophosphamide
Cyclophosphamide is an alkylating chemotherapeutic agent, employed mainly for treating various types of cancer including lymphomas, leukaemias, and some solid tumours. It works by interfering with DNA replication, thus inhibiting cell division. It is not used for treating ALS.

Interferon-alpha
Interferon-alpha does not confer a survival benefit in patients with ALS either. Similar to interferon-beta, interferon-alpha has antiviral properties and can modulate immune responses. It's used predominantly for treating hepatitis C and certain haematological malignancies like hairy cell leukaemia but not for neurodegenerative diseases like ALS.

stem: A 32-year-old woman presents to the neurology clinic with a 6-week history of progressive stiffness and weakness in both legs, causing difficulty walking. She has no bowel or bladder symptoms. Examination reveals increased tone and brisk reflexes in both lower limbs, with bilateral extensor plantar responses. Upper limb examination is normal. Sensation is intact throughout. MRI brain from last year showed several periventricular white matter lesions; she did not attend follow-up at that time. Which diagnosis most likely explains her current presentation?
explanation:
Multiple sclerosis
Multiple sclerosis is a cause of spastic paraparesis. Multiple sclerosis is the best answer because it commonly affects young women and can present with signs of upper motor neuron (UMN) dysfunction in the lower limbs, such as spastic paraparesis. The presence of prior periventricular white matter lesions on MRI supports dissemination in space—a key MS diagnostic criterion according to UK guidelines. Although sensory symptoms are common, pure motor presentations do occur if plaques predominantly involve corticospinal tracts; relapses may also be incomplete or show gradual progression over weeks. The absence of upper limb findings further localises pathology to the spinal cord or brain affecting leg fibres.

Primary lateral sclerosis
Primary lateral sclerosis is a rare motor neurone disease variant causing slowly progressive UMN signs without lower motor neuron involvement or significant sensory changes, typically presenting after age 40 and progressing over years rather than weeks. It would not explain the prior white matter lesions on MRI nor fit this patient's age and subacute course.

Transverse myelitis
Transverse myelitis usually causes bilateral sensory loss below a spinal level, often with bladder/bowel dysfunction due to involvement of both ascending and descending tracts across a transverse segment of cord. This patient has no sensory deficit or sphincter disturbance, making isolated transverse myelitis unlikely.

Cervical spondylotic myelopathy
Cervical spondylotic myelopathy, while capable of causing spastic paraparesis via cord compression, generally occurs in older adults due to degenerative changes; it rarely causes isolated lower limb UMN signs without any upper limb involvement or preceding neck symptoms at this age.

Hereditary spastic paraplegia
Hereditary spastic paraplegia presents as a slowly progressive familial disorder beginning in childhood or early adulthood, characterised by insidious onset rather than subacute progression over weeks and would not account for previous disseminated white matter lesions on MRI.

stem: A 23-year-old man presents with recurrent headaches. These typically occur 2 or 3 times a month and are characterised by severe, right-sided headaches which are throbbing in nature and last around 8-12 hours. When he gets the headaches he finds it hard to carry on working and tends to go and lie down in a dark room. The headaches so far have responded poorly to paracetamol. Which one of the following medications should be prescribed to help reduce the frequency of these headaches?
explanation:
Propranolol
This is a classic history of migraine, prophylaxis should be offered with propranolol or topiramate.

Ibuprofen
Ibuprofen is not specifically mentioned for prophylaxis in this context.

Pizotifen
Pizotifen is not mentioned in the explanation.

Zolmitriptan
Zolmitriptan is used in the acute treatment of migraine, not for prophylaxis.

Carbamazepine
Carbamazepine is not mentioned in the explanation.

stem: A 55-year-old man presents with a worsening early morning headache. He has now also developed persistent nausea. A systematic enquiry was otherwise unremarkable. On examination, you note that he is unable to recognise simple objects when his eyes are closed. A neurological examination was otherwise unremarkable. What area of the brain is affected?
explanation:
Parietal lobe
Parietal lobe lesions may cause astereognosis. Parietal lobe is correct. Astereognosis is defined as the inability to identify objects by touch, despite intact elementary tactile, proprioceptive, and thermal sensation. It occurs due to a lesion in the parietal lobe.

Inferior frontal gyrus
Inferior frontal gyrus is incorrect. Lesions in this part of the brain result in Broca's dysphasia characterised by non-fluent speech but normal comprehension.

Lateral geniculate nucleus
Lateral geniculate nucleus is incorrect. This is a component of the thalamus which is a very important component of the visual pathway. A lesion of this nucleus produces moderately to completely congruent visual field defects.

Medial geniculate nucleus
Medial geniculate nucleus is incorrect. The medial geniculate nucleus is part of the auditory thalamus and represents the thalamic relay between the inferior colliculus and the auditory cortex. Although the medial geniculate nucleus is a well-known integration centre for the central auditory pathways, auditory symptoms caused by damage to these nuclei are rarely described. However, there are some case reports of auditory hallucinations.

Temporal lobe
Temporal lobe is incorrect. The function of the temporal lobe centres around auditory stimuli, memory, and emotion.

stem: A 33-year-old man presents to the emergency department with recurrent headaches and sweating. He has no past medical history. At the time of examination, the headache has resolved but the blood pressure is 210/94 mmHg. Examination demonstrates no skin lesions and a non-tender thyroid with no nodules. A CT head is normal but a CT chest, abdomen, and pelvis demonstrates a lesion on the left adrenal gland and an exophytic lesion in the right kidney. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Von Hippel-Lindau syndrome
Von Hippel-Lindau syndrome is correct. The patient presents with episodic headaches, sweating and very elevated blood pressure. The existence of an adrenal lesion in this context suggests a phaeochromocytoma. The exophytic lesion in the kidney suggests renal carcinoma. The most likely explanation for these findings is Von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) syndrome, which is a rare multisystem genetic disorder resulting in cysts and tumours (which may undergo malignant transformation) in multiple organs. Other possible features are retinal and cerebellar haemangioblastomas and pancreatic cysts.

Birt-Hogg-Dube Syndrome
Birt-Hogg-Dube Syndrome is incorrect. This rare genetic skin disorder can be associated with the development of renal cancer. Phaeochromocytoma is not a feature and the skin is normal in this case, making this diagnosis unlikely.

Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 (MEN1)
Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 (MEN1) is incorrect. This is a disorder associated with the development of tumours in endocrine organs (typically pituitary, parathyroid and pancreatic for MEN1). Phaeochromocytoma is rare for this disorder and renal cancer is not a feature.

Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2 (MEN2)
Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2 (MEN2) is incorrect. This is another form of multiple endocrine neoplasia. In this form, phaeochromocytoma is common (up to 50%). However, medullary thyroid cancer is essentially ubiquitous (~98%) and renal cancer is not a feature. Therefore, the absence of an abnormal thyroid and the presence of renal cancer make VHL syndrome more likely.

Polycystic kidney disease
Polycystic kidney disease is incorrect. The lesion in the kidney is exophytic (meaning it grows outward from the epithelium of the affected organ - suggesting a tumour) rather than cystic. Furthermore, there is only one lesion rather than multiple. Finally, phaeochromocytoma is not a feature of polycystic kidney disease.

stem: A 62-year-old man in a hospital neurology clinic has 6 months of an evening urge to move his legs with unpleasant sensations, relieved by movement and disrupting sleep. His partner reports repetitive leg jerks during the night. He has type 2 diabetes and a past gambling disorder. Examination is normal. He takes metformin and sertraline. Ferritin 120 µg/L (30 - 400) What is the most appropriate initial pharmacological treatment?
explanation:
Gabapentin
Gabapentin: This is the best initial pharmacological treatment for restless legs syndrome (RLS) in this scenario. Current UK practice and guidelines increasingly favour alpha-2-delta ligands (gabapentin or pregabalin) as first-line pharmacotherapy for persistent RLS because they effectively reduce sensory discomfort and periodic limb movements while avoiding the high rates of augmentation and impulse-control disorders seen with dopamine agonists. His ferritin is normal, so iron replacement is not indicated, and non-pharmacological measures alone have failed, given 6 months of sleep-disrupting symptoms. Gabapentin is particularly suitable here as it also addresses neuropathic-type discomfort and is useful if coexisting pain is suspected (e.g., in diabetes). The patient’s history of gambling disorder is a red flag for dopamine agonists, which can precipitate or worsen impulsive behaviours. Gabapentin’s main adverse effects are dizziness, somnolence and ataxia; dose adjustment is required in chronic kidney disease, but no severe renal impairment is presented. It has no significant interaction with sertraline. Overall, an alpha-2-delta ligand is first-line, and gabapentin is an evidence-based, guideline-consistent choice.

Pramipexole
Pramipexole: Although pramipexole is effective and historically used for RLS, it is no longer preferred as first-line due to the substantial risk of augmentation (earlier onset/worsening of symptoms, spread to arms, higher doses needed) and impulse-control disorders (e.g., pathological gambling, hypersexuality). This patient’s past gambling disorder is a clear contraindication to favouring a dopamine agonist when alternatives exist. In UK practice, pramipexole is typically reserved for cases where alpha-2-delta ligands are unsuitable or ineffective, after careful counselling about risks. It would not be the most appropriate initial choice when gabapentin or pregabalin can be used, particularly with a normal ferritin and persistent nocturnal symptoms. While pramipexole can be considered in carefully selected patients, the clinical context here strongly argues against it as first-line.

Ropinirole
Ropinirole: Similar to pramipexole, ropinirole is a non-ergot dopamine agonist that reduces RLS symptoms but carries the same key problems: augmentation with long-term use and a significant risk of impulse-control disorders. Given the patient’s history of gambling disorder, a dopamine agonist poses avoidable risk. UK guidance has shifted away from routine first-line dopamine agonists for exactly these reasons, especially in individuals vulnerable to behavioural adverse effects. Ropinirole is therefore not the most appropriate initial treatment. It may be considered in selected cases where alpha-2-delta ligands are contraindicated or poorly tolerated, with close monitoring for augmentation and impulsivity, but that is not the case here.

Levodopa
Levodopa: Levodopa can provide short-term relief and is sometimes used for intermittent RLS (e.g., occasional episodes or pre-travel dosing), but it has high rates of augmentation and rebound with regular nightly use. For a patient with chronic nightly symptoms causing sleep disturbance over months, levodopa is not recommended as first-line. It is generally avoided for regular use in RLS due to these complications, and better long-term tolerance exists with alpha-2-delta ligands. In this case —persistent symptoms, normal ferritin, and a behavioural risk profile that disfavors dopamine agents—levodopa would be an inferior initial choice compared to gabapentin.

Clonazepam
Clonazepam: Benzodiazepines are not first-line for RLS. While clonazepam may improve sleep continuity and can reduce arousals associated with periodic limb movements, it does not target the core pathophysiology of RLS and carries risks of sedation, cognitive impairment, falls (especially in older adults), and dependence. UK practice generally reserves benzodiazepines for very selected cases (e.g., refractory insomnia due to RLS/PLMS) when other options have failed or are contraindicated. In a 62-year-old with clear RLS features, normal ferritin, and prior gambling disorder, clonazepam is not the most appropriate initial choice. An alpha-2-delta ligand such as gabapentin is preferred as first-line therapy.

stem: An 18-year-old male gives a history of early morning jerking movements of his arm. After a night of heavy drinking and sleep deprivation, he has a generalised tonic-clonic seizure at 5am. An EEG reveals generalised spike and wave discharges. What is the most appropriate choice of antiepileptic?
explanation:
Sodium valproate
Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy (the diagnosis here), is a common form of idiopathic generalised epilepsy, representing 10% of all patients with epilepsy. This disorder typically first manifests itself between the ages of 10 and 18 with brief episodes of involuntary muscle twitching occurring early in the morning. Most patients also have generalised seizures that affect the entire brain and others have absence seizures. The most effective medication for this disorder is sodium valproate.

stem: A 72-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department. Whilst walking back from a friends house he slipped on some ice and fell backwards, landing on his right arm and banging his head on the kerb in the process. His past medical history includes atrial fibrillation for which he takes bisoprolol and warfarin. A routine INR taken four days ago was 2.2. There are no signs of any external injury to his right arm or scalp. What is the most appropriate course of action with relation to his head injury?
options: Arrange a CT head scan to be performed within 8 hours
Discharge with standard head injury advice
Discharge with standard head injury advice + advise he stops warfarin for 5 days
explanation:
Arrange a CT head scan to be performed within 8 hours
Patients who've had a head injury and are on warfarin need to have a CT scan, regardless of whether they have risk factors for an intracranial injury.

stem: A 60-year-old woman presents with a tremor. Which one of the following features would suggest a diagnosis of essential tremor rather than Parkinson's disease?
options: Tremor is worse when the arms are outstretched
explanation:
Tremor is worse following alcohol
Essential tremor symptoms are usually eased by alcohol.

Difficulty in initiating movement
Difficulty in initiating movement (bradykinesia) is typical of Parkinson's.

Postural instability
Postural instability is typical of Parkinson's.

Unilateral symptoms
Unilateral symptoms (initially) are typical of Parkinson's.

stem: A 68-year-old man presents to the emergency department with sudden-onset difficulty in speaking and comprehending language. He also has significant weakness of the right arm. He has a past medical history of diabetes and hypertension. After examination, a CT head scan shows left-sided cerebral hypoattenuation, indicating ischaemia. Given the likely diagnosis, he is referred to the appropriate team and spends a considerable amount of time in hospital. After discharge, the community team follows him up and wishes to measure his level of disability and dependence with regards to daily living. Which of the following is best for this purpose?
explanation:
Barthel scale
The Barthel index is a scale that measures disability or dependence in activities of daily living in stroke patients. This patient has had a stroke - the Barthel scale allows for the measurement of disability or dependence in activities of daily living in stroke patients.

FAST test
FAST is an acronym, often advertised to the general public, used to help recognise the early signs of stroke and improve responsiveness to their needs. It stands for facial drooping, arm weakness, speech difficulties, and 'time to call the emergency services'. It would not be used in the longer-term assessment of post-stroke disability.

MUST
The MUST, or 'Malnutrition Universal Screening Tool', is used to identify malnourished adults or those at risk of malnutrition. Whilst it may be useful in stroke patients, especially in those who have difficulty with food intake post-stroke, it is not specifically measuring disability in stroke patients as the Barthel scale does.

ROSIER scale
The ROSIER scale, or 'Recognition of Stroke in the Emergency Room', is used in an emergency setting to differentiate acute stroke from stroke mimics. It would not play a role in longer-term stroke assessment.

Waterlow score
The Waterlow score is used to estimate the risk of development of a pressure sore in a patient, factoring in variables such as mobility. Whilst it also may be useful in a stroke patient who has lost their mobility, it is not specifically designed to assess disability in stroke patients like the Barthel score.

stem: You are a CT1 in Acute Medicine covering a general medical ward at night. You are asked to see a 60-year-old patient with known myasthenia gravis who is complaining of increased breathlessness and fatigue. Which of the following antibiotics is most likely to be responsible for a myasthenic crisis?
explanation:
Gentamicin
Aminoglycosides, including gentamicin, are relatively contra-indicated in myasthenia as they are more commonly associated with exacerbations. The mechanism is thought to be competitive inhibition of the release of acetylcholine at the presynaptic membrane of the neuromuscular junction.

Metronidazole
Although metronidazole is occasionally associated with exacerbation in myasthenic patients, it is usually well tolerated in this population.

Clarithromycin
Although macrolides, such as clarithromycin, are occasionally associated with exacerbation in myasthenic patients, they are usually well tolerated in this population.

Amoxicillin
Amoxicillin is generally considered to be safe in myasthenia gravis.

stem: A 64-year-old woman presents with migraine and her daughter says that she noticed that when she asked her mum to repeat a phrase she said she could not. The patient has been having migraines for years and they have always been accompanied by a visual aura of flashing lights and nil else. There are no focal neurological signs and CT brain is unremarkable. Upon further questioning, the patient can follow simple and complex commands (open eyes and touch left hand to right ear) and when asked can name 4 animals in a minute. She is also fluent and understandable when asking her general questions. However, when the patient is asked to repeat 3 simple words and a sentence she cannot. What is this type of dysphasia?
explanation:
Conductive dysphasia
Conduction dysphasia: speech fluent, but repetition poor. Comprehension is relatively intact. Conductive dysphasia is correct as this dysphasia is characterised by word finding difficulties (hence only 4 animals named) and difficulty in repeating phrases. However, people with conduction difficulties still have intact language comprehension and relatively fluent speech and the sentence structure is intact, but may lack meaning.

Anomic dysphasia
Anomic dysphasia is incorrect as this describes a dysphasia with characteristic word finding difficulties with the use of generic fillers (e.g. 'thing') or circumlocution. People with this dysphasia are fluent, their comprehension is intact and repetition of words/phrases good.

Broca's dysphasia
Broca's dysphasia is incorrect as this describes a dysphasia where the speech is non-fluent and repetition of words is also poor. Comprehension is normal in Broca's.

Transcortical motor dysphasia
Transcortical motor dysphasia is incorrect. This dysphasia presents similarly to Broca's dysphasia, but in transcortical motor there are strong repetition skills; speech is non-fluent and comprehension intact.

Wernicke's dysphasia
Wernicke's dysphasia is incorrect as this results from damage to Wernicke's area in the temporal lobe and impairs language comprehension, repetition of words and phrases. In Wernicke's dysphasia speech is fluent with intact sentence structure but lacks meaning.

stem: A 23-year-old woman undergoes a planned lumbar puncture (LP) as part of neurological investigations for possible multiple sclerosis. During the consent process, she expresses concern about a post-LP headache. What is the mechanism of post-LP headaches?
options: Leaking cerebrospinal fluid from the dura
explanation:
Leaking cerebrospinal fluid from the dura
Leaking of cerebrospinal fluid from the dura is the most likely explanation for post-lumbar puncture headaches. It is thought that ongoing leak of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) through the puncture site causes ongoing CSF loss, leading to low pressure. A post-LP headache is typically frontal or occipital and occurs within three days. It is normally associated with worsening on standing and improvement when lying down. Treatment in severe cases includes an epidural blood patch, but most resolve on their own.

Vertebral body injury
Vertebral body injury would not cause headaches.

Nerve injury
Nerve injury would not cause headaches.

Bleeding into cerebrospinal fluid
Bleeding into cerebrospinal fluid would not cause headaches.

Too much cerebrospinal fluid removed
The loss of cerebrospinal fluid volume during lumbar puncture does not cause pain.

stem: A 35-year-old woman presents to her GP with three weeks of tingling in her right hand and left foot. She has no significant past medical history and is on no regular medications. One year previously, she had an episode of visual blurring in her left eye that lasted for a week before resolving. She did not seek medical attention at the time. On clinical examination, there was reduced sensation in her right hand and left foot. Flexing her neck elicited paraesthesia in the upper limbs. Her vision was normal. Which of the following clinical features is more common early in the course of this disease?
explanation:
Lethargy
Lethargy is a very common early symptom of multiple sclerosis. Lethargy is the correct answer.

Cognitive decline
All of the other features are more common in advanced multiple sclerosis.

Difficulty swallowing
All of the other features are more common in advanced multiple sclerosis.

Muscle contractures
All of the other features are more common in advanced multiple sclerosis.

Speech disturbance
All of the other features are more common in advanced multiple sclerosis.

stem: Which one of the following medications is most useful for helping to prevent attacks of Meniere's disease?
explanation:
Betahistine
The correct answer is Betahistine. Betahistine is a histamine analogue that works by improving the microcirculation and pressure of the inner ear, which helps to relieve symptoms associated with Meniere's disease such as vertigo, tinnitus, hearing loss and aural fullness. It is commonly used in the UK for the prophylaxis of this condition due to its effectiveness and relatively low side effect profile.

Promethazine
Promethazine and Prochlorperazine are both antiemetics that can be used to manage acute episodes of vertigo associated with Meniere's disease. However, they do not prevent attacks from occurring. Instead, these medications work by blocking dopamine receptors in the brain's vomiting centre and chemoreceptor trigger zone, respectively. This helps to reduce nausea and vomiting during an attack but does not address the underlying pathology causing the symptoms.

Prochlorperazine
Promethazine and Prochlorperazine are both antiemetics that can be used to manage acute episodes of vertigo associated with Meniere's disease. However, they do not prevent attacks from occurring. Instead, these medications work by blocking dopamine receptors in the brain's vomiting centre and chemoreceptor trigger zone, respectively. This helps to reduce nausea and vomiting during an attack but does not address the underlying pathology causing the symptoms.

Chlorphenamine
Chlorphenamine is an antihistamine primarily used for symptomatic relief of allergic conditions including rhinitis and urticaria. While it may have some minor effects on reducing fluid build-up in the inner ear due to its antihistamine properties, it is not typically used in the management or prevention of Meniere's disease.

Cinnarizine
Cinnarizine is an antihistamine and calcium channel blocker that can also be used in managing vertigo symptoms. However, like Promethazine and Prochlorperazine, it does not prevent attacks from occurring but rather provides symptomatic relief during an episode of vertigo.

stem: A 33-year-old woman presents to her GP with headaches. She initially noted unilateral, throbbing headaches that occurred every few weeks and would be relieved by lying in a darkened room. The patient began to use regular paracetamol, ibuprofen and codeine for these headaches, taking them daily. She now describes a constant headache that she feels all across her head and is not relieved by lying in a darkened room. Her neurological examination is unremarkable. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Taper off current analgesia whilst introducing propranolol
Taper off current analgesia whilst introducing topiramate
Wean down dose of codeine and stop paracetamol/ibuprofen immediately
Wean down dose of paracetamol/ibuprofen and stop codeine immediately
explanation:
Wean down dose of codeine and stop paracetamol/ibuprofen immediately
Wean down dose of codeine and stop paracetamol/ibuprofen immediately is correct. This patient initially described migraine-like symptoms and began to use daily analgesia. The headache then became a medication overuse headache, the treatment for which is the cessation of the analgesia. The paracetamol and ibuprofen can be stopped abruptly, but the codeine requires gradual dose reduction to avoid withdrawal symptoms.

Stop all analgesia immediately
Stop all analgesia immediately is incorrect. Whilst the paracetamol and ibuprofen can be stopped abruptly, the codeine must be withdrawn gradually to avoid withdrawal symptoms.

Taper off current analgesia whilst introducing propranolol
Taper off current analgesia whilst introducing propranolol is incorrect. The paracetamol and ibuprofen can be stopped abruptly and do not need to be tapered or weaned. Because this patient's primary problem is now medication overuse headache, this must be treated first. The treatment for this involves cessation of current analgesia. Once the analgesia has been withdrawn, propranolol could be introduced if the patient was still struggling with migraine symptoms.

Taper off current analgesia whilst introducing topiramate
Taper off current analgesia whilst introducing topiramate is incorrect. The paracetamol and ibuprofen can be stopped abruptly and do not need to be tapered or weaned. Because this patient's primary problem is now medication overuse headache, this must be treated first. The treatment for this involves cessation of current analgesia. Once the analgesia has been withdrawn, migraine prophylaxis could be considered if the patient was still struggling with migraine symptoms. Topiramate would, however, not be the first choice as this patient is a female of child-bearing age and topiramate is associated with a risk of teratogenicity. Propranolol would therefore be preferred as prophylaxis if required.

Wean down dose of paracetamol/ibuprofen and stop codeine immediately
Wean down dose of paracetamol/ibuprofen and stop codeine immediately is incorrect. These options are the wrong way around; in medication overuse headache the paracetamol and ibuprofen can be stopped abruptly but the codeine dose should be gradually reduced to avoid withdrawal symptoms.

stem: A 21-year-old female is seen in the first seizure clinic in the outpatient department. Both the EEG and MRI brain are normal. A decision is made not to start her on anti-epileptic medication. What restrictions on driving should she be informed about?
options: No restrictions, no need to inform DVLA if not on medication
Cannot drive for 1 month from date of seizure
Cannot drive for 6 months from date of seizure
Cannot drive for 1 year from date of seizure
explanation:
Cannot drive for 6 months from date of seizure
Patients cannot drive for 6 months following a first unprovoked or isolated seizure if brain imaging and EEG normal. The correct answer is Cannot drive for 6 months from date of seizure. According to DVLA guidelines, after a first unprovoked seizure, a person must not drive for 6 months from the date of the seizure, and they must notify the DVLA. This applies regardless of whether anti-epileptic medication is started or not. The 6-month restriction allows time to assess the risk of seizure recurrence and ensures road safety.

No restrictions but inform DVLA
No restrictions but inform DVLA is incorrect. Simply informing the DVLA without any driving restriction would be unsafe and does not comply with current guidelines. There must be a period of driving cessation after a seizure to ensure public safety.

No restrictions, no need to inform DVLA if not on medication
No restrictions, no need to inform DVLA if not on medication is incorrect. The requirement to notify the DVLA and stop driving applies regardless of whether medication is prescribed. The occurrence of a seizure itself, not the treatment, is what determines the driving restrictions.

Cannot drive for 1 month from date of seizure
Cannot drive for 1 month from date of seizure is incorrect. This duration is too short to adequately assess the risk of seizure recurrence. A one-month restriction would be insufficient to ensure road safety.

Cannot drive for 1 year from date of seizure
Cannot drive for 1 year from date of seizure is incorrect. While a one-year driving ban applies in some circumstances (such as in cases of established epilepsy or when seizures occur exclusively during sleep), it is excessive for a single unprovoked seizure where investigations are normal. The evidence-based guideline of 6 months provides an appropriate balance between safety and maintaining quality of life.

stem: A 62-year-old man comes into the emergency department due to increased double vision. He has been finding it increasingly difficult to walk down stairs because he is seeing two of every step. However, he is able to walk upstairs without any problems. The patient also reports trouble whilst reading the newspaper. Upon further questioning he denies any recent eye trauma, headache or any weakness or numbness of his limbs. He suffers from hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus, both of which are well controlled. The patient is a non-smoker and denies use of recreational drugs or alcohol. Which of the following structures has most likely been affected?
explanation:
Trochlear nerve
This patient likely has trochlear nerve palsy (CN IV). Microvascular disease can involve CN IV in older patients with cardiovascular risk factors. The trochlear nerve innervates the superior oblique muscle which causes the eye to internally rotate and depress while adducted. Patients with trochlear nerve palsy usually present with vertical diplopia, most noticeable when the affected eye looks down and nasally. Clinical examination would show impairment of downgaze when the affected eye is adducted.

Abducens nerve
Abducens nerve (CN VI) innervates the lateral rectus which abducts the eye. A lesion affecting this nerve would cause horizontal diplopia and inward deviation of the eye.

Oculomotor nerve
The oculomotor nerve (CN III) innervates the superior and inferior recti, medial rectus, and inferior oblique muscles. Palsies to this nerve would present with impaired horizontal eye movement and weak adduction of the affected eye.

Optic nerve
Loss of vision would result from damage to the optic nerve (CN II).

Trigeminal nerve
The trigeminal nerve does not supply motor function to the ocular muscles.

stem: A 75-year-old man is brought to the emergency department with sudden onset numbness affecting his face and limbs. He has a past medical history of hypertension and hypercholesterolaemia. His medications are amlodipine and atorvastatin. On examination, he is ataxic and there is nystagmus. Right-sided ptosis and miosis are noted. There is an absence of right-sided facial sensation and left-sided arm and leg sensation. There is no weakness. What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Lateral medullary syndrome
Lateral medullary syndrome is correct. The sudden onset of symptoms suggests a vascular event. The lateral medullary syndrome is caused by a posterior inferior cerebellar artery lesion. It causes cerebellar signs (ataxia, nystagmus), ipsilateral facial numbness and Horner's syndrome (ptosis, miosis) and contralateral sensory loss.

Benedikt syndrome
Benedikt syndrome is incorrect. This is a syndrome caused by a lesion (infarction, haemorrhage, tumour or infection) in the tegmentum of the midbrain and cerebellum. Occlusion of the posterior cerebral artery is a possible cause. It causes 3rd nerve palsy, cerebellar ataxia and movement disorders (including tremor and chorea).

Millard-Gubler syndrome
Millard-Gubler syndrome is incorrect. This is caused by a lesion affecting the pons. It results in ipsilateral 6th and 7th nerve palsies and contralateral hemiparesis.

Nothnagel syndrome
Nothnagel syndrome is incorrect. This is an uncommon midbrain syndrome, which involves the tectum of the midbrain and superior cerebellar peduncle. It can be caused by stroke or neoplasm. It causes an ipsilateral 3rd nerve palsy and limb ataxia.

Weber syndrome
Weber syndrome is incorrect. This is a stroke that affects the medial portion of the midbrain. It can be caused by the occlusion of a branch of the posterior cerebral artery. It causes contralateral hemiparesis and a 3rd nerve palsy, neither of which are present in this case.

stem: A 24-year-old female presents with a headache. She has a past history of epilepsy and is known to suffer from migraines, but has previously managed attacks with a combination of paracetamol and metoclopramide. This combination is however not working for the current episode. What second line medication is it most appropriate to use?
explanation:
Zolmitriptan + paracetamol
Migraine acute: triptan + NSAID or triptan + paracetamol. Epilepsy is not a contraindication to the use of triptans.

Codeine + paracetamol
Opioids are not recommended in the management of migraine.

stem: A 30-year-old lady presents with acute occipital headache associated with vomiting, photophobia and stiff neck. There is no history of rash or fever. She has a past medical history of phaeochromocytoma for which she had surgery. She reports that her father died of kidney cancer and her brother is blind in his right eye due to a bleed in the eye. What is the unifying diagnosis?
explanation:
Von Hippel Lindau disease
This patient has von Hippel Lindau disease which is characterised by retinal and cerebellar haemangiomas, renal cysts with transformation to renal cell carcinoma, and phaeochromocytoma. Neurological signs can be due to compression by haemangiomas, or an acute headache due to intracerebral or subarachnoid haemorrhage as in this patient.

Polycystic kidney disease
Polycystic kidney disease is associated with subarachnoid haemorrhage due to berry aneurysms, but the other pointers in the history of a phaeochromocytoma and a family history of retinal bleeding and renal cell carcinoma do not fit with PKD.

Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1
Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 is associated with parathyroid disease, pancreatic endocrine tumours and pituitary tumours.

Tuberous sclerosis
Tuberous sclerosis is associated with hamartomas of the brain, eye and kidneys but would have characteristic skin signs present such as angiofibroma, shagreen patches and adenoma sebaceum.

Alport syndrome
Alport syndrome is not associated with intracerebral bleeding.

stem: A 57-year-old Polish patient, who just moved to the UK 6 months ago, presents to the emergency department following a fall. You notice that he has a wide-based gait, bilateral hand tremor and a nystagmus. Which medication is he likely to be taking?
explanation:
Phenytoin
Phenytoin use is a cause of the cerebellar syndrome. Phenytoin is the correct answer as this patient is displaying classical signs of phenytoin toxicity. The clinical features described - wide-based ataxic gait, tremor, and nystagmus - are characteristic of phenytoin's adverse effects on the cerebellum. Phenytoin is still commonly prescribed as first-line antiepileptic therapy in many Eastern European countries, including Poland, whereas in the UK it is now considered a second-line agent. The therapeutic window of phenytoin is narrow, and toxicity can occur even within the therapeutic range, particularly in chronic use.

Ethosuximide
Ethosuximide is incorrect as it is primarily used for absence seizures and does not typically cause cerebellar signs. Its main adverse effects include gastrointestinal disturbances, headaches, and rarely psychotic symptoms. It would be an unusual choice for an adult patient.

Levetiracetam
Levetiracetam is incorrect because while it can cause neurological side effects, these typically manifest as behavioural changes, irritability, and mood disturbances rather than cerebellar signs. Levetiracetam is commonly used in the UK but does not typically cause the combination of symptoms described.

Lamotrigine
Lamotrigine is incorrect as its main adverse effects include skin rashes (which can be severe, such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome), headaches, and diplopia. While it can cause ataxia, it rarely presents with the classical triad of cerebellar signs described in this case.

Sodium valproate
Sodium valproate is incorrect because although it can cause tremor, its typical adverse effects include weight gain, hair loss, and teratogenicity. While it can cause ataxia, the combination of prominent cerebellar signs is more characteristic of phenytoin toxicity. Additionally, valproate-induced tremor tends to be fine rather than the coarse tremor typically seen with phenytoin.

stem: A 55-year-old man presents to his general practitioner with reports of recurrent episodes of the room spinning. He has no past medical history. He denies hearing loss or aural fullness. The patient experiences this commonly when he is in bed and each episode lasts 10-20 seconds. This has been ongoing for months and was preceded by an upper respiratory tract infection. He is well in between episodes. The examination is unremarkable. What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo
Typical BPPV history: vertigo triggered by change in head position (e.g. rolling over in bed or gazing upwards) may be associated with nausea each episode typically lasts 10-20 seconds. The patient gives a clear history of short-lasting stereotyped episodes of vertigo. Given this is commonly occurring when he is in bed, it suggests that rolling over in bed is contributory, which would be typical of this diagnosis (brought about by changes in head position).

Meniere's disease
Meniere's disease is incorrect. This can cause recurrent episodes of vertigo. However, it will be unrelated to head position, episodes typically last 2-3 hours, and there may be other associated features like hearing loss and a sensation of aural fullness.

Multiple sclerosis
Multiple sclerosis is incorrect. Vertigo is uncommon in MS. If it occurs, it is unlikely to be short-lasting. Additionally, there would typically be other associated features e.g. clinical signs of an upper motor neuron disorder or optic neuritis. It would be unrelated to the position a patient takes.

Posterior circulation stroke
Posterior circulation stroke is incorrect. If the patient had a stroke, it would be a sudden onset of persistent vertigo rather than recurrent episodes with periods of being well in between. The examination may be abnormal.

Viral labyrinthitis
Viral labyrinthitis is incorrect. This can cause vertigo. However, it would typically cause vertigo after an infection that would result in one continuous episode that subsequently resolves rather than recurrent episodes. In this case, the infection that preceded the symptoms is unrelated. Furthermore, viral labyrinthitis causes hearing loss (unlike vestibular neuritis), which is absent here and makes the diagnosis unlikely.

stem: A 75-year old gentleman presents with a short history of neck pain, paraesthesia in his finger tips and progressive leg weakness. Following a MRI scan of his spine, he is diagnosed with degenerative cervical myelopathy due to a C4/5 disc prolapse. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
options: Analgesia and review in 4 weeks time
Analgesia, a hard cervical collar and review in 4 weeks
explanation:
Cervical decompressive surgery
All patients with degenerative cervical myelopathy should be urgently referred for assessment by specialist spinal services (neurosurgery or orthopaedic spinal surgery). This is due to the importance of early treatment. The timing of surgery is important, as any existing spinal cord damage can be permanent. Early treatment (within 6 months of diagnosis) offers the best chance of a full recovery but at present, most patients are presenting too late. In one study, patients averaged over 5 appointments before diagnosis, representing >2 years. Currently, decompressive surgery is the only effective treatment. It has been shown to prevent disease progression. Close observation is an option for mild stable disease, but anything progressive or more severe requires surgery to prevent further deterioration. Prompt diagnosis and onward referral are therefore key to ensuring good outcome for your patients. There are national initiatives to raise awareness of the condition to try and improve referral times (www.myelopathy.org).

Cervical nerve root injection
All of the other listed options in this question do not control the patients primary pathology.

Analgesia and referral to physiotherapy
All of the other listed options in this question do not control the patients primary pathology. Physiotherapy should only be initiated by specialist services, as manipulation can cause more spinal cord damage.

Analgesia and review in 4 weeks time
All of the other listed options in this question do not control the patients primary pathology.

Analgesia, a hard cervical collar and review in 4 weeks
All of the other listed options in this question do not control the patients primary pathology.

stem: A 62-year-old patient presents to the emergency department with severe nausea and vomiting. She describes the onset as fairly sudden, with no obvious cause. She has no significant past medical history except for hypertension and takes regular amlodipine for this. On examination, there are no specific findings. As part of initial management, she is given an antiemetic. Approximately 30 minutes later, she starts to complain of palpitations and lightheadedness. An urgent ECG is performed, which demonstrates polymorphic ventricular tachycardia. What antiemetic was she most likely to have been given?
explanation:
Ondansetron
5-HT3 antagonists such as ondansetron can predispose to prolonged QT interval and increased risk of polymorphic VT. This patient appears to have developed Torsades de Pointes (TdP), judging from the description of polymorphic ventricular tachycardia. This is typically caused by a prolonged QT interval, which in turn is known to be caused by 5-HT3 antagonists such as ondansetron. The risk is increased when using large doses, generally over 16mg in adults or 8mg in the elderly, or when there are short intervals between doses (less than 4 hours apart).

Aprepitant
Aprepitant is incorrect. This is a neurokinin receptor antagonist that is mainly used for chemotherapy-induced nausea and is not associated with QT prolongation.

Cyclizine
Cyclizine is an example of an antihistamine-based antiemetic. It is not known to prolong the QT interval.

Hyoscine
Hyoscine is an anticholinergic sometimes used for antiemetic purposes. It is not typically linked with QT prolongation or TdP.

Nabilone
Nabilone is a cannabinoid anti-emetic which is also sometimes considered for refractory chemotherapy-induced nausea. It is not a cause of QT prolongation.

stem: A 67-year-old man presented to the emergency department with sudden onset double vision on rightward gaze. He had a background of ischaemic heart disease and hypercholesterolemia. He smoked 10 cigarettes per day. On examination, he was found to have a normal gait and a normal peripheral neurological examination. Examination of the cranial the left eye did not adduct on rightward gaze and the right eye exhibited nystagmus. The pupils were equal and reactive the light. The emergency department team arrange an urgent MRI of the brain to rule out a possible stroke. Where is the neurological lesion that would account for the clinical presentation?
explanation:
Left medial longitudinal fasciculus
Internuclear ophthalmoplegia is due to a lesion in the medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF), which is located in the paramedian area of the midbrain and the pons. The patient has presented with a typical history and examination of internuclear ophthalmoplegia. In order to generate conjugate eye movements, a signal is sent from the paramedian pontine reticular formation (PPRF) to the pontine abducens nucleus. A signal is then sent from the abducens nucleus to the ipsilateral lateral rectus muscle via the abducens nerve and to the contralateral oculomotor nucleus to control the contralateral medial rectus muscle. Fibres from the abducens nucleus cross the midline of the brainstem and form a highly myelinated tract, the MLF, which travels up the contralateral side of the brainstem to the oculomotor nucleus. The contralateral medial rectus muscle is then innervated from the oculomotor nucleus in the midbrain. The eye which fails to adduct is ipsilateral to the lesion in the MLF as the oculomotor nucleus does not receive a signal from the contralateral abducens nucleus to adduct. This results in a failure of conjugate gaze and diplopia. The horizontal nystagmus of the right eye above is explained by Hering's law of equal innervation, whereby the 'weak, medial rectus muscle prompts the cortex to increase innervation to the oculomotor nucleus. This prompts an equally increased, and in this case, excessive innervation to the contralateral abducens nucleus, resulting in horizontal nystagmus of the right eye.

Left oculomotor nucleus
The left and right oculomotor nuclei are incorrect. The nuclei of the oculomotor nerve innervate ipsilaterally, emerging from the medial aspect of the cerebral peduncles. Hence a lesion of the left oculomotor nucleus would affect the left eye and lesion of the right oculomotor nucleus would affect the right eye. Lesions of the oculomotor nuclei would result in more profound ophthalmoplegias with the eye often resting in the 'down and out' position, due to unopposed lateral rectus and superior oblique contraction.

Right abducens nucleus
A lesion of the right abducens nucleus is incorrect. The right abducens nerve is functioning in the scenario above as the patient can look to the right and so we can assume that the nucleus is functioning also. The fact that the right eye exhibits nystagmus is related to Hering's law as mentioned above.

Right oculomotor nucleus
The left and right oculomotor nuclei are incorrect. The nuclei of the oculomotor nerve innervate ipsilaterally, emerging from the medial aspect of the cerebral peduncles. Hence a lesion of the left oculomotor nucleus would affect the left eye and lesion of the right oculomotor nucleus would affect the right eye. Lesions of the oculomotor nuclei would result in more profound ophthalmoplegias with the eye often resting in the 'down and out' position, due to unopposed lateral rectus and superior oblique contraction.

stem: A 52-year-old man with a history of epilepsy is reviewed. Since having his medication change he has experienced a 'numbness' of his hands and feet. On examination he has reduced sensation in a glove-and-stocking distribution associated with a reduced ankle reflex. He is also noted to have lymphadenopathy in the cervical and inguinal region and some bleeding around the gums. Which one of the following medications is he most likely to have been taking?
explanation:
Phenytoin
The correct answer is Phenytoin. The patient's presentation of peripheral neuropathy, lymphadenopathy, and bleeding gums suggests that he has been taking phenytoin. Phenytoin is an antiepileptic drug that can cause side effects such as peripheral neuropathy, characterized by numbness and reduced sensation in a glove-and-stocking distribution. Additionally, phenytoin can cause gingival hyperplasia, which may lead to bleeding gums. Lymphadenopathy is another potential side effect of phenytoin.

Carbamazepine
Carbamazepine is an antiepileptic drug that can cause side effects such as dizziness, ataxia, and diplopia. While it has been associated with some cases of peripheral neuropathy, it is not commonly linked to lymphadenopathy or bleeding gums.

Topiramate
Topiramate is another antiepileptic medication that can cause side effects like weight loss, cognitive impairment, and kidney stones. It is not typically associated with peripheral neuropathy, lymphadenopathy, or bleeding gums.

Sodium valproate
Sodium valproate is an antiepileptic drug that can cause gastrointestinal disturbances, tremor, and hair loss. It does not typically cause peripheral neuropathy or the other symptoms described in this case.

Lamotrigine
Lamotrigine is an antiepileptic medication known for causing skin rashes (including Stevens-Johnson syndrome), headache, and dizziness. Peripheral neuropathy, lymphadenopathy, and bleeding gums are not common side effects of lamotrigine.

stem: An 18-year-old woman presents for a routine neurology review. She has a longstanding history of seizures, occurring several times per day. During these episodes, she completely stops what she is doing and becomes unresponsive to voice or tactile stimulation. Her eyelids rapidly flutter for approximately 20 seconds, before the episode finishes. She is able to quickly resume activity after this. She has trialled a number of different medications over the years, with varying degrees of success. What medication is likely to have been avoided throughout?
explanation:
Carbamazepine
Carbamazepine is contraindicated in absence seizures. This patient's history is a clear description of absence seizures. These may start during early school age if part of childhood absence epilepsy (CAE), or during puberty if part of juvenile absence epilepsy (JAE). A number of anticonvulsants may be used to manage the condition. However, carbamazepine should be avoided as it is known to exacerbate absence seizures.

Ethosuximide
Ethosuximide is generally considered a first-line agent in the management of absence seizures. It is not contraindicated in their management.

Lamotrigine
Lamotrigine is not contraindicated in the management of absence seizures. It may be used as a second-line option, particularly in females.

Levetiracetam
Levetiracetam is another second-line agent in the management of absence seizures, alongside lamotrigine, especially in females.

Sodium valproate
Sodium valproate is a second-line option for absence seizures - not contraindicated. It is generally used in males, given its teratogenicity.

stem: A 62-year-old man is admitted to the Emergency Department with a left hemiplegia. His symptoms started around 5 hours but he initially thought he had slept in an awkward position. He has no past medical history of note but on examination is found to have and irregular pulse of 150 / min. The ECG confirms atrial fibrillation. A CT head is immediately arranged and reported as normal. What is the most appropriate initial management?
explanation:
Aspirin
Rate control should also be initiated. The 2004 RCP guidelines recommend that anticoagulation should be commenced 14 days after an ischaemic stroke. Earlier anticoagulation may exacerbate any secondary haemorrhage. Dipyridamole should not be used in the acute phase. Aspirin is the most appropriate initial management in this scenario.

Aspirin + dipyridamole
Dipyridamole should not be used in the acute phase.

Alteplase
He is outside the thrombolysis window so alteplase is not an option.

Warfarin
The 2004 RCP guidelines recommend that anticoagulation should be commenced 14 days after an ischaemic stroke. Earlier anticoagulation may exacerbate any secondary haemorrhage.

stem: A 37-year-old carpenter presents to his GP with a history of clumsiness at work worsening over the last 6 months. He has noticed 'fumbling' for tools on several occasions and is particularly concerned he has fallen repeatedly due to 'tripping over his feet'. He is normally fit and well apart from well controlled type 1 diabetes and has no other symptoms. Insulin is his only medication. There is no family history of illness. On examination of this patient's reflexes he has absent ankle jerks and extensor plantars. Sensation is intact. Which of the following is a possible cause for his symptoms?
explanation:
Diabetic neuropathy
Diabetic neuropathy, myasthenia gravis and Guillain Barre syndrome would cause lower motor neuron signs only.

Myasthenia gravis
Diabetic neuropathy, myasthenia gravis and Guillain Barre syndrome would cause lower motor neuron signs only.

Progressive supranuclear palsy
Progressive supranuclear palsy would present with Parkinsonism and falls.

Motor neuron disease
Extensor plantars + absent ankle jerk → mixed UMN + LMN signs - motor neuron disease, subacute combined degeneration of cord, syringomyelia.

Guillain Barre syndrome
Diabetic neuropathy, myasthenia gravis and Guillain Barre syndrome would cause lower motor neuron signs only.

stem: A 40-year-old woman presents with recurrent episode of vertigo associated with a feeling or 'fullness' and 'pressure' in her ears. She thinks her hearing is worse during the attacks. Clinical examination is unremarkable. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Meniere's disease
The most likely diagnosis for this patient is Meniere's disease. Meniere's disease is characterized by recurrent episodes of vertigo, fluctuating hearing loss, and a feeling of fullness or pressure in the affected ear. The exact cause of Meniere's disease is unknown, but it is thought to be related to an imbalance in the endolymphatic fluid within the inner ear. The unremarkable clinical examination further supports this diagnosis.

Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo
Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV) is another possible cause of vertigo; however, it typically presents with brief episodes of vertigo triggered by specific head movements or changes in position. BPPV is caused by dislodged otoliths within the semicircular canals of the inner ear, leading to inappropriate stimulation of the vestibular system. This patient's symptoms do not align with this presentation as her vertigo seems to be unrelated to head movement or position.

Acoustic neuroma
Acoustic neuroma, also known as vestibular schwannoma, is a benign tumour arising from Schwann cells that surround the vestibulocochlear nerve (cranial nerve VIII). While acoustic neuromas can present with progressive hearing loss and tinnitus, they usually cause only mild or no vertigo. Furthermore, these symptoms would generally not have a recurrent pattern as described by the patient.

Cholesteatoma
A cholesteatoma is an abnormal growth of skin cells within the middle ear that can lead to erosion of surrounding structures and complications such as hearing loss and dizziness. However, cholesteatomas typically present with other symptoms such as chronic foul-smelling otorrhea and conductive hearing loss which are not mentioned in this case.

Somatisation
Lastly, somatisation refers to the manifestation of psychological distress through physical symptoms. While somatisation could theoretically cause a wide range of symptoms, including vertigo and hearing loss, the specific pattern of this patient's symptoms - recurrent episodes of vertigo with associated ear fullness and fluctuating hearing loss - is more consistent with Meniere's disease.

stem: You are asked to see a 21-year-old woman on the medical take who presents with a 2-day history of blurred vision and pain in her right eye which worsened after her morning bath. She had similar symptoms 6 months ago affecting her right eye but these resolved spontaneously and she did not seek medical attention. Examination reveals a central scotoma and impaired colour vision on Ishihara plates in the right eye. Examination is otherwise unremarkable. A contrast MRI brain shows T2 enhancement of the right optic nerve but no other abnormalities. Lumbar puncture demonstrates oligoclonal bands in the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). Her mother has multiple sclerosis (MS) and she is understandably anxious to discuss her diagnosis and treatment options. Which of the following is the most appropriate action?
options: Reassure her she does not have MS and discharge
Give steroids and arrange MRI whole spine
Give steroids and arrange repeat MRI brain as a neurology outpatient
explanation:
Give steroids and arrange MRI whole spine
This is the best option. By doing an MRI spine you can determine if there are lesions separated in space and time. Steroids would treat her current optic neuritis.

Start Beta-interferon
Beta-interferon is used in certain MS patients who meet specific criteria. It reduces the frequency of attacks. It is inappropriate to start in this scenario as you are not even able to confirm a diagnosis of MS.

Reassure her she does not have MS and discharge
You cannot exclude MS with the information available and so it would be wrong (and frankly negligent) to reassure and discharge her (on the basis of probability it's very likely that she has/will develop MS in the future but again on the limited information you have available you can't make that diagnosis).

Perform visual evoked potentials
Visual evoked potentials are used in investigating MS but wouldn't add anything in this scenario. You already know she has optic neuritis and the MRI brain has shown a demyelinating lesion.

Give steroids and arrange repeat MRI brain as a neurology outpatient
Giving steroids would help her current optic neuritis but simply repeating the MRI brain at a later date is inappropriate.

stem: A 54-year-old woman presents with sudden onset of memory loss. Her husband states that for a period of 8 hours she was disoriented in time and place, but could remember who she was and was able to recognise family members. She has no recollection of the events. There is no history of any traumatic events. The mental state examination is otherwise normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Transient global amnesia
The most likely diagnosis is transient global amnesia (TGA) which is characterised by the acute onset of anterograde amnesia (the inability to form new memories). It usually resolves within 24 hours.

Bipolar affective disorder
Bipolar affective disorder is incorrect. There are no clinical features (e.g. mania, or delusions) to suggest an underlying bipolar disorder.

Dissociation
Dissociation is incorrect. Dissociation is a mental process where a person disconnects from their thoughts, feelings, memories or sense of identity.

Factitious amnesia
Factitious amnesia is incorrect. A factitious disorder is a condition in which a person, without a malingering motive, acts as if they have an illness by deliberately producing, feigning, or exaggerating symptoms, purely to attain (for themselves or for another) a patient's role. Although this remains within the differential, there is nothing to suggest a factitious disorder in this case.

Fugue state
Fugue state is incorrect. A dissociative fugue is a temporary state where a person has memory loss (amnesia) and ends up in an unexpected place. People with this symptom can't remember who they are or details about their past. The fugue state can last for days, months or longer. The short duration in this case favours a diagnosis of TGA.

stem: A 42-year-old woman is referred to the clinic having been diagnosed with a phaeochromocytoma after originally presenting with episodes of headaches, tachycardia and sweating. Given its relatively rare frequency, the patient is screened for an underlying cause. Following investigations an autosomal dominant condition that predisposes patients to neoplasia is confirmed. The syndrome is due to an abnormal gene located on the short arm of chromosome 3 and is associated with visceral cysts and tumours. What cancer is most commonly associated with this patient's syndrome?
explanation:
Renal cell
The commonest cancer associated with the condition is renal cell carcinoma and therefore this should be screened for in any patient confirmed with VHL syndrome.

Adrenal cortex
VHL syndrome is mostly associated with phaeochromocytoma, a tumour of the adrenal gland affecting the inner medulla region, not the outer adrenal cortex.

Ovarian
Defects of the ovaries are not commonly associated with the condition.

Pancreatic
Pancreatic cyst is one of the most common features of VHL syndrome however malignancy of the organ is rare and far less common than renal cell cancers.

Parafollicular cells
Although predominately endocrine organs the thyroid and parathyroid are not commonly affected in VHL syndrome and therefore parafollicular cell cancer is rare.

stem: A 60-year-old gentleman with a background of lumbar spondylosis and chronic back pain presents with gradually worsening bilateral upper limb paraesthesias and leg stiffness. Which one of the investigations below is diagnostic for his likely condition?
explanation:
MRI Cervical spine
The presence of upper limb neurological symptoms indicates that there is pathology either within his cervical spinal cord or brain. Brain disease is more likely to cause unilateral problems. A MRI lumbar spine would therefore not provide a unifying diagnosis here. In the context of known lumbar degenerative spine, degenerative cervical myelopathy is the number one differential for this presentation. An MRI of the cervical spine is the gold standard test where cervical myelopathy is suspected. It may reveal disc degeneration and ligament hypertrophy, with accompanying cord signal change. It is not uncommon for patients to suffer from tandem (cervical and lumbar) stenosis.

Nerve conduction studies and EMG
Other investigations (e.g. nerve conduction studies, EMG) may be performed when the clinical picture is unclear. These can help to exclude mononeuropathies and other lower motor neuron disorders.
