Transient global amnesia is a clinical syndrome of uncertain aetiology, characterised by a discrete episode lasting for a few hours (always less than 24 hours) of anterograde amnesia, retrograde amnesia, repetitive questioning with an absence of other cognitive or neurological impairments. Diagnostic criteria (in addition to the above features) are as follows; reliable witness to episode, the absence of head trauma or loss of consciousness at the onset, preserved personal identity and absence of epileptic features. The clinical features in this case conform to the classical description of transient global amnesia so closely.

Epilepsy
Epilepsy can present with discreet episodes of amnesia. This syndrome is called transient epileptic amnesia. Features that suggest epilepsy are; shorter duration (should be less than 1 hour), multiple attacks, onset on waking from sleep and accompanying epileptic features - e.g. motor automatism, stereotyped behaviours, limb shaking.

Transient psychogenic amnesia
Distinguishing transient global amnesia from transient psychogenic amnesia can be very difficult, however, transient global amnesia is the most likely diagnosis in this case due to the clinical features conforming to the classical description of transient global amnesia so closely.

Brain tumour
There are a small number of case reports where a brain tumour has been implicated in transient global amnesia, however, this is very rare.

Transient ischaemic attack
A transient ischaemic attack can present with isolated amnesia, however, this again is exceedingly rare.

stem: A 20-year-old male patient presents to the GP surgery with a 2-year history of upper back pain, shoulder and arm weakness. On inspection, you notice that he has an asymmetric smile. On further examination, there is marked weakness and wasting of the right facial muscles, right trapezius, deltoid and biceps muscles. There is also winging of the right scapula. There is some weakness and wasting of the same muscle groups on the left side but to a much lesser extent. A type of muscular dystrophy is suspected. What is the inheritance pattern of this condition?
explanation:
Autosomal dominant
Facioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy is an autosomal dominant disorder. This patient presents with the classic appearance of facioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy, which is an autosomal dominant disorder. There is typically an asymmetric pattern.

Autosomal recessive
The other inheritance patterns are not applicable to this condition.

X-linked recessive
The other inheritance patterns are not applicable to this condition.

X-linked dominant
The other inheritance patterns are not applicable to this condition.

Idiopathic
This condition is not idiopathic.

stem: A 31-year-old woman presents with a 4 month history of headache. She has brought a headache diary which demonstrates that her symptoms are present on around 20-25 days of each month. The headache is typically unilateral and she is currently taking paracetamol 1g qds and ibuprofen 400mg tds everyday to try and relieve her symptoms. A diagnosis of medication overuse headache is suspected. What is the most appropriate management?
explanation:
Abruptly stop analgesics
Medication overuse headache simple analgesia + triptans: stop abruptly opioid analgesia: withdraw gradually This answer may seem counterintuitive but it is line with recent guidelines from SIGN, please see the link provided.

stem: A 36-year-old man presents with 4 days of progressive limb weakness and difficulty mobilising. He describes the upper arms and legs as having been affected first, followed by the lower limbs and now the digits. Alongside this, he is also experiencing double vision. He has no significant past medical history but did experience suspected food poisoning with diarrhoea 2 weeks ago. On examination, power is 1/5 in all limbs. Tendon reflexes are reduced. Ophthalmoplegia is evident on cranial nerve examination. What antibody is classically associated with the underlying condition?
explanation:
Anti-GQ1b
Miller Fisher syndrome - areflexia, ataxia, ophthalmoplegia. This patient's presentation is most suggestive of Miller-Fisher syndrome (MFS), a variant of Guillain-Barre syndrome (GBS). This is an immunemediated demyelination of the peripheral nervous system, classically triggered by an infection such as Campylobacter jejuni - the history of diarrhoea alludes to this. As seen here, MFS presents with descending paralysis, rather than the ascending paralysis seen in other forms of GBS, along with ophthalmoplegia and areflexia. It is most strongly associated with the anti-GQ1b antibody, which is present in 90% of cases.

Anti muscle-specific tyrosine kinase (anti-MuSK)
Anti-MuSK antibody is incorrect. This is associated with myasthenia gravis (MG), not MFS. MG would instead present with excessive fatiguability and diurnal variation, and reflexes would be preserved. This scenario is more in keeping with MFS.

Anti-GM1
The anti-GM1 antibody is associated with GBS. However, it is only present in 25% of patients. With regard to MFS specifically, anti-GQ1b is the correct answer.

Anti-acetylcholine receptor (anti-AChR)
The anti-AChR antibody is associated with MG. This would instead present with diurnal variation, excessive fatiguability and preserved reflexes, whereas the scenario here is more fitting with MFS.

Anti-voltage-gated calcium channel (anti-VGCC)
The anti-VGCC antibody is associated with Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (LEMS). This is typically a paraneoplastic disorder and is often a differential of MG, although LEMS typically shows improvement following exercise, rather than excessive fatiguability. The history of diarrhoea in this scenario, along with descending paralysis, favours a diagnosis of MFS.

stem: A 72-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by her daughter who reports sudden onset confusion 3 hours ago. The patient speaks fluently in long sentences but uses incorrect words and makes up words that don't exist. She appears unaware of these errors. When asked to follow simple commands, she seems unable to understand. Examination reveals a right homonymous hemianopia. CT head shows an acute infarct. Which anatomical area is most likely affected?
explanation:
Superior temporal gyrus
Wernicke's aphasia is due to a lesion of the superior temporal gyrus. This patient presents with classic features of Wernicke's (receptive) aphasia: fluent speech with paraphasic errors and neologisms ('word salad'), impaired comprehension, and lack of awareness of errors. The superior temporal gyrus, located in the posterior superior temporal lobe, contains Wernicke's area which is responsible for language comprehension and the formation of coherent speech content. It is typically supplied by the inferior division of the left middle cerebral artery. Lesions in this area disrupt the ability to understand spoken and written language, and whilst speech remains fluent with normal prosody and rhythm, the content is nonsensical due to word substitutions and invented words. The associated right homonymous hemianopia suggests involvement of the left optic radiation, consistent with a posterior left hemisphere stroke affecting the temporal lobe.

Inferior frontal gyrus
Inferior frontal gyrus contains Broca's area and lesions here cause Broca's (expressive) aphasia. This is characterised by non-fluent, effortful, halting speech with relatively preserved comprehension. Patients are typically aware of their errors and become frustrated. The speech pattern described in this scenario is fluent, making Broca's aphasia unlikely. Additionally, Broca's area is supplied by the superior division of the middle cerebral artery and would not typically cause a homonymous hemianopia.

Arcuate fasciculus
Arcuate fasciculus is the white matter tract connecting Wernicke's and Broca's areas. Lesions cause conduction aphasia, characterised by fluent speech with good comprehension but severely impaired repetition. Patients are typically aware of their errors and attempt to self-correct. The key distinguishing feature is that comprehension remains intact in conduction aphasia, unlike in this case where the patient cannot follow simple commands.

Angular gyrus
Angular gyrus lesions can cause alexia with agraphia and are associated with Gerstmann syndrome (agraphia, acalculia, finger agnosia, and leftright disorientation). Whilst the angular gyrus is involved in language processing, particularly reading, it does not typically produce the fluent aphasia with severely impaired comprehension seen in this patient. The clinical picture is more consistent with a primary receptive aphasia.

Precentral gyrus
Precentral gyrus contains the primary motor cortex and lesions cause contralateral weakness rather than aphasia. Whilst strokes affecting this area may be associated with dysarthria (a motor speech disorder affecting articulation), they do not cause the language comprehension and content problems seen in this patient. The fluent nature of the speech and the specific pattern of language dysfunction point to a temporal rather than frontal motor area lesion.

stem: A 72-year-old man is reviewed on the stroke unit 3 days after an ischaemic stroke. A CT head on admission excluded haemorrhage, and he was commenced on aspirin 300mg daily. He is medically stable and plans are being made for his long-term secondary prevention. He has no known drug allergies or history of peptic ulcer disease. What is the most appropriate long-term antiplatelet medication to start after 14 days?
explanation:
Clopidogrel
Clopidogrel is the preferred antiplatelet for secondary prevention following stroke. The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guideline NG128 on Stroke and TIA recommends clopidogrel monotherapy as the first-line long-term antiplatelet for secondary prevention in patients who have had an ischaemic stroke. This patient has had a confirmed ischaemic stroke and is being planned for long-term secondary prevention. The standard UK protocol is to treat with aspirin 300mg daily for the first 14 days, after which the patient should be switched to long-term clopidogrel 75mg once daily. This recommendation is based on evidence suggesting that clopidogrel offers a favourable balance of efficacy in preventing further vascular events and a better safety/tolerability profile compared to the combination of aspirin and dipyridamole.

Aspirin
Aspirin as a long-term monotherapy is not the first-line choice for secondary prevention after an ischaemic stroke. While aspirin 300mg is correctly initiated immediately and continued for 14 days, NICE guidelines recommend switching to a more effective long-term agent thereafter. Long-term aspirin monotherapy is reserved for patients who are intolerant of or have a contraindication to clopidogrel. As the patient in the scenario has no known allergies or contraindications, clopidogrel is the preferred agent.

Aspirin plus modified-release dipyridamole
Aspirin plus modified-release dipyridamole was previously the recommended first-line treatment for secondary prevention following an ischaemic stroke. However, NICE guidelines were updated following trials, such as the TARDIS trial, which showed that this combination was not more effective than clopidogrel monotherapy and was associated with a higher rate of bleeding and treatment discontinuation due to side effects (most commonly headache). Therefore, this regimen has been superseded by clopidogrel and is no longer the recommended first-line option.

Apixaban
Apixaban is a direct oral anticoagulant (DOAC). Anticoagulation is the cornerstone of secondary stroke prevention for patients with a cardioembolic source, most commonly atrial fibrillation (AF). The scenario does not provide any evidence to suggest the patient has AF (e.g., an irregularly irregular pulse or known history). In the absence of an indication for anticoagulation, an antiplatelet agent is the appropriate choice for preventing further atherothrombotic events.

Ticagrelor
Ticagrelor is a potent P2Y12 inhibitor, similar to clopidogrel. While it is a key antiplatelet in the management of acute coronary syndromes (often in combination with aspirin), its role in the long-term secondary prevention of ischaemic stroke is not as established as first-line therapy in UK guidelines. NICE recommends clopidogrel as the primary agent for this indication. Using ticagrelor would be an off-guideline choice in this standard post-stroke scenario.

stem: A 34-year-old female with a history of primary generalised epilepsy presents to her GP as she plans to start a family. She currently takes lamotrigine as monotherapy. What advice should be given regarding the prevention of neural tube defects?
options: Folic acid 400 mcg per day once pregnancy has been confirmed
Folic acid 1 mg per day once pregnancy has been confirmed
Folic acid 5 mg per day starting now
Folic acid 10 mg per day starting now
Folic acid 400 mcg per day starting now
explanation:
Folic acid 5 mg per day starting now
The correct answer is that folic acid 5 mg per day should be started now. Women taking anti-epileptic medications, including lamotrigine, have an increased risk of having a baby with neural tube defects. The UK epilepsy guidelines recommend that all women with epilepsy who are planning pregnancy should take high-dose folic acid (5 mg daily) before conception and continue until the end of the first trimester. This higher dose is necessary because anti-epileptic drugs interfere with folate metabolism. Starting before conception is crucial as neural tube closure occurs very early in pregnancy, often before the woman knows she is pregnant.

Folic acid 400 mcg per day once pregnancy has been confirmed
Folic acid 400 mcg per day once pregnancy has been confirmed is incorrect because this is the standard dose recommended for women without risk factors, and waiting until pregnancy is confirmed would be too late to prevent neural tube defects, which develop in the first few weeks after conception.

Folic acid 1 mg per day once pregnancy has been confirmed
Folic acid 1 mg per day once pregnancy has been confirmed is incorrect for the same reasons - the dose is insufficient for women on anti-epileptic medications, and starting after pregnancy confirmation would be too late to provide optimal protection.

Folic acid 10 mg per day starting now
Folic acid 10 mg per day starting now is incorrect because this dose is unnecessarily high and exceeds the recommended dose for women taking anti-epileptic medications. There is no evidence that doses higher than 5 mg provide additional benefit.

Folic acid 400 mcg per day starting now
Folic acid 400 mcg per day starting now is incorrect because although the timing of starting before conception is appropriate, this is the standard dose recommended for women without risk factors and is insufficient for women taking anti-epileptic medications who require the higher 5 mg dose.

stem: A 32-year-old woman is brought to her GP by her husband who is worried about her behaviour. He is concerned that the patient seems to be mentally 'slowing down' and seems increasingly disorientated and clumsy. The patient has been diagnosed with multiple sclerosis and was started on a new medication by her neurologist two months ago. On examination, she has dysarthria and an ataxic gait. A neurology consultation was sought, and the reactivation of a certain polyomavirus was found to be the cause of the new symptoms. What medication had the patient taken that might lead to such a reactivation?
explanation:
Natalizumab
Natalizumab can cause reactivation of the JC virus causing progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML). The correct answer is natalizumab, which can cause reactivation of the John Cunningham virus (JC) leading to progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML). The symptoms of progressive ataxia, dysarthria, cognitive impairment and generalised weakness raise the possibility of progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) and this is further supported by the identification of a polyomavirus cause. Natalizumab is a recombinant monoclonal antibody used in the management of multiple sclerosis (MS). It can cause reactivation of the (JC) virus, which causes PML when it infects the oligodendrocytes.

Beta-interferon
Beta-interferon can be used in the management of MS but is very rarely associated with PML. It is not as effective as newer medications such as natalizumab.

Glatiramer acetate
Glatiramer acetate is an immunomodulating drug used to treat MS that is less effective than newer monoclonal antibody therapies such as natalizumab. There is no association with PML.

Ocrelizumab
Ocrelizumab is a humanized anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody used to treat MS but is only very rarely associated with PML.

Riluzole
Riluzole is not used in the treatment of MS, it is used in the management of motor neurone disease.

stem: A 28-year-old woman attends neurology outpatient clinic for review. She underwent a lumbar puncture 36 hours ago as part of investigation for suspected multiple sclerosis. She reports a severe headache that began yesterday afternoon. The headache is significantly worse when standing and improves markedly when lying flat. Neurological examination is normal. Paracetamol provides minimal relief. Which modification to the lumbar puncture technique would have been most likely to prevent this complication?
options: Removing a smaller volume of cerebrospinal fluid
Ensuring bed rest for 4 hours post-procedure
Replacing the stylet before needle withdrawal
explanation:
Using a pencil point needle
The use of pencil point (atraumatic) needles reduces the risk of post-lumbar puncture headache. Using a pencil point needle is the correct answer and represents the most effective modification to reduce post-lumbar puncture headache risk. Pencil point (atraumatic) needles have a rounded tip with a side opening for CSF flow, which separates rather than cuts dural fibres during insertion. This design allows the dura to re-seal more effectively after needle withdrawal, significantly reducing CSF leakage through the puncture site. Multiple studies have demonstrated that pencil point needles substantially reduce the incidence of post-dural puncture headache compared to conventional cutting needles. The mechanism relates to the preservation of dural architecture - by separating rather than severing collagen fibres, the dural defect is smaller and closes more readily. This patient's presentation is classic for post-dural puncture headache with its positional nature (worse upright, better recumbent) and timing within 48 hours of the procedure. Had a pencil point needle been used initially, her risk of developing this complication would have been markedly reduced.

Using a smaller gauge needle
Using a smaller gauge needle is partially correct as smaller needles do reduce the risk of post-lumbar puncture headache by creating a smaller dural defect. However, the evidence suggests that needle type (pencil point versus cutting) has a more significant impact on headache incidence than needle size alone. While using both a smaller gauge and a pencil point needle would be ideal, if only one modification could be made, switching to a pencil point design would provide greater benefit. The question asks for the modification most likely to prevent the complication, making needle type the superior answer.

Removing a smaller volume of cerebrospinal fluid
Removing a smaller volume of cerebrospinal fluid is incorrect as the volume of CSF removed during lumbar puncture has not been shown to influence the risk of post-dural puncture headache. The headache results from ongoing CSF leakage through the dural puncture site rather than from the volume initially removed for diagnostic purposes. Standard diagnostic lumbar puncture typically removes 10-20ml of CSF, and this volume does not correlate with headache incidence in clinical studies.

Ensuring bed rest for 4 hours post-procedure
Ensuring bed rest for 4 hours post-procedure is incorrect as bed rest following lumbar puncture has been extensively studied and does not reduce the incidence of post-dural puncture headache. This is a common misconception, and many centres have abandoned routine post-procedure bed rest based on evidence showing no benefit. The patient can mobilise immediately after the procedure without increasing headache risk, making this modification ineffective for prevention.

Replacing the stylet before needle withdrawal
Replacing the stylet before needle withdrawal would be beneficial and does reduce the risk of post-dural puncture headache, though the evidence for this is less robust than for pencil point needles. The proposed mechanism is that replacing the stylet prevents a strand of arachnoid matter from being drawn into the needle track, which could theoretically maintain a CSF fistula. While this is good practice and should be done, the magnitude of risk reduction is smaller compared to using a pencil point needle design.

stem: A 45-year-old lady presents with a 2-month history of left-hand weakness. She has no past medical history. On examination, there is a mild weakness of the left upper and lower limbs with a right-sided facial weakness which spares the forehead. Where is the lesion?
explanation:
Right pons
A right cerebral lesion would give left upper and lower limb weakness. It would also cause a left-sided facial weakness. A left cerebral lesion would give right upper and lower limb weakness with right facial weakness. A cervical spinal cord lesion would not cause a facial weakness. We are left with the pons. The pons is above the level of decussation of the corticospinal tracts so a pontine lesion would cause a contralateral limb weakness. Based on this information alone you can conclude that option 3 must be the correct answer without needing to understand why it has caused an ipsilateral facial weakness. The facial motor nucleus is located in the pons and supplies the ipsilateral facial muscles.

Right cerebrum
A right cerebral lesion would give left upper and lower limb weakness. It would also cause a left-sided facial weakness.

Left cerebrum
A left cerebral lesion would give right upper and lower limb weakness with right facial weakness.

Cervical spinal cord
A cervical spinal cord lesion would not cause a facial weakness.

stem: A 50-year-old man presents with right-sided ear pain and facial weakness. He had flu-like symptoms of fever and headache for three days before the rash appeared. On examination, there is a right-sided facial nerve palsy. A vesicular rash is seen on otoscopy. How should this patient be managed?
explanation:
Oral aciclovir and corticosteroids
Treatment of Ramsay Hunt syndrome consists of oral aciclovir and corticosteroids. Ramsay Hunt syndrome (herpes zoster oticus) is caused by the reactivation of the varicella-zoster virus in the geniculate ganglion of the seventh cranial nerve. This patient presents with typical features of the disease including ear pain, facial nerve palsy, and a vesicular rash around the ear. Other features include vertigo and tinnitus. Full recovery is more likely if antiviral treatment is started within 72 hours of the onset of symptoms. First-line treatment includes aciclovir 800 mg orally five times daily for 7 days and prednisone 60 mg orally daily for 5 days. Steroids are thought to be helpful in Ramsay-Hunt syndrome due to their strong anti-inflammatory action. This is thought to reduce oedema in the affected nerves and result in shorter disease duration. However, trial evidence supports combining aciclovir and steroids, rather than steroids alone. There is evidence that treating Ramsay Hunt syndrome with a combination of oral aciclovir and steroids reduces disease severity and duration.

Corticosteroids only
Steroids are thought to be helpful in Ramsay-Hunt syndrome due to their strong anti-inflammatory action. This is thought to reduce oedema in the affected nerves and result in shorter disease duration. However, trial evidence supports combining aciclovir and steroids, rather than steroids alone.

Intravenous aciclovir
Generally, unless the patient is systemically unwell, aciclovir is given orally rather than intravenously for Ramsay-Hunt syndrome.

Oral aciclovir only
Trial evidence supports combining aciclovir and steroids, rather than aciclovir alone.

Reassurance
Reassurance alone is an incorrect answer. There is evidence that treating Ramsay Hunt syndrome with a combination of oral aciclovir and steroids reduces disease severity and duration.

stem: Which one of the following antibodies are associated with painful sensory neuropathy in patients with small cell lung cancer?
explanation:
Anti-Hu
The correct answer is Anti-Hu. Anti-Hu antibodies are associated with paraneoplastic neurological syndromes, including painful sensory neuropathy, which often precedes the diagnosis of small cell lung cancer. These antibodies target neuronal cells leading to various neurological manifestations including peripheral neuropathy. The presence of these antibodies in a patient presenting with unexplained neurological symptoms should prompt a search for an underlying malignancy, particularly small cell lung cancer.

Anti-Ri
Anti-Ri antibodies are also associated with paraneoplastic neurological syndromes but they are most commonly linked with opsoclonus-myoclonus syndrome (dancing eyes-dancing feet syndrome) and rarely with sensory neuropathy. They are typically seen in patients with breast cancer or ovarian cancer, rather than small cell lung cancer.

Anti-GAD
Anti-GAD (glutamic acid decarboxylase) antibodies are primarily associated with type 1 diabetes mellitus and stiff person syndrome. They target the enzyme GAD that is involved in the synthesis of gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA), an inhibitory neurotransmitter in the brain. They do not have a specific link to painful sensory neuropathy or small cell lung cancer.

Anti-Ro
Anti-Ro, also known as SS-A, is one of the autoantibodies produced in Sjogren's syndrome and systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). It is not specifically linked to any paraneoplastic syndromes or malignancies.

Anti-Yo
Anti-Yo antibodies are related to paraneoplastic cerebellar degeneration and predominantly found in patients with gynaecological cancers such as ovarian and breast cancers. They do not have a direct association with painful sensory neuropathy or small cell lung cancer.

stem: A 19-year-old female university student presents to the first seizure clinic after her flatmate became worried she had a fit first thing in the morning after a night out. This seizure is the first she has had in her entire life. She does not drink or take recreational drugs but did feel sleep-deprived and dizzy prior to the seizure. The flatmate shows a video that reveals the seizure appearing to be tonic-clonic in nature, involving arms and legs, no incontinence, no tongue-biting and no post-ictal drowsiness. Blood tests, lumbar puncture, CT head, MRI brain and electroencephalogram (EEG) are all unremarkable. How long should this patient be advised they cannot drive for?
explanation:
6 months
Patients cannot drive for 6 months following a first unprovoked or isolated seizure if brain imaging and EEG are normal. 6 months is the correct option. The above seizure at this stage is most likely a result of vasovagal syncope due to exhaustion and sleep deprivation. Vasovagal syncope can result in collapse and subsequent jerking movements of the limbs, with a lack of epileptic seizure-associated symptoms such as incontinence, tongue-biting or post-ictal confusion. If the brain imaging and EEG are normal after a first seizure, the patient must be informed that they cannot drive for 6 months after the date of the seizure.

1 month
1 month is incorrect as it is not a length of period for a driving ban for any seizures.

2 years
2 years is incorrect in this case as this option is too long for this type of seizure described.

3 months
3 months is incorrect as it is not a length of period for a driving ban for any seizures.

12 months
12 months is an incorrect option in this case. 12 months driving ban applies to individuals who have had an epilepsy diagnosis or due to an abnormality in imaging or EEG. Epileptics who have had no seizures whilst awake for 12 months can return to driving if the Driving and Vehicle Licensing Agency (DVLA) are satisfied with the absence of seizures.

stem: A 48-year-old man presents to his GP with a number of symptoms that have come on over the past few days. His vision is blurred and his right eye is painful, as well as having a generalised headache. On examination, the right eye has deviated inferiorly and laterally. There is visible ptosis of the upper right lid, and the pupil is dilated. It does not respond to light. This eye does not follow movements well, but the left eye appears unaffected and is normal upon testing. Where is the most likely location of the lesion?
explanation:
Posterior communicating artery
Painful third nerve palsy = posterior communicating artery aneurysm. The cluster of symptoms described here points towards a third (oculomotor) nerve palsy, with the eye classically deviated 'down and out' and the presence of ptosis. The presence of pupil dilation and pain points towards a compressive lesion. This is most commonly a posterior communicating artery aneurysm and requires urgent intervention.

Anterior cerebral artery
The anterior cerebral artery is incorrect. This does not have a direct physical relationship to the oculomotor nerve and would be very unlikely to present with these signs and symptoms.

Internal carotid artery
The internal carotid artery runs through the cavernous sinus alongside the oculomotor nerve. An aneurysm of this can compress the nerve; however, aneurysms of the posterior communicating artery are more likely to do so.

Medulla
The medulla is not relevant to this presentation. Several cranial nerves arise from the medulla - the oculomotor nerve does not.

Oculomotor nucleus
The oculomotor nerve arises from the oculomotor nucleus of the midbrain. A lesion here would be unlikely to cause a painful palsy.

stem: You review a 70-year-old woman four days after she was admitted with a suspected stroke. Unfortunately she has been left with right sided sensory loss affecting her arms more than the legs and a right sided homonymous hemianopia. Functionally she has difficulty dressing her self. Examination of her cranial nerves is unremarkable. What area is the stroke most likely to have affected?
explanation:
Middle cerebral artery
This patient presents with a classic middle cerebral artery (MCA) stroke syndrome. The MCA supplies a large portion of the lateral cerebral hemisphere, including the lateral frontal, temporal, and parietal lobes. The patient's symptoms of right-sided sensory loss affecting the arms more than the legs is consistent with involvement of the left primary sensory cortex in the parietal lobe, which has a larger representation for the upper limbs compared to the lower limbs. The difficulty with dressing herself suggests apraxia, which is also consistent with parietal lobe involvement. While the homonymous hemianopia is more typically associated with posterior cerebral artery territory, it can occur with large MCA strokes that extend posteriorly to involve the optic radiations.

Lacunar
Lacunar strokes are small infarcts (typically <15mm) in the deep white matter, basal ganglia, or brainstem, caused by occlusion of small penetrating arteries. They typically present with one of five classic syndromes: pure motor hemiparesis, pure sensory stroke, ataxic hemiparesis, dysarthria-clumsy hand syndrome, or sensorimotor stroke. The combination of sensory loss, homonymous hemianopia, and apraxia (difficulty dressing) indicates a larger cortical stroke rather than a lacunar infarct.

Anterior cerebral artery
The anterior cerebral artery (ACA) supplies the medial surface of the frontal and parietal lobes, including the lower limb motor and sensory cortices. ACA strokes typically cause contralateral lower limb weakness and sensory loss, with relative sparing of the face and upper limb. This patient's presentation with arm sensory loss greater than leg involvement is the opposite pattern to what would be expected in an ACA stroke. Additionally, homonymous hemianopia is not a feature of ACA territory infarcts.

Posterior cerebral artery
While the posterior cerebral artery (PCA) does supply the occipital lobe and medial temporal lobe, and PCA strokes commonly cause homonymous hemianopia, they typically do not cause the pattern of sensory loss described (arms more than legs) or the functional difficulty with dressing (suggesting parietal lobe involvement). PCA strokes may cause visual field defects, alexia, colour agnosia, and sometimes memory impairment, but not the combination of symptoms presented in this case.

Posterior inferior cerebellar artery
The posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA) supplies the inferior cerebellum and lateral medulla. PICA territory infarcts typically present with Wallenberg syndrome (lateral medullary syndrome), characterised by ipsilateral facial sensory loss, ipsilateral Horner's syndrome, ipsilateral cerebellar signs, ipsilateral palatal weakness, and contralateral spinothalamic sensory loss. The patient's presentation with homonymous hemianopia and cortical sensory loss affecting the arm more than the leg is not consistent with a PICA territory infarct.

stem: A 62-year-old man is referred to the neurology clinic with worsening symptoms over the past few months. The neurologist suspects the patient has progressive supranuclear palsy. Which one of the following features is least likely to be seen in this patient?
explanation:
Impairment of horizontal gaze
Impairment of vertical gaze is seen in progressive supranuclear palsy. Horizontal gaze impairment is sometimes seen later as the disease progresses, but would be atypical in a newly diagnosed patient.

stem: A 67-year-old man is reviewed in the neurology clinic due to concerns about increasing clumsiness. Examination reveals an ataxic gait and increased upper limb tone with cog-wheel rigidity. Blood pressure is 135/80 lying and 95/70 standing. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Multiple system atrophy
Whilst postural hypotension may be seen in Parkinson's disease the ataxic gait points towards a diagnosis of multiple system atrophy.

Parkinson's disease
Whilst postural hypotension may be seen in Parkinson's disease the ataxic gait points towards a diagnosis of multiple system atrophy.

stem: A 76-year-old man presents with an 18-month history of neck stiffness. He complains of numbness in his fingers and difficulty picking up small objects. Recently he has felt increasingly unsteady and had a fall. On examination, he has hyperreflexia in his arms and legs. Which of the following is the most appropriate management plan?
explanation:
Cervical decompression surgery
Cervical spondylitic myelopathy is caused by advanced osteoarthritis of the cervical spine causing compression of the cervical cord. The most likely diagnosis is cervical spondylotic myelopathy. All patients with cervical spondylotic myelopathy should be assessed by a spinal surgeon. Surgery is recommended in patients with moderate or severe cervical spondylotic myelopathy and in those with disease progression. Decompressive surgery can halt disease progression and improve pain, function, and quality of life.

Infliximab
Infliximab is not indicated for cervical spondylotic myelopathy.

Steroids
Steroids are not the primary treatment for cervical spondylotic myelopathy.

Carpal tunnel surgery
Carpal tunnel surgery is not indicated for cervical spondylotic myelopathy.

Riluzole
Riluzole is not indicated for cervical spondylotic myelopathy.

stem: A 55-year-old man presents to his GP with visual disturbance. On examination, the patient is noted to have visual field abnormalities; he is unable to perceive stimuli in the superior temporal field of his left eye and the superior nasal field of his right eye. The GP requests an MRI urgently. Where is a lesion most likely to be found?
explanation:
Right temporal lobe
Right temporal lobe is correct. A lesion here would produce a left-sided homonymous superior quadrantanopia as described in the question stem.

Left parietal lobe
Left parietal lobe is incorrect. This would produce a right-sided homonymous inferior quadrantanopia.

Left temporal lobe
Left temporal lobe is incorrect. A lesion here would cause right-sided homonymous superior quadrantanopia.

Optic chiasm
Optic chiasm is incorrect. This would cause bitemporal hemianopia.

Right parietal lobe
Right parietal lobe is incorrect. A lesion here would result in a left-sided homonymous inferior quadrantanopia.

stem: A 28-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with a 3-day history of fever, malaise, and a painful rash that began on her face and chest before spreading to her limbs. The rash consists of target-like lesions with central blistering. She has painful oral ulceration and conjunctival injection. She was started on lamotrigine 6 weeks ago following her first generalised tonic-clonic seizure. Examination reveals widespread epidermal detachment affecting approximately 8% of her body surface area. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
options: Discontinue lamotrigine and start high-dose corticosteroids
Discontinue lamotrigine and provide supportive care
Continue lamotrigine and start topical corticosteroids
Discontinue lamotrigine and start intravenous immunoglobulin
Continue lamotrigine and start oral antihistamines
explanation:
Discontinue lamotrigine and provide supportive care
This patient presents with classic features of Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS), a severe cutaneous adverse reaction characterised by target-like lesions, mucosal involvement, and epidermal detachment affecting less than 10% of body surface area. Lamotrigine is a well-recognised cause of SJS, particularly within the first 8 weeks of treatment. The immediate priority is discontinuation of the offending drug and supportive care including fluid management, wound care, pain control, and monitoring for complications such as secondary infection. Early recognition and drug cessation is crucial as continued exposure can lead to progression to toxic epidermal necrolysis. Supportive care in a burns unit or intensive care setting may be required depending on severity.

Discontinue lamotrigine and start high-dose corticosteroids
While drug discontinuation is essential, the use of systemic corticosteroids in SJS/TEN remains controversial. Current evidence suggests corticosteroids may increase the risk of complications including secondary infection and delayed healing, and they are generally not recommended in established SJS/TEN.

Continue lamotrigine and start topical corticosteroids
Continuing the causative medication would be dangerous and could lead to progression to toxic epidermal necrolysis, which carries significant mortality. Topical treatments are insufficient for this systemic condition.

Discontinue lamotrigine and start intravenous immunoglobulin
Discontinue lamotrigine and start intravenous immunoglobulin is partially correct regarding drug cessation but IVIG use in SJS/TEN lacks strong evidence and is not considered first-line treatment. Some studies suggest potential benefit but this remains controversial.

Continue lamotrigine and start oral antihistamines
This approach fails to address the serious nature of SJS and continuing the causative drug could be life-threatening. Antihistamines are inadequate treatment for this severe condition.

stem: A 71-year-old man is admitted to the Emergency Department. His family report that since yesterday he has been very 'clumsy' and unsteady on his feet. This morning he started to complain of numbness down his left side. On examination you notice that he has a right-sided Horner's syndrome and horizontal nystagmus. Examination of the peripheral nervous system confirms the sensory loss on the left side. Where is the lesion most likely to be?
explanation:
Posterior inferior cerebellar artery
The correct answer is Posterior inferior cerebellar artery. This patient's clinical presentation with ataxia, sensory loss on the left side, right-sided Horner's syndrome, and horizontal nystagmus is consistent with lateral medullary syndrome, also known as Wallenberg syndrome. Lateral medullary syndrome is caused by a lesion in the dorsolateral part of the medulla oblongata, which is supplied by the posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA). PICA occlusion results in ischemia to this region and causes these characteristic neurological deficits.

Lateral sinus thrombosis
Lateral sinus thrombosis is an incorrect answer because it typically presents with symptoms such as headache, fever, ear pain, and tenderness over the mastoid process due to venous congestion and increased intracranial pressure. It would not cause the specific pattern of sensory loss and other neurological findings seen in this patient.

Posterior cerebral artery
Posterior cerebral artery occlusion primarily affects the occipital lobe and can result in visual field deficits (homonymous hemianopia), memory impairment, or cortical blindness. The patient's symptoms do not fit this vascular territory.

Middle cerebral artery
Middle cerebral artery occlusion typically presents with contralateral hemiparesis and/or sensory loss affecting mainly the face and upper extremity, aphasia if dominant hemisphere is affected or neglect if nondominant hemisphere is affected. It does not explain Horner's syndrome or nystagmus found in this patient.

Anterior inferior cerebellar artery
Anterior inferior cerebellar artery occlusion can lead to lateral pontine syndrome (also known as AICA syndrome) which may present with vertigo, hearing loss, ipsilateral facial paralysis or paresis, ataxia and nystagmus. However, it does not cause contralateral sensory loss or Horner's syndrome as seen in this patient.

stem: A 21-year-old man presents with a short history of severe headache, fever and neck stiffness. An initial CT brain is normal and you proceed to perform a lumbar puncture. His lumbar puncture results are as follows. Appearance Cloudy Opening pressure 31cmCSF (5 - 20) WBC count 357 cells/µL (99% polymorphs) (<1) Glucose 0.4mmol/L (2.5 - 3.5) Protein 1.3g/L (0.18 - 0.45) The patient is started on IV antibiotics and steroids and after a few days begins to recover. He asks you about his prognosis and asks if he is likely to be left with any long-lasting effects of this illness. What is the most common complication of his condition?
explanation:
Sensorineural hearing loss
Sensorineural hearing loss is the most common complication following meningitis. This patient has bacterial meningitis. His history is suggestive of meningitis and this is confirmed on the lumbar puncture. He has a high white cell count, high protein and low glucose which are the typical findings of bacterial meningitis. There is also the high opening pressure and the cloudy CSF which suggest infection. All of the above options can be complications of meningitis but sensorineural hearing loss is the most common, occurring in 34% of cases.

Adrenal insufficiency
Adrenal insufficiency is incorrect. It is a rare but recognised complication of meningococcal meningitis and is caused by adrenal haemorrhage. This is known as Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome.

Cognitive impairment
Cognitive impairment is also incorrect as it occurs in about 9% of cases.

Conductive hearing loss
Conductive hearing loss is not correct. Meningitis does not cause conductive hearing loss but does cause sensorineural hearing loss as described above.

Epilepsy
Epilepsy is incorrect. Ongoing seizures are present following 13% of cases of bacterial meningitis.

stem: A 33-year-old Indian man presented with a 5-day history of fevers, vomiting and dizziness. He had recently come back from a trip to Kerala and had been treated with a two-week course of clarithromycin for a bout of prolonged severe sinusitis by his GP. This was due to the fact that he had been suffering from severe frontal headaches, difficulty sleeping and periorbital swelling. He has a background of tuberculosis (TB) and is currently on treatment with rifampicin and isoniazid. On examination, there was some slurring dysarthria and mild coarse nystagmus to the left. His observation shows a temperate of 38.3ºC, pulse 93 beats per minute, blood pressure 120/80mmHg and oxygen saturation 93% on room air. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Cerebellar abscess
Cerebellar abscesses are most commonly caused by otogenic diseases like mastoiditis and sinusitis infections. Brain abscesses are focal areas of intracerebral pus collection which occur due to a number of causes. In particular, cerebellar abscesses most commonly occur due to infections such as mastoiditis and sinusitis infections.

TB meningitis
TB meningitis would present with fever and chills, neck stiffness, photophobia associated with mental changes.

Cerebellar metastases
Cerebellar metastases would present with headaches (the most common symptom of brain metastases), nausea, vomiting, difficulty walking, seizures with speech disturbance.

Cerebellar haemorrhage
Cerebellar haemorrhage is a more acute vascular event which would have a quicker onset and likely present with stronger neurological signs with sudden onset headache, dizziness, vomiting, vertigo, truncal ataxia and impairment of consciousness.

Chronic sinusitis
Chronic sinusitis is referred to when the cavities around nasal passages known as sinuses - remain inflamed and swollen for at least 12 weeks, in spite of various treatment attempts.

stem: A 62-year-old man with a history of hypertension and epilepsy is noted to have gingival hyperplasia on examination in the cardiology clinic. Which one of the following drugs is most likely to be responsible?
explanation:
Nifedipine
Nifedipine is a calcium channel blocker used in the treatment of hypertension. One of its well-documented side effects is gingival hyperplasia, which occurs due to an overgrowth of the gum tissue. The exact mechanism of this side effect is not fully understood but it's suggested that nifedipine may alter collagen metabolism, thereby leading to an accumulation of extracellular matrix and resultant gingival overgrowth.

Sodium valproate
Sodium valproate is an antiepileptic drug used for the management of seizures. Its common side effects include gastrointestinal disturbances, tremor, weight gain and hair loss. Gingival hyperplasia is not typically associated with sodium valproate use.

Lisinopril
Lisinopril is an angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor used in the management of hypertension and heart failure. Common side effects are cough, dizziness, rash and renal impairment. It does not commonly cause gingival hyperplasia.

Atorvastatin
Atorvastatin belongs to the statin group of drugs and is primarily used for lowering cholesterol levels in patients at high risk of cardiovascular disease. While it can cause various side effects such as myalgia, hepatic impairment or even rhabdomyolysis in severe cases, gingival hyperplasia isn't a known complication associated with atorvastatin use.

Carbamazepine
Carbamazepine, another antiepileptic drug like sodium valproate, has several potential adverse effects including dizziness, ataxia and blood dyscrasias but it doesn't typically result in gingival hyperplasia either.

stem: A 33-year-old man is seen in the Emergency Department with a fall. He is a known alcoholic and drank a bottle of vodka and 2 cans of cider in the last 24 hours. He is started on a chlordiazepoxide reducing regimen by the junior doctor. He is post-taken by the medical consultant who examines him requests that he is urgently started on Pabrinex as he has features consistent with Wernicke's encephalopathy. Which of the following is a feature of Wernicke's encephalopathy?
explanation:
Ophthalmoplegia
Confusion, gait ataxia, nystagmus + ophthalmoplegia are features of Wernicke's encephalopathy. A useful mnemonic to remember the features of Wernicke's encephalopathy is CAN OPEN: Confusion, Ataxia, Nystagmus, Ophthalmoplegia, PEripheral Neuropathy.

Dysarthria
Dysarthria and tremor are multifactorial symptoms of neurological/systemic disease.

Retrograde amnesia
Retrograde amnesia and confabulation are features of Korsakoff's psychosis.

Confabulation
Retrograde amnesia and confabulation are features of Korsakoff's psychosis.

Tremor
Dysarthria and tremor are multifactorial symptoms of neurological/systemic disease.

stem: A 25-year-old female with a history of bilateral vitreous haemorrhage is referred due to progressive ataxia. What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Von Hippel-Lindau syndrome
Von Hippel-Lindau syndrome is the correct diagnosis in this case. The combination of bilateral vitreous haemorrhage and progressive ataxia in a young patient strongly suggests Von Hippel-Lindau syndrome (VHL). VHL is an autosomal dominant condition characterised by the development of multiple tumours, particularly retinal and cerebellar haemangioblastomas. The retinal haemangioblastomas can cause vitreous haemorrhage, while cerebellar haemangioblastomas typically present with progressive ataxia. The age of presentation is typically in young adulthood, consistent with this 25-year-old patient.

Neurofibromatosis type I
Neurofibromatosis type I is incorrect because while it can affect the nervous system, it typically presents with café-au-lait spots, axillary freckling, and cutaneous neurofibromas. Ocular manifestations usually include Lisch nodules and optic pathway gliomas, not vitreous haemorrhage. Ataxia is not a typical presenting feature.

Neurofibromatosis type II
Neurofibromatosis type II is incorrect because it characteristically presents with bilateral vestibular schwannomas leading to hearing loss and tinnitus. While it can cause various ocular problems, including cataracts and retinal hamartomas, vitreous haemorrhage is not typical. The predominant neurological symptoms are usually related to VIII nerve dysfunction rather than ataxia.

Tuberose sclerosis
Tuberose sclerosis is incorrect because its classic triad includes seizures, learning disability, and facial angiofibromas. While it can cause retinal hamartomas, these rarely cause vitreous haemorrhage. Cerebellar involvement causing ataxia is not a typical feature of tuberose sclerosis.

Sarcoidosis
Sarcoidosis is incorrect because while it can cause both neurological and ocular manifestations, the pattern would be different. Ocular sarcoidosis typically causes uveitis rather than vitreous haemorrhage, and neurological involvement usually presents with cranial nerve palsies, meningitis, or mass lesions. The combination of bilateral vitreous haemorrhage and ataxia would be unusual for sarcoidosis.

stem: A 62-year-old woman is taken to the emergency department by her son, after she reported experiencing sudden-onset weakness of the legs. On examination, she has spastic paresis bilaterally of the lower limbs. A full neurological examination is conducted and she is also found to have loss of pain and temperature sensation of the lower limbs. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Subacute combined degeneration of the cord
explanation:
Anterior spinal artery syndrome
Bilateral spastic paresis and loss of pain and temperature sensation - anterior spinal artery occlusion. The correct answer is anterior spinal artery syndrome - this is due to occlusion of the anterior spinal artery. This is a rare occurrence, affecting the lateral corticospinal and spinothalamic tracts and the level of and below the lesion. It results in bilateral spastic paresis and bilateral loss of temperature and pain sensation.

Brown-Sequard syndrome
Brown-Sequard syndrome is also rare and refers to hemisection of the cord. This would affect the lateral corticospinal tract, spinothalamic tract and dorsal columns. It results in a unique picture of ipsilateral spastic paresis below the lesion, ipsilateral loss of proprioception and vibration sensation, and contralateral loss of pain and temperature sensation. The scenario described here is more in keeping with anterior spinal artery occlusion.

Multiple sclerosis
Multiple sclerosis usually presents asymmetrically, with varying tracts involved - rather than symmetrically as seen here.

Subacute combined degeneration of the cord
Subacute combined degeneration of the cord (usually due to vitamin B12 deficiency) affects the lateral corticospinal tract, dorsal columns and spinocerebellar tracts. It also results in bilateral spastic paresis, similarly to the condition seen here, but would lead to bilateral loss of proprioception and vibration sensation, rather than pain and temperature sensation.

Syringomyelia
Syringomyelia affects the ventral horns and lateral spinothalamic tract. It results in flaccid paresis, rather than spastic paresis, but also causes loss of pain and temperature sensation.

stem: Six months ago, a 33-year-old female patient attended her GP with recurrent episodes of unilateral headache with aura. The GP diagnosed her with migraine and advised the use of paracetamol as needed, and provided a repeat prescription of sumatriptan. She has attended her GP surgery again today to discuss the headaches. She explains that sumatriptan and paracetamol adequately suppressed the migraine symptoms, and so she started taking them both daily, or every other day, in the hope of preventing the migraines altogether. Over the past couple of months, however, the headaches have been recurring almost-daily, and sometimes more intensely than prior to starting medication. There are no red flags in the history, nor any visual disturbances. She continues to take the medications, although they seem to provide no benefit anymore. Given the likely diagnosis, what is the most appropriate management?
options: Give high-flow oxygen therapy for 15-20 minutes
explanation:
Stop her medications abruptly
The correct answer is stopping her medications abruptly. This patient's history is strongly suggestive of medication overuse headache, given the frequent use of paracetamol and a triptan, and subsequent recurrence of headache symptoms. For simple analgesia and triptans, the guidelines recommend stopping the medications abruptly.

Add ibuprofen
Adding ibuprofen is incorrect - this would not solve the underlying problem of triptan and paracetamol overuse, and may make the headache worse.

Change to subcutaneous sumatriptan
Subcutaneous sumatriptan is incorrect - this is a treatment for cluster headaches, which would present differently to this scenario. A cluster headache history would describe severe, unilateral, orbital pain episodes, associated with at least one of: lacrimation, conjunctival injection, nasal congestion, forehead/facial sweating or flushing.

Withdraw her medications gradually
Withdrawing her medications gradually is incorrect - this is the management for opioid-induced medication overuse headaches.

Give high-flow oxygen therapy for 15-20 minutes
High-flow oxygen therapy for 15-20 minutes is incorrect - this is a treatment for cluster headaches, which would present differently to this scenario. A cluster headache history would describe severe, unilateral, orbital pain episodes, associated with at least one of: lacrimation, conjunctival injection, nasal congestion, forehead/facial sweating or flushing.

stem: A 15-year-old girl and her mother present to the clinic. They describe an episode last week to you. She had been at a sleepover at her friend's house and studying hard for her school examinations. In the morning, when she returned home, she was drinking a cup of tea with her mother and her arm suddenly jerked and the tea flew everywhere. She remained conscious throughout. Her mother also described intermittent 'blank spells' where she notices her daughter staring blankly for a few seconds before recovering. The girl is otherwise well. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy
Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy is classically associated with seizures in the morning/following sleep deprivation. The description of preceding absence episodes followed by myoclonus is most typical of juvenile myoclonic epilepsy. As in this case, the condition most typically occurs in adolescent females following a period of sleep deprivation, suggested by exam stress and sleepovers in this vignette. There is usually a good response to sodium valproate.

Benign rolandic epilepsy
Benign rolandic epilepsy typically occurs in younger children than in this vignette. It also more commonly presents with paraesthesia than myoclonus and absence episodes.

Lennox-Gestaut syndrome
Lennox-Gestaut syndrome presents in early childhood in children younger than described in this vignette. Although it also presents with absence episodes and jerks, 90% of children have an underlying learning difficulty, which is not described in this vignette.

Typical absence seizures
Although this vignette describes absence episodes, typical absence seizures occur in younger children and are not associated with the myoclonus described in this vignette.

West's syndrome
West's syndrome is also known as infantile spasms. This condition occurs in infancy, unlike in this vignette. Children display a typical spasm beginning with flexion of the head, trunk and limbs followed by extension of the arms, which can repeat many times in a row. This condition is also associated with progressive learning difficulties, which is not described in this vignette.

stem: A patient presenting to the emergency department undergoes a CT head scan. The report describes a hypodense collection around the convexity of the brain that is not limited to suture lines. What is the most likely radiological diagnosis?
explanation:
Chronic subdural haematoma
On CT imaging, a chronic subdural haematoma will appear as a hypodense (dark), crescentic collection around the convexity of the brain.

Subarachnoid haemorrhage
Subarachnoid haemorrhage are typically seen as hyperdensity within the basal cisterns and sulci of the subarachnoid space.

Extradural haematoma
Extradural haematomas are limited by suture lines whereas subdural haematomas are not.

Acute subdural haematoma
On CT imaging, acute haematomas appear bright (hyperdense) whereas chronic haematomas appear dark (hypodense).

Intracerebral haematoma
Intraparenchymal haematomas arise within the brain substance.

stem: A 49-year-old man is prescribed procyclidine for Parkinson's disease. What is the mechanism of action?
explanation:
Antimuscarinic
Procyclidine, a drug commonly used in the treatment of Parkinson's disease, works primarily through an antimuscarinic mechanism of action. It blocks muscarinic acetylcholine receptors in the central and peripheral nervous system. This results in a reduction of cholinergic activity which helps to balance the dopamine-acetylcholine ratio in the brain, thereby alleviating symptoms associated with Parkinson's disease such as tremors, rigidity and bradykinesia.

Dopamine receptor agonist
While it is true that some drugs used for Parkinson's disease work by directly stimulating dopamine receptors (e.g., pramipexole and ropinirole), procyclidine does not fall into this category. Its primary mechanism of action is antimuscarinic, rather than dopaminergic.

Decarboxylase inhibitor
Decarboxylase inhibitors like carbidopa or benserazide are often given alongside levodopa to prevent its peripheral conversion to dopamine before reaching the brain. However, this is not how procyclidine works.

Dopamine receptor antagonist
Dopamine receptor antagonists block dopamine receptors and are typically used to treat conditions like schizophrenia or bipolar disorder where there may be an overactivity of dopamine neurotransmission. Using a dopamine antagonist would likely worsen symptoms of Parkinson's disease.

Monoamine Oxidase-B inhibitor
While MAO-B inhibitors such as selegiline and rasagiline do have a role in managing Parkinson's disease by slowing down the breakdown of dopamine in the brain, this does not describe the mechanism of action for procyclidine.

stem: An 80-year-old right-handed woman has recently been admitted with an acute ischaemic stroke affecting part of the left hemisphere. She is seen in clinic a month later. She is able to understand questions and produce fluent connected speech, however she frequently substitutes incorrect sounds. When she makes an error she notices but finds it difficult to correct the error. She is unable to repeat phrases. What type of aphasia does she have?
explanation:
Conduction aphasia
Conduction dysphasia: speech fluent, but repetition poor. Comprehension is relatively intact. This woman has likely had a stroke affecting the arcuate fasciculus in her dominant hemisphere, the connection between Wernicke's and Broca's area. She has conduction aphasia, with fluent speech and good comprehension but word finding difficulties and difficulty repeating phrases.

Anomic aphasia
Anomic aphasia is a deficit of expressive language which results primarily in word finding difficulties.

Broca's aphasia
Broca's aphasia results in non-fluent, laboured and halting speech.

Global aphasia
Global aphasia causes severe expressive and receptive deficits.

Wernicke's aphasia
Wernicke's aphasia results in neologisms and nonsense sentences which is fluent.

stem: A 56-year-old woman comes for review. Around 4 weeks ago she had a blistering rash under her right breast which extended around to the back. A diagnosis of shingles was made. Unfortunately since that time she has been experiencing severe 'shooting' pains. The skin is also very tender to touch. Neither paracetamol nor ibuprofen have helped her symptoms. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
explanation:
Amitriptyline
This lady has developed post-herpetic neuralgia. NICE recommend using amitriptyline, duloxetine, gabapentin or pregabalin first-line.

stem: A 53-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with a sudden-onset, severe headache, describing it as the worst of her life. She had been sitting at her desk when the headache came on. She has associated nausea and vomiting. On examination, she has some neck stiffness and photophobia and appears drowsy. A CT scan shows hyperdense across the basal cisterns and sulci. Which of the following is indicated in managing the complications of this condition?
explanation:
Nimodipine
Nimodipine is used to prevent vasospasm in aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhages. The condition being described here is subarachnoid haemorrhage (SAH), given the sudden-onset severe headache, signs of meningism and CT findings. Nimodipine should be given as a 21-day course to prevent vasospasm - it is a dihydropyridine calcium-channel blocker (CCB) that targets brain vasculature.

Amlodipine
Amlodipine is another dihydropyridine CCB but is not used in the management of SAH. It is commonly used as a first-line drug to manage hypertension in those over 55 years old.

Diltiazem
Diltiazem is a non-dihydropyridine CCB and is used in the management of angina and hypertension - as a non-dihydropyridine CCB, it also slows the heart rate. It is not indicated for SAH.

Felodipine
Felodipine, like amlodipine, is another dihydropyridine CCB. It is also used to manage hypertension, but not SAH.

Nifedipine
Nifedipine is another dihydropyridine CCB. It can also be used to manage hypertension and is also the first-line treatment for the symptoms of Raynaud's syndrome. It is not indicated for SAH.

stem: Which one of the following is least characteristic of Wernicke's encephalopathy?
explanation:
Confabulation
An inability to acquire new memories and confabulation suggests the development of Korsakoff's syndrome.

stem: A 55-year-old man is seen in the neurology clinic with sensory loss. On examination he has loss of fine touch, joint position sense and temperature sensation bilaterally in the lower limbs, extending from his knees down, as well as in his fingertips. His motor function is 5/5 in all four limbs. His medications include: calcichew, alfacalcidol, sodium bicarbonate and ramipril Which of the following is most likely to be the cause of these clinical findings?
explanation:
Chronic kidney disease
Uraemic polyneuropathy is predominantly sensory. Of the above, CKD (leading to uraemia) is the only option to cause a predominantly sensory polyneuropathy.

Guillain-Barre syndrome
Guillain-Barre syndrome and lead poisoning cause a polyneuropathy which is predominantly motor.

Lead poisoning
Guillain-Barre syndrome and lead poisoning cause a polyneuropathy which is predominantly motor.

Polio
Polio and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis affect the anterior horn cells of the motor tract, within the spinal cord. As such, they cause a motor deficit.

Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis
Polio and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis affect the anterior horn cells of the motor tract, within the spinal cord. As such, they cause a motor deficit.

stem: A 63-year-old man is prescribed selegiline for Parkinson's disease. What is the mechanism of action?
explanation:
Monoamine Oxidase-B inhibitor
Selegiline is a selective and irreversible inhibitor of Monoamine Oxidase-B (MAO-B). This enzyme is involved in the breakdown of dopamine in the brain. By inhibiting MAO-B, selegiline increases the availability of dopamine, helping to alleviate symptoms of Parkinson's disease.

Dopamine receptor antagonist
Antagonists block or suppress the action of dopamine receptors rather than enhancing their activity. Using a dopamine receptor antagonist would likely exacerbate Parkinson's symptoms, as this condition is characterized by reduced dopaminergic activity in certain parts of the brain.

Dopamine receptor agonist
While these drugs do indeed mimic the action of dopamine and can be used in Parkinson's disease management, they are not the mechanism by which selegiline works.

Antimuscarinic
Antimuscarinics work by blocking muscarinic acetylcholine receptors and are used to counteract an imbalance between cholinergic and dopaminergic neurotransmission seen in Parkinson's disease. However, selegiline does not have antimuscarinic properties.

Catechol-O-Methyl Transferase inhibitor
These drugs inhibit Catechol-O-Methyl Transferase (COMT), an enzyme that breaks down dopamine and levodopa (a precursor to dopamine often used in treatment). Although COMT inhibitors can be useful adjuncts in treating Parkinson's disease, they represent a different class of drugs from selegiline.

stem: Which one of the following features is most likely to be seen following facial nerve paralysis?
explanation:
Hyperacusis
The correct answer is Hyperacusis, which is an increased sensitivity to sound. In facial nerve (cranial nerve VII) paralysis, such as in Bell's palsy, damage to the nerve affects the stapedius muscle, which is innervated by the stapedial branch of the facial nerve. The stapedius muscle normally dampens loud sounds by pulling on the stapes bone in the middle ear. When this muscle is paralysed, it cannot contract to protect the inner ear from loud sounds, resulting in hyperacusis.

Hyperlacrimation
Hyperlacrimation (excessive tearing) is incorrect because facial nerve paralysis typically causes decreased tear production due to parasympathetic dysfunction affecting the greater petrosal nerve, which supplies the lacrimal gland. In fact, patients often experience dry eye (xerophthalmia) and require artificial tears.

Hyperesthesia
Hyperesthesia (increased sensitivity to touch) is incorrect because the facial nerve is primarily a motor nerve, with some special sensory (taste) and parasympathetic functions. It does not carry general sensory information from the face, which is the role of the trigeminal nerve (CN V).

Hyperalgesia
Hyperalgesia (increased sensitivity to pain) is incorrect for the same reason as hyperesthesia. Pain sensation in the face is carried by the trigeminal nerve, not the facial nerve. Facial nerve lesions do not directly affect pain perception.

Hypersalivation
Hypersalivation (excessive saliva production) is incorrect because facial nerve paralysis typically results in decreased salivation due to parasympathetic dysfunction affecting the chorda tympani nerve, which supplies the submandibular and sublingual salivary glands. Patients often complain of dry mouth (xerostomia).

stem: A 40-year-old man presents with a 4-day history of vertigo. This seems to have followed a viral upper respiratory tract infection in the past week. He is generally fit and well. His symptoms are associated with some nausea but there is no hearing loss or tinnitus. On examination fine horizontal nystagmus is noted. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Vestibular neuronitis
The correct answer is Vestibular neuronitis, which is a self-limiting condition characterised by acute onset vertigo following a viral illness. The patient's presentation is classic: recent viral upper respiratory tract infection, followed by acute vertigo with nausea and horizontal nystagmus, but crucially without auditory symptoms. The vestibular nerve inflammation is typically unilateral, causing an acute vestibular syndrome with preservation of hearing, as the cochlear division is spared.

Viral labyrinthitis
Viral labyrinthitis is incorrect because although it also commonly follows a viral infection and presents with vertigo, it characteristically involves both the vestibular and cochlear portions of the inner ear. Therefore, patients typically present with hearing loss and/or tinnitus in addition to vertigo, which this patient does not have.

Transient ischaemic attack
Transient ischaemic attack is incorrect as vertigo from a TIA is typically brief (minutes), accompanied by other neurological symptoms, and would be unusual to persist for 4 days. Additionally, the history of preceding viral illness and the patient's relatively young age make a vascular cause less likely.

Acoustic neuroma
Acoustic neuroma is incorrect because this benign tumour typically presents with gradual, unilateral hearing loss and tinnitus as primary symptoms. Vertigo may occur but is usually not the predominant feature, and the symptoms develop gradually rather than acutely.

Meniere's disease
Meniere's disease is incorrect because it classically presents with episodic attacks of vertigo lasting 20 minutes to 12 hours, accompanied by fluctuating hearing loss, tinnitus, and aural fullness. This patient's continuous vertigo for 4 days and lack of auditory symptoms make Meniere's disease unlikely.

stem: A 25-year-old man is referred to neurology by his GP. Over the last six months he has been experiencing neck pain and stiffness and arm weakness. He is normally fit and well and denies any history of trauma, bowel or bladder problems or erectile dysfunction. He drinks five pints of beer per week. On examination, there is a small area of erythema with central blistering on his right elbow which he had not noticed previously. Pin-prick sensation is reduced in the C5-6 dermatomes bilaterally. Fine touch, proprioception and vibration sensation are intact throughout. Forearm flexion is weak bilaterally with reduced biceps tendon reflexes. Forearm extension is weak on the right with a brisk triceps reflex. He is alert and orientated. His cranial nerves are intact. His coordination and gait are normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord
explanation:
Syringomyelia
Syringomyelia classically presents with cape-like loss of pain and temperature sensation due to compression of the spinothalamic tract fibres decussating in the anterior white commissure of the spine. This patient is presenting with symptoms consistent with a lesion around the C4-C5 level affecting the anterior white commissure, anterior horns, and the corticospinal tract. The spinothalamic tract (pain and temperature sensation) decussates 1-2 spinal levels above the level of entry in the anterior white commissure. This results in loss of pain/pinprick sensation on examination and a possible unnoticed burn injury e.g., from reaching inside an oven. The anterior horns carry lower motor neurones. These are being affected bilaterally at the level of the lesion, resulting in a lower motor neurone pattern of weakness around the C4-5-6 myotome. In this case, it is causing incomplete paresis (rather than paralysis) of the biceps because biceps is supplied by C5-7 via the musculocutaneous nerve. The corticospinal tract carries upper motor neurones to lower spinal levels. Compression at C4-5 is causing an upper motor neurone pattern below the level of the lesion.

Friedreich's ataxia
Friedreich's ataxia is a genetic progressive neurodegenerative disorder. It causes degeneration of the corticospinal tracts, dorsal columns, and spinocerebellar tracts, as well as hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and diabetes. Symptoms include ataxia, slurred speech, spasticity, dysphagia, limb sensory loss, and vision and hearing loss. Symptoms are usually apparent by adolescence, and the absence of ataxia makes Friedreich's ataxia less likely.

Multiple sclerosis
While multiple sclerosis (MS) is a cause of sensory disturbance and upper motor neurone lesions, diagnosis requires lesions separated in space and time - the lesions may be asymmetrical and at different spinal levels. The lesion pattern here is more suggestive of syringomyelia. Additionally, MS does not typically cause lower motor neurone lesions (apart from cranial nerve lesions and some reports of demyelination affecting the ventral horns).

Subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord
Subacute combined degeneration of the cord (SACD) causes a lesion of the dorsal columns, then later the corticospinal tracts and spinothalamic tract. SACD occurs due to vitamin B12, vitamin E, and copper deficiency. It causes loss of vibration and proprioception (later other sensory modalities), sensory gait ataxia, distal muscle weakness, and dementia. SACD is more common in older adults with malabsorption or poor nutrition.

Syringobulbia
Syringobulbia is a similar disorder to syringomyelia where a syrinx affects the brainstem. It causes cranial nerve abnormalities e.g., trigeminal pain and temperature sensation loss, nystagmus, dysphagia, palatal weakness, and tongue atrophy.

stem: A 55-year-old builder comes to see you about his ongoing back pain. He was diagnosed several months ago with a prolapsed intervertebral disc which is still causing him a lot of pain, limiting his ability to work. He is currently on 75mg of amitriptyline which has been up titrated over several weeks; he reports he has not noticed much improvement. Prior to amitriptyline, he was on pregabalin which was stopped due to side effects. What is the next appropriate step in his management?
explanation:
Stop amitriptyline and start duloxetine
Stopping amitriptyline and starting duloxetine is the correct option. NICE recommends for neuropathic pain that if the first-line drug treatment does not work doctors should try one of the other 3 drugs. They are typically used as monotherapy, i.e. if not working then drugs should be switched, not added. This man has already tried pregabalin which he did not tolerate due to side effects. He is currently on a high dose of amitriptyline which is not controlling his pain.

Add duloxetine
Adding duloxetine is incorrect as drugs should be used as monotherapy.

Add gabapentin
Adding gabapentin is incorrect as drugs should be used as monotherapy. Furthermore, this man has not tolerated pregabalin in the past, this makes gabapentin a less good choice than duloxetine.

Increase amitriptyline
Increasing amitriptyline is incorrect as this man is already on a very high dose of amitriptyline and has not noticed an improvement in his pain. If he was on a lower dose and reported some improvement, increasing the dose should be considered.

Stop amitriptyline and start gabapentin
Stopping amitriptyline and starting gabapentin would be an option. However, this man has previously had side effects with pregabalin, therefore duloxetine is a better option in this case.

stem: A 33-year-old woman presents with a one-week history of strange behaviour, confusion and abnormal movements. She initially exhibited anxiety, but her symptoms have progressed to include disorganised speech and intermittent unresponsiveness. On exam, she is febrile and agitated, with myoclonic jerks of the upper limbs. MRI of the brain shows no abnormalities and cerebrospinal fluid analysis reveals lymphocytic pleocytosis with elevated protein levels. Further testing identifies antibodies against NMDA receptors. What type of cancer is most commonly associated with this patient’s condition?
explanation:
Ovarian teratoma
Ovarian teratoma is associated with Anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis. Ovarian teratoma is strongly associated with anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis, a paraneoplastic autoimmune condition characterised by psychiatric symptoms, seizures, and dyskinesias. This link is due to teratomas often containing neural tissue, which can trigger an autoimmune response against NMDA receptors in the brain. Early recognition of this association is crucial as removal of the teratoma can significantly improve outcomes. Young women, like this patient, are particularly susceptible, and screening for an ovarian teratoma is an essential step in managing anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis.

Breast cancer
Breast cancer is associated with certain paraneoplastic syndromes, such as paraneoplastic cerebellar degeneration mediated by anti-Yo antibodies, but it does not typically lead to anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis. While breast cancer can rarely trigger autoimmune neurological syndromes, the absence of specific neural tissue in the tumour reduces the likelihood of an immune response against NMDA receptors, making it an improbable explanation for this patient’s presentation.

Colorectal adenocarcinoma
Colorectal adenocarcinoma is not associated with paraneoplastic encephalitis or NMDA receptor antibodies. It is typically linked to systemic symptoms like cachexia or local invasion effects rather than autoimmune neurological syndromes. While colorectal cancer can metastasise to the brain, its mechanism is unrelated to the autoimmune encephalitis seen in anti-NMDA receptor conditions, making it an unlikely diagnosis in this patient.

Glioblastoma
Glioblastoma, a primary brain tumour, can cause neurological symptoms such as seizures, personality changes, and cognitive decline due to its mass effect and direct invasion of brain tissue. However, these symptoms are not due to autoimmune mechanisms, and glioblastoma is not associated with anti-NMDA receptor antibodies. The patient’s presentation, combined with normal MRI findings and the presence of NMDA receptor antibodies, rules out glioblastoma as the underlying cause.

Small cell lung cancer (SCLC)
SCLC is associated with paraneoplastic syndromes such as Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome and SIADH, but not anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis. SCLC triggers autoimmune responses against other neuronal components, typically affecting the peripheral nervous system or causing endocrine dysregulation. While SCLC can produce a broad range of paraneoplastic syndromes, its pathology does not involve NMDA receptor antibodies, making it an unlikely cause in this case.
