Indomethacin functions through this mechanism and serves as a non-steroidal antiinflammatory drug (NSAID) for treating short-lasting unilateral neuralgiform headache attacks. These headaches are characterised by intense sharp pain but do not involve papilloedema; therefore, this choice is incorrect.

Serotonin receptor antagonist
Serotonin receptor antagonist is incorrect. Triptans operate via serotonin antagonism and are used primarily for acute migraine management; however, migraines usually manifest as episodic and unilateral rather than constant and global pain without associated papilloedema, rendering this option invalid.

stem: Which one of the following dopamine receptor agonists used in the management of Parkinson's disease is least associated with pulmonary, retroperitoneal and pericardial fibrosis?
explanation:
Ropinirole
The correct answer is Ropinirole. Ropinirole is a non-ergot derived dopamine receptor agonist used in the management of Parkinson's disease. It has been shown to have the least association with pulmonary, retroperitoneal and pericardial fibrosis. This is because ergot-derived dopamine agonists such as Pergolide, Lisuride, Bromocriptine and Cabergoline are associated with an increased risk of these fibrotic reactions due to their mechanism of action on serotonin 5-HT2B receptors which can cause fibrotic changes in tissues.

Pergolide
Pergolide is an ergot-derived dopamine receptor agonist that was widely used in the management of Parkinson's disease. However, it has been withdrawn from several markets including the UK due to its high association with heart valve disease and fibrotic reactions including those affecting the lungs, retroperitoneum and pericardium.

Lisuride
Lisuride, another ergot-derived dopamine receptor agonist has also been linked to serious fibrotic complications although it continues to be used in some countries under strict monitoring for these side effects.

Bromocriptine
Bromocriptine is another ergot derivative that has been associated with pulmonary, retroperitoneal and pericardial fibrosis. Although its use in Parkinson's disease has declined over time due to these safety concerns, it remains available for use in specific clinical scenarios such as hyperprolactinemia.

Cabergoline
Cabergoline, yet another ergot-derived dopamine receptor agonist has also been implicated in causing fibrotic reactions. It carries a black box warning about this risk and requires regular monitoring for signs and symptoms of fibrosis during treatment.

stem: A 66-year-old woman is taken to the emergency department by her son, who suspects that she may have had a stroke. On examination, she has right-sided facial pain and temperature sensation loss. She has left-sided arm and leg pain, with associated temperature sensation loss of the left arm and leg. Ataxia is also demonstrated, as well as nystagmus. Given the findings, which artery is most likely to have been affected?
explanation:
Posterior inferior cerebellar artery
Lateral medullary syndrome can be caused by PICA strokes. The cluster of signs and symptoms described here are indicative of lateral medullary syndrome, also known as Wallenberg syndrome. This is most commonly due to blockage of the posterior inferior cerebellar artery, causing ischaemia of the lateral part of the medulla oblongata in the brainstem. The loss of temperature sensation, and pain, arise from the involvement of the lateral spinothalamic tract.

Anterior cerebral artery
Strokes involving the anterior cerebral artery classically present with contralateral hemiparesis and sensory deficits, with the lower extremities being affected worse than upper. The opposite side of the face being affected in this scenario points more towards lateral medullary syndrome here.

Anterior inferior cerebellar artery
A stroke involving the anterior inferior cerebellar artery would present with symptoms similar to lateral medullary syndrome - this artery supplies the pons and the cluster of signs is known as lateral pontine syndrome. In addition to the findings of lateral medullary syndrome, facial paralysis and deafness would be expected, which are not described in this scenario.

Middle cerebral artery
Middle cerebral artery involvement would present with contralateral hemiparesis, with upper extremities affected more than lower. Contralateral homonymous hemianopia may also be present, and aphasia. These are not mentioned in this scenario.

Posterior cerebral artery
Posterior cerebral artery involvement would present with contralateral homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing, and visual agnosia.

stem: An 80-year-old man presents with sudden-onset difficulty walking and a droopy eyelid. He noticed slurred speech a few weeks ago, but as this resolved after 10 minutes he did not seek medical attention. On general examination, he has an ataxic gait and loss of sensation in his right arm and leg. On examination of his cranial nerves, he has nystagmus to the left, ptosis, meiosis and loss of sensation on the lefthand side of the face. Where is the likely arterial lesion?
explanation:
Posterior inferior cerebellar
Lateral medullary syndrome - PICA lesion - cerebellar signs, contralateral sensory loss & ipsilateral Horner's. Posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA) is the correct answer. Left-sided Horner's syndrome depicted here with cerebellar signs and a contralateral sensory loss of the limbs is consistent with a left-sided PICA infarct. The lateral brainstem signs involve the sympathetic outflow tract, (hence Horner's with ptosis and meiosis), spinocerebellar tract (hence cerebellar signs), the sensory nucleus of cranial nerve V (hence the sensation over the left-hand side of the face would be affected) and spinothalamic tract (hence pain and temperature loss on the contralateral, right side in this case).

Anterior inferior cerebellar
Anterior inferior cerebellar artery (AICA) is incorrect as this does not affect the same region as the PICA and hence produces a different neurological deficit. The AICA lesions are less well known and have been purported to cause central vestibular loss and hearing loss, since the inner ear, lateral pons and anterior inferior cerebellum are supplied.

Pontine
Pontine is incorrect because this artery causes a variety of syndromes, with none of the syndromes creating the lateral medullary syndrome associated with PICA infarct. Pontine infarcts can cause the locked-in syndrome, pure motor hemiparesis, sensorimotor deficits, ataxic hemiparesis and more rarely dysarthria-clumsy hand syndrome.

Posterior cerebral
Posterior cerebral is an incorrect answer. The posterior cerebral artery supplies the occipital lobe therefore an infarct here would cause a visual field loss or homonymous hemianopia to the contralateral side.

Superior cerebellar
Superior cerebellar is an incorrect answer as infarction in the superior cerebellar artery does not cause the brainstem signs seen in this case of PICA infarction. Superior cerebellar artery stroke commonly results in vertigo, dizziness, nystagmus, ataxias and sometimes mild hemiparesis.

stem: A 24-year-old patient is referred to the neurology clinic. She has been experiencing intermittent jerking of her right upper limb. There is no loss of awareness during these episodes. They occur frequently and she finds them distressing. Her past medical history is unremarkable other than an episode of hypoxia at birth. The examination at the time of review is unremarkable. MRI brain Encephalomalacia affecting the left motor cortex Despite the use of levetiracetam, her symptoms persist. What is the most appropriate medication to choose at this point?
explanation:
Lamotrigine
Lamotrigine is the correct answer. The patient presents with simple focal seizures (i.e. seizures affecting one part of the body with preserved awareness). This is likely a consequence of perinatal hypoxic brain injury in this context. The first choice medication in this circumstance to prevent further seizures is either lamotrigine or levetiracetam. If one fails to adequately control seizures, the other is generally trialled.

Carbamazepine
Carbamazepine is incorrect. This is a possible option to treat refractory focal seizures that have not responded to either lamotrigine or carbamazepine. It is not the first-line option.

Clobazam
Clobazam is incorrect. This is typically used as an add-on therapy in difficult-to-control epilepsy on standard treatment. It would not be used as first-line treatment or monotherapy.

Lorazepam
Lorazepam is incorrect. This is used in acute active (typically generalized seizures) treatment. In this context, the patient is not seizing and requires treatment to prevent further seizures. Lorazepam is addictive, short-acting, and can cause drowsiness so this would not be appropriate.

Sodium valproate
Sodium valproate is incorrect. This medication is effective in most forms of epilepsy. However, it is teratogenic and is a less suitable option for women of childbearing age.

stem: A 66-year-old woman presents with a six-month history of urinary frequency and incontinence. She has a background in relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis (MS). A urine dip is normal. What is the most appropriate next step in her management?
options: Ultrasound kidneys, ureters and urinary bladder (KUB)
explanation:
Ultrasound kidneys, ureters and urinary bladder (KUB)
This patient has neurogenic bladder dysfunction secondary to MS. The next appropriate step in her management is thus to arrange an ultrasound KUB, to assess her bladder emptying - this will then determine what treatment options are available to her.

Botulinum toxin type A injections
NICE guidelines state botulinum injections may be considered for the treatment of urinary incontinence in neurological disease but only in patients (without a significant post-void residual volume) who have found anti-cholinergic medication ineffective.

Intermittent self-catheterisation
Intermittent self-catheterisation is only of benefit if the patient has a significant post-void residual volume and ultrasound KUB is first required to assess this. If the patient does not have a significant post-void residual volume, then intermittent self-catheterisation will not be a beneficial treatment option.

Micturating cystogram
A micturating cystogram is a fluoroscopic study of the lower urinary tract, in which contrast is introduced into the bladder using a catheter. It is used to evaluate the anatomy and function of the lower urinary tract system and tends to be the investigation of choice for suspected vesicoureteral reflux. Whilst it can also be used in the assessment of neurogenic bladder dysfunction, it would not be used as a first-line imaging modality and so is not the appropriate next step in this example.

Oxybutynin
Oxybutynin is an anticholinergic medication, which may be of use in neurogenic bladder dysfunction if there is no significant post-void residual volume. If the patient has a significant post-void residual volume, however, the use of anticholinergic medications will likely precipitate urinary retention. As such, US KUB is required to assess bladder emptying before such drugs are trialled.

stem: A 42-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with sudden-onset severe headache that peaked within 2 minutes. She describes it as 'the worst headache of my life' and reports photophobia. Examination reveals neck stiffness but no focal neurological deficit. A non-contrast CT head performed 4 hours after symptom onset shows no abnormalities. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
explanation:
Consider alternative diagnosis
According to current UK guidelines, if a CT head is performed within 6 hours of symptom onset for suspected subarachnoid haemorrhage and is normal, lumbar puncture should not be performed. Instead, clinicians should consider alternative diagnoses. This represents a significant change from previous practice where lumbar puncture was routinely performed after a normal CT. The rationale is that CT scanning within 6 hours has very high sensitivity (approaching 100%) for detecting subarachnoid haemorrhage, making the additional yield from lumbar puncture minimal whilst exposing patients to unnecessary risk and delay in considering other causes of their symptoms.

Lumbar puncture in 8 hours
Lumbar puncture in 8 hours is incorrect. This reflects outdated practice. Previously, lumbar puncture was recommended when CT was normal, with timing at least 12 hours after symptom onset to allow xanthochromia to develop. However, current guidelines specifically advise against lumbar puncture when CT within 6 hours is normal, as the diagnostic yield is extremely low and may delay consideration of alternative diagnoses.

CT angiogram of the head
CT angiogram of the head is not appropriate at this stage. CT angiography is used to identify vascular lesions such as aneurysms or arteriovenous malformations after subarachnoid haemorrhage has been confirmed. Since the CT head is normal and performed within the critical 6-hour window, subarachnoid haemorrhage is effectively excluded, making angiography unnecessary.

MRI brain with gadolinium
MRI brain with gadolinium is not the next appropriate step. Whilst MRI can detect subarachnoid haemorrhage, it is not superior to CT within the acute timeframe and is not recommended as a first-line investigation. The normal CT within 6 hours effectively excludes subarachnoid haemorrhage, making further imaging to detect blood products unnecessary.

Repeat CT head in 12 hours
Repeat CT head in 12 hours is not indicated. The sensitivity of CT for subarachnoid haemorrhage within 6 hours of symptom onset is extremely high, and repeating the scan would not add diagnostic value. This approach would also delay consideration of alternative diagnoses that could explain the patient's thunderclap headache and meningism.

stem: A 40-year-old presents with generalised weakness and visual issues. She reports first noticing some blurring and double vision 4 days ago. A day later she then developed difficulty getting up from a chair and lifting her arms up which seems to have spread now to her hands and feet. She reports returning from a hiking tour in Central America 2 weeks ago where she was treated with antibiotics for an infection. On exam, she has proximal muscle weakness and an ataxic gait. Her sensation is normal throughout but reflexes are diminished. Eye weakness with diplopia is also noted. Given the patient's likely diagnosis, what is the most likely causative pathogen?
explanation:
Campylobacter jejuni
Guillain-Barre syndrome is classically triggered by Campylobacter jejuni infection. This patient has presented with the typical findings of Miller-Fisher syndrome, a variant of Guillain-Barre syndrome. The condition is classically associated with ophthalmoplegia, which normally develops first, a descending paralysis with areflexia and ataxia. As with Guillain-Barre syndrome, Miller-Fisher syndrome is often triggered by an infection, the commonest being Campylobacter jejuni which accounts for approximately 30% of cases. Campylobacter jejuni is common throughout the developing world including Central America where food hygiene may be reduced and therefore contamination risk higher.

Borrelia burgdorferi
Borrelia burgdorferi is the causative infective agent in Lyme disease. It is transmitted by tick bites, therefore there is normally a history of exposure with the patient recently spending time somewhere ticks are present, i.e., a woodland area. Lyme disease can present with a variety of symptoms but typically is associated with an erythema migrans rash, muscle and joint pain before progressing to arrhythmias, etc. A descending weakness is not commonly seen in Lyme disease.

Cytomegalovirus
Cytomegalovirus (CMV) is a recognised infective agent triggering Guillain-Barre syndrome and its variants, however, it is far less commonly associated with the condition than Campylobacter jejuni. CMV has also been associated with triggering other auto-immune conditions including myocarditis and possibly type 1 diabetes.

Epstein-Barr virus
Although rare, Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) has been associated with Guillain-Barre syndrome and its variants, however, far less so than Campylobacter jejuni. EBV has been associated with other conditions including multiple sclerosis and rheumatoid arthritis.

Trypanosoma cruzi
Trypanosoma cruzi is the causative infective agent of Chagas disease, also known as American trypanosomiasis, spread by insects known as Triatominae that are present throughout Central and South America. The condition normally comprises an acute stage, which develops a few weeks after the insect bite and includes mild symptoms of fever and malaise followed by a chronic stage which develops over many years and consists of chronic fatigue, enlargement of the liver, spleen, and lymph nodes. If untreated, patients can eventually progress to developing cardiac issues such as arrhythmias and cardiomyopathies. Chagas disease is not associated with neuropathies or eye issues as seen in this patient.

stem: A 55-year-old man presents complaining of visual disturbance. Examination reveals a right congruous homonymous hemianopia with macula sparing. Where is the lesion most likely to be?
explanation:
Left occipital cortex
The correct answer is the Left occipital cortex. A congruous homonymous hemianopia with macula sparing is indicative of a lesion in the occipital lobe, particularly in the primary visual cortex. The term 'congruous' refers to the mirror-image nature of the visual field defect in both eyes, which suggests that the lesion is located posterior to the optic tract. The term 'macula sparing' refers to the preservation of central vision, which is a characteristic feature of lesions in the occipital lobe due to dual blood supply from both middle and posterior cerebral arteries.

Right optic nerve
The Right optic nerve option would typically present as monocular vision loss rather than homonymous hemianopia. Damage at this level would affect only one eye because it occurs before the decussation (crossing) of optic nerve fibres at the chiasm.

Right optic radiation
A lesion in the Right optic radiation would result in a left homonymous hemianopia. This is because right optic radiations carry information from left visual fields after decussation has occurred at the level of the optic chiasm.

Left optic tract
A lesion in the Left optic tract would lead to a right homonymous hemianopia but it would be incongruous rather than congruous. Incongruity typically indicates a lesion anterior to the lateral geniculate nucleus i.e., at the level of either optic tract or chiasm.

Optic chiasm
An injury at the level of Optic chiasm, such as caused by pituitary adenomas or craniopharyngiomas, usually leads to bitemporal hemianopia (loss of the outer/temporal half of visual field in both eyes). This occurs due to damage to crossing nasal fibres from each retina that carry temporal visual field information.

stem: A 68-year-old man presents to the emergency department 90 minutes after sudden onset left-sided weakness and dysphasia. CT head excludes haemorrhage. He is assessed by the stroke team and deemed suitable for thrombolysis. His observations show heart rate 88/min, respiratory rate 16/min, oxygen saturations 97% on room air, temperature 36.8°C, and blood pressure 192/116 mmHg. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
options: Repeat blood pressure measurement in 15 minutes
explanation:
Administer intravenous labetalol
Hypertension (>185/110 mmHg) in the setting of acute ischaemic stroke should be treated prior to thrombolysis. Administer intravenous labetalol is the correct answer. This patient has an acute ischaemic stroke and is within the 4.5-hour window for thrombolysis. However, his blood pressure of 192/116 mmHg exceeds the threshold of 185/110 mmHg required before thrombolysis can be safely administered. According to the National Clinical Guideline for Stroke, blood pressure must be lowered to below 185/110 mmHg prior to thrombolysis to reduce the risk of haemorrhagic transformation. Intravenous labetalol is commonly used for rapid blood pressure control in this setting. The patient is otherwise suitable for thrombolysis, having presented within 90 minutes of symptom onset with haemorrhage excluded on CT. Once blood pressure is adequately controlled, thrombolysis can proceed. This represents a critical step in the acute management pathway, as failure to control blood pressure would represent a relative contraindication to thrombolysis, potentially denying the patient this time-critical treatment.

Administer alteplase immediately
Administer alteplase immediately is incorrect. Whilst this patient is within the therapeutic window and has had haemorrhage excluded, proceeding with thrombolysis when blood pressure exceeds 185/110 mmHg significantly increases the risk of haemorrhagic transformation. This represents a relative contraindication to thrombolysis. The guidelines are clear that blood pressure must be controlled first. Administering alteplase without blood pressure control would be unsafe practice and could result in serious complications including intracerebral haemorrhage.

Administer aspirin 300mg
Administer aspirin 300mg is incorrect in this immediate context. Whilst aspirin 300mg should be given as soon as possible after haemorrhagic stroke has been excluded, it should not be given before thrombolysis. The patient is a candidate for thrombolysis (once blood pressure is controlled), and aspirin administration should be delayed until after thrombolytic therapy. Giving aspirin before thrombolysis would increase bleeding risk. Aspirin would be appropriate if the patient were not suitable for thrombolysis.

Arrange urgent CT angiography
Arrange urgent CT angiography is not the immediate priority. Whilst CT angiography may be useful for identifying large vessel occlusion and planning potential thrombectomy, the immediate management priority is controlling blood pressure to enable thrombolysis. The patient is already within the thrombolysis window, and delaying treatment to arrange further imaging without first addressing the blood pressure would waste valuable time. CT angiography could be considered after thrombolysis has been initiated or alongside blood pressure management.

Repeat blood pressure measurement in 15 minutes
Repeat blood pressure measurement in 15 minutes is incorrect as it represents unnecessary delay. The blood pressure reading of 192/116 mmHg clearly exceeds the threshold, and waiting to repeat the measurement without intervening would waste precious time in an acute stroke where 'time is brain'. Active blood pressure reduction should be initiated immediately. Whilst blood pressure can fluctuate, this reading is sufficiently elevated that intervention is warranted without delay.

stem: A 19-year-old female presents complaining of visual disturbance. Examination reveals a bitemporal hemianopia with predominately the lower quadrants being affected. What is the most likely lesion?
explanation:
Craniopharyngioma
Craniopharyngioma is indeed the correct answer. Craniopharyngiomas typically arise from remnants of Rathke's pouch above the pituitary gland and compress the optic chiasm from above. This superior compression characteristically causes a bitemporal hemianopia that affects the inferior fields first (as the crossing fibers in the superior chiasm are compressed first), which matches the description in this case. These tumors commonly present in children or young adults.

Brainstem lesion
Brainstem lesion is incorrect as brainstem lesions typically cause cranial nerve palsies, long tract signs, or internuclear ophthalmoplegia rather than visual field defects.

Frontal lobe lesion
Frontal lobe lesion is incorrect as frontal lobe lesions do not typically cause visual field defects unless they extend posteriorly to involve the optic radiation.

Pituitary macroadenoma
Pituitary macroadenoma is incorrect because while it can cause bitemporal hemianopia, it typically grows upward from below the chiasm and affects the superior visual fields first (opposite to this case).

Right occipital lesion
Right occipital lesion is incorrect as this would cause a left homonymous hemianopia rather than a bitemporal defect. Occipital lesions affect the contralateral visual field and do not cause bitemporal defects.

stem: A worried mother brings in her 13-year-old girl who has been dropping things in the morning due to sudden jerks in her arms. Her teacher has also reported that in the first hours of class she sometimes seems to 'zone out' and not listen at all. Her mother is worried that she may have epilepsy, as the child's aunt does. The child has been otherwise developing normally and is clinically well today. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy
Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy is classically associated with seizures in the morning/following sleep deprivation. Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy (JME), also known as Janz syndrome, typically presents in teenage years with a triad of: Myoclonic seizures (sudden, shock-like muscle jerks), present in all cases by definition, these may cause patients to drop things. Generalised tonic-clonic seizures, present in 2/3 of the cases, may develop later. Absence seizures (daytime 'staring spells'), present in 1/3 of the cases. All of the different types of seizures in JME are more likely to occur in the morning, within hours of waking, and are worsened/triggered by sleep deprivation. JME is more common in girls. Up to 50% of cases may be photosensitive. EEG may show generalised spike and wave or polyspike and slow-wave discharges. Treatment is with sodium valproate.

Atonic seizures
Atonic seizures are a type of generalised seizures characterised by loss of tone. While dropping things can be a feature in atonic seizures, they are more commonly described as 'drop attacks', where patients suddenly fall or limp, or their head may slump. Atonic seizures would not explain the staring spells.

Focal seizures
Focal seizures (partial seizures) can be divided into focal aware (simple partial), awareness unknown, or focal impaired awareness (complex partial). They may be motor (e.g. Jacksonian march), non-motor (e.g. jamais vu) or have other features such as aura. In this child, the presence of 'staring spells' (absence seizures) rules out partial seizures, as they are a generalised form of seizures.

Infantile spasms
Infantile spasms (West's syndrome) are brief spasms in the first few months of life (up to 6 months) associated with progressive developmental delay and a poor prognosis. This child does not have developmental delay and her age makes this diagnosis extremely unlikely.

Lennox-Gastaut syndrome
Lennox-Gastaut syndrome may be the progression into early childhood (onset around 1-5 years) of infantile spasms, typically presenting with falls, jerks and atypical absence seizures and in most cases associated with considerable developmental delay. Again, this child does not have developmental delay and her age makes this diagnosis less likely.

stem: A 25-year-old woman presents with recurrent attacks of 'dizziness'. These attacks typically last around 30-60 minutes and occur every few days or so. During an attack 'the room seems to be spinning' and the patient often feels sick. These episodes are often accompanied by a 'roaring' sensation in the left ear. Otoscopy is normal, Weber's test localises to the right ear, and Rinne's test shows air conduction greater than bone conduction bilaterally. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Meniere's disease
The correct answer is Meniere's disease. This condition is characterised by episodic vertigo, tinnitus (often described as a 'roaring' sensation), and sensorineural hearing loss. The symptoms typically last from 20 minutes to several hours. Meniere's disease is thought to be caused by an excess of endolymph in the inner ear, although the exact cause remains unknown. The presentation of this patient with recurrent episodes of vertigo accompanied by tinnitus localising to one ear makes Meniere's disease the most likely diagnosis.

Acoustic neuroma
Acoustic neuroma, also known as vestibular schwannoma, usually presents with unilateral sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus and imbalance rather than true vertigo. It is a slow-growing benign tumour of the eighth cranial nerve. However, it would not typically cause episodic symptoms as described in the question.

Vestibular neuritis
Vestibular neuritis is typically characterised by a single episode of severe vertigo lasting days rather than recurrent episodes. It often follows a viral infection and may be associated with nausea and vomiting but does not typically cause tinnitus or hearing loss.

Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo
Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV) causes brief episodes of mild to intense dizziness that are triggered by specific changes in the position of your head. Episodes are often less than one minute and occur when moving in certain directions or at certain times, such as rolling over in bed or looking up. BPPV would not explain the 'roaring' sensation in her ear.

Multiple sclerosis
Multiple sclerosis can certainly present with vertigo but would usually have other neurological symptoms too such as visual disturbances or limb weakness which are not mentioned here. Multiple sclerosis also tends to present with more persistent symptoms rather than episodic ones.

stem: A 49-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department complaining of visual disturbance. Examination reveals a right incongruous homonymous hemianopia. Where is the lesion most likely to be?
explanation:
Left optic tract
Left optic tract is the correct answer because a lesion here would cause a right homonymous hemianopia that is typically incongruous (meaning slightly different between the two eyes). The optic tract carries fibers from both retinas that represent the contralateral visual field, after they have partially crossed at the chiasm.

Left optic radiation
Left optic radiation would also cause a right homonymous hemianopia, but these lesions typically produce more congruous defects (more similar between the two eyes) because the fibers are more organized at this point in the pathway.

Right optic tract
Right optic tract would cause a left homonymous hemianopia, which doesn't match the clinical presentation.

Right optic radiation
Right optic radiation would also cause a left homonymous hemianopia, again not matching the symptoms described.

Optic chiasm
Optic chiasm lesions typically cause bitemporal hemianopia due to compression of the crossing nasal retinal fibers, not a homonymous defect. This pattern is classically seen with pituitary tumors.

stem: A 20-year-old man presents with recent episodes of severe, stabbing pain in the right eye. These episodes typically occur once a day and last around 30 minutes. His wife reports him pacing around and shouting with the pain. She also reports that his right eye appears red and that he has clear nasal discharge during the episodes. Given the likely diagnosis, which one of the following should you advise the patient to avoid to help prevent further episodes?
explanation:
Alcohol
Alcohol is a common trigger for cluster headaches. This patient's symptoms are suggestive of cluster headaches, a primary headache disorder characterised by severe unilateral orbital or temporal pain, typically lasting 15-180 minutes and occurring once to eight times a day. Attacks often occur in clusters (hence the name), with periods of remission between clusters. During attacks, patients often appear restless or agitated and may exhibit autonomic symptoms such as conjunctival injection (red eye), lacrimation, nasal congestion or rhinorrhoea (clear nasal discharge) on the side of the headache. Alcohol is known to be a trigger for attacks during a cluster period but not during remission periods.

Opioid medications including codeine
Opioid medications including codeine are incorrect because they do not precipitate cluster headaches. However, they are generally avoided in management due to the risk of medication overuse headache and dependence.

Stress
Stress is also incorrect. While stress can trigger migraines and tension-type headaches, it is not typically associated with triggering cluster headaches.

Sunlight
Exposure to Sunlight, unlike some other types of headache such as migraine, is not known to trigger cluster headaches and thus this option is incorrect.

Excessive exercise
Excessive exercise does not typically precipitate cluster headaches either. In fact, aerobic exercise has been shown to have a preventive effect on several types of primary headache disorders. Therefore this option is also incorrect.

stem: A 21-year-old musician is brought to hospital after collapsing on stage. There was no loss of consciousness and he sustained only minor bruising to his knees. Another musician onstage at the time notes he had been laughing at the time before his legs suddenly 'gave way' and his mouth twitched for a few seconds. The patient reports a similar episode occurring a few days previously. He has been extremely fatigued over the last several months, which he had attributed to touring. ECG and blood tests are normal. What is the most likely underlying diagnosis?
explanation:
Narcolepsy
Laughter → fall/collapse ?cataplexy The event described is characteristic of cataplexy which can feature phasic muscle jerking around the mouth. In the context of 'extreme fatigue', cataplexy is highly specific for narcolepsy.

Gelastic seizures
Gelastic seizures are not caused by laughter but the outburst of laughter is the seizure itself- this can be caused by brain neoplasms.

Tourette's syndrome
Tourette's syndrome presents with verbal and physical 'tics'.

Lennox Gaustaut syndrome
Lennox Gastaut syndrome normally presents in childhood and can cause drop attacks but these are characterised by a single, generalized myoclonic jerk that precedes tonic contraction of axial muscles.

stem: A 75-year-old man attends the falls clinic with a 1-month history of increased falls. He reports falling five times over the past month. Previously, he was independently mobile, but now requires the assistance of a walking frame. His wife reports intermittent episodes of confusion followed by lucid periods. He has a history of hypertension, alcoholic fatty liver disease, and gout. On examination, he has normal power and sensation in the upper limbs. In the lower limbs, power is generally good, but he has a shuffling gait. Cranial nerve examination is unremarkable except for an inability to abduct his left eye on lateral gaze. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Subdural haematoma
In the elderly, especially those with a history of alcohol misuse, recurrent falls and fluctuating confusion should raise concern for a subdural haematoma. The left abducens (cranial nerve VI) palsy may represent a false localising sign due to raised intracranial pressure or midline shift from a space-occupying lesion. A CT head should be performed to assess for a subdural haematoma, which typically appears as a crescentshaped collection of blood, most often due to rupture of bridging veins.

Hepatic encephalopathy
Hepatic encephalopathy is a differential in patients with alcohol-related liver disease. However, in the absence of decompensation features (e.g. ascites, jaundice) and the presence of a focal cranial nerve deficit, it is less likely.

Lewy body dementia
Lewy body dementia can present with fluctuating cognition, hallucinations, and Parkinsonism (e.g. shuffling gait, rigidity). However, it would not explain the acute onset or cranial nerve palsy.

Normal-pressure hydrocephalus
Normal-pressure hydrocephalus presents with the classic triad of gait disturbance (typically a magnetic, broad-based gait), cognitive impairment, and urinary incontinence. It tends to develop gradually, whereas this case is more acute and focal.

Wernicke's encephalopathy
Wernicke’s encephalopathy is possible given the history of alcohol misuse. It typically presents with ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, and confusion. However, the isolated abducens palsy without nystagmus or cerebellar signs, and the pattern of fluctuating confusion, point more towards a structural lesion such as a subdural haematoma.

stem: A 45-year-old woman who had chemotherapy 15 days ago for locally advanced breast cancer presents to the emergency department with weakness of both legs which has come on over the previous 12 hours. She has been mostly well since chemotherapy, although does report suffering from painful blisters in a strip across the right side of her chest last week. On examination, she has a temperature of 37.8ºC and is rather distressed. Power is 3/5 throughout both legs. There is clonus with upgoing plantars bilaterally, reflexes are brisk. There is loss of fine touch sensation below the umbilicus. Examination of the upper limbs and cranial nerves is normal. Which of the following is the most likely cause of her current presentation?
explanation:
Varicella myelitis
Spastic paraparesis can be caused by transverse myelitis. The symmetrical leg weakness with upper motor neurone signs describes the clinical picture of spastic paraparesis. In addition, there is a sensory level - pointing towards a spinal lesion. The history of a blistering rash that sounds dermatomal should raise suspicions of varicella, which can cause transverse myelitis (focal inflammation of the spinal cord).

Venous sinus thrombosis
Venous sinus thrombosis presents with headache, fever and cranial nerve palsies.

Guillain-Barre syndrome (GBS)
GBS and vincristine neuropathy are pathologies of the peripheral nerves and therefore lower motor neurone (LMN) signs would be expected.

Vincristine neuropathy
GBS and vincristine neuropathy are pathologies of the peripheral nerves and therefore lower motor neurone (LMN) signs would be expected.

Cauda equina syndrome
Leg weakness in the context of malignancy should always raise suspicions of cauda equina syndrome, however, it also causes LMN signs. Additionally, as the cauda equina starts at L1/2 its compression cannot cause a sensory level at T10 (umbilicus). Malignant cord compression would be in the differential diagnosis.

stem: Which one of the following is least likely to cause a raised protein level in the cerebrospinal fluid?
explanation:
Systemic lupus erythematous
The correct answer is Systemic lupus erythematous (SLE). SLE is a chronic autoimmune disease that affects various systems in the body. It does not typically cause raised protein levels in the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). Although neurological manifestations can occur in SLE, known as neuropsychiatric systemic lupus erythematosus (NPSLE), these do not typically result in raised CSF protein levels. NPSLE can present with a variety of symptoms such as cognitive dysfunction, mood disorders, seizures, and psychosis but CSF analysis usually shows normal or mildly elevated protein level.

Tuberculous meningitis
Tuberculous meningitis, caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, often presents with a significantly raised CSF protein level. This is due to the inflammatory response triggered by the infection which increases permeability of the blood-brain barrier leading to an influx of proteins into the CSF.

Guillain-Barre syndrome
Guillain-Barre syndrome is another condition that causes raised CSF protein levels. It's an autoimmune disorder affecting peripheral nerves resulting in ascending paralysis. A characteristic feature of Guillain-Barre syndrome on lumbar puncture is albuminocytologic dissociation where there's a high protein level without a corresponding increase in cell count.

Fungal meningitis
Fungal meningitis, caused by fungi like Cryptococcus neoformans or Candida species, also results in elevated CSF protein levels due to similar mechanisms as tuberculous meningitis - inflammation and increased permeability of blood-brain barrier.

Froin's syndrome
Froin's syndrome is characterized by spinal blockage leading to xanthochromia (yellow appearance of CSF due to breakdown of red blood cells), high CSF protein levels and the presence of clots in the CSF. The high protein level results from local production within the blocked segment and reduced absorption due to blockage.

stem: A 54-year-old man presents with a persistent tremor. On examination there is 6-8 Hz tremor of the arms which is worse when his arms are outstretched. His father suffered from a similar complaint. What is the most suitable first-line treatment?
explanation:
Propranolol
Propranolol is the treatment of choice for essential tremor. Propranolol is the correct answer as it is the first-line treatment for essential tremor, which this patient likely has based on the clinical presentation. Essential tremor typically presents with a bilateral postural tremor of 4-12 Hz (commonly 6-8 Hz) that is worse with arm extension, and there is often a positive family history. Beta-blockers, particularly propranolol, are the most effective first-line treatment, working by blocking peripheral beta-adrenergic receptors. The typical starting dose is 20-40mg twice daily.

Amitriptyline
Amitriptyline is incorrect as it is not indicated for essential tremor. While it may be used to treat other neurological conditions such as neuropathic pain or migraine prophylaxis, it can actually worsen tremor as a side effect due to its anticholinergic properties.

D-penicillamine
D-penicillamine is incorrect as it is primarily used in Wilson's disease, a genetic disorder of copper metabolism. While Wilson's disease can cause tremor, the presentation would typically include other features such as liver disease, psychiatric symptoms, and Kayser-Fleischer rings. Additionally, the age of onset is usually much younger.

Levodopa
Levodopa is incorrect as it is the primary treatment for Parkinson's disease. While parkinsonian tremor can appear similar, it is typically a 4-6 Hz rest tremor that improves with action, unlike this patient's postural tremor. The absence of other parkinsonian features (bradykinesia, rigidity) also makes Parkinson's disease unlikely.

Diazepam
Diazepam is incorrect as while benzodiazepines can temporarily reduce tremor severity, they are not recommended as first-line treatment due to their sedating effects and risk of dependence. They may be used as an adjunct therapy in severe cases or for occasional use in specific situations where the tremor is particularly troublesome.

stem: A 21-year-old man presents with progressive hearing loss as well as an on-off ringing affecting both ears. The patient is otherwise well with no other medical conditions. He does however reports that both his father and grandparents had similar issues at a young age and eventually required surgical intervention. External and otoscope examinations are normal however Rinne and Weber's tests reveal a bilateral conductive hearing loss. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Otosclerosis
Otosclerosis is characterised by conductive hearing loss, tinnitus and positive family history. This patient has presented with features in keeping with the condition of the middle ear otosclerosis. In otosclerosis, the normal bones of the ear's bony labyrinth are replaced by vascular spongy bone. There is normally a family history of the condition as it is caused by a combination of genetic and environmental factors (e.g. viral infections), with patients experiencing symptoms from their 20s onwards. As otosclerosis is due to a disruption of the bony labyrinth, with the stapes at the oval window becoming fixated, it results in progressive conductive deafness however otoscope examination will commonly reveal a normal tympanic membrane. Treatment is dependant on the extent of the otosclerosis and hearing loss but can range from hearing aids to a stapedectomy, where a portion of the sclerotic stapes footplate is removed and replaced with an implant.

Alport syndrome
Alport syndrome is an inherited defect of type IV collagen, normally presenting in childhood. The condition typically results in progressive renal failure and a sensorineural hearing loss, not a conductive hearing loss as described here. Other features of the syndrome include ocular issues, smooth muscle tumours (leiomyomas) and rarely aortic dissection.

Cerumen
Cerumen is the medical term for ear wax, referring to the secretion from the ceruminous and sebaceous glands of the outer ear. Excessive cerumen can result from several conditions and causes a conductive hearing loss however the waxy substance will be present in the ear canal and therefore seen on otoscope examination.

Cholesteatoma
A cholesteatoma is a collection of keratinised squamous epithelium that forms within the middle ear space. Symptoms develop as the collection progressively expands causing destruction of the surrounding tissues and bone resulting in retraction or perforation of the tympanic membrane as well as chronic drainage from the ear secondary to infection. As such in cholesteatoma, otoscopic examination of the ear will nearly always be abnormal.

Microtia
Microtia is a congenital deformity of unclear cause where the external aspect of the ear is underdeveloped. Microtia can be unilateral or bilateral and is graded based on the extent of the underdevelopment. If significant, children can have reduced hearing as sound is unable to travel into the inner ear. As a deformity of the external ear examination will be abnormal in microtia.

stem: A 67-year-old man presents to his GP with numbness in his feet and recurrent falls over the past month. He describes difficulty walking. His GP recently started him on folate for a macrocytic anaemia. He takes no other regular medications. He does not drink alcohol. On examination, he has an ataxic gait and Romberg's test is positive. Examination of his lower limbs demonstrates an increase in tone and bilateral weakness. He has absent ankle and knee jerks with upgoing plantars. Light touch and vibration sense is reduced bilaterally. What is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
options: Subacute combined degeneration of the cord
explanation:
Subacute combined degeneration of the cord
Subacute combined degeneration of the cord involves degeneration of the posterior and lateral columns of the spinal cord, often due to vitamin B12 deficiency. Damage to the posterior columns - loss of proprioception, light touch and vibration sense (sensory ataxia and a positive Romberg's test). Damage to lateral columns - spastic weakness and upgoing plantars (UMN signs). Damage to peripheral nerves - absent ankle and knee jerks (LMN signs). When there is a mix of UMN and LMN signs in a patient, always consider SCDC. Replacing folate without vitamin B12 (hinted at in this case) can precipitate subacute combined degeneration of the cord in a patient who is vitamin B12 deficient. Always ensure vitamin B12 levels are checked (and replenished) before giving folate for a macrocytic anaemia.

Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis
Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis is a subtype of motor neurone disease. This may present with mixed UMN and LMN signs but no associated sensory deficits.

Guillain-Barre syndrome
Guillain-Barre syndrome is an inflammatory peripheral neuropathy so will not present with UMN signs. There is nothing in the history to suggest a recent bacterial or viral infection.

Myasthenia gravis
Myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune disease affecting the neuromuscular junction so will not present with UMN signs or sensory loss.

Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease
Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease is a hereditary sensory and motor peripheral neuropathy. UMN signs are not present in these patients. However, patients can present with LMN signs in all limbs and reduced sensation (more pronounced distally).

stem: A 45-year-old woman presents with pain associated with muscle spasticity in the context of relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis. Baclofen is initiated with the aim of reducing spasticity. What is the mechanism of action of this medication?
explanation:
Gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) receptor agonist
Baclofen is an agonist of GABA receptors that acts in the central nervous system. Baclofen is an agonist of GABA receptors and is used as a muscle relaxant to treat spasticity conditions such as multiple sclerosis and cerebral palsy.

Gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) receptor antagonist
Baclofen is an agonist rather than antagonist at GABA receptors. An example of a GABA antagonist is flumazenil.

N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor (NMDA) receptor agonist
Baclofen exerts its effects at GABA rather than NMDA receptors. An example of an NMDA agonist is the toxin responsible for Amanita muscaria poisoning.

N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor (NMDA) receptor antagonist
Baclofen exerts its effects at GABA rather than NMDA receptors. An example of an NMDA antagonist is memantine, used in moderate to severe Alzheimer's dementia.

Muscarinic M3 receptor antagonist
Baclofen exerts its effects at GABA rather than muscarinic receptors. An example of a commonly used muscarinic M3 receptor antagonist is buscopan, used to treat pain associated with bowel wall spasm and respiratory secretions during end-of-life care.

stem: A 43-year-old woman attends the emergency department with acute confusion, left sided leg weakness and behavioural disturbance. She has a past medical history of multiple sclerosis for which she is taking natalizumab. She is haemodynamically stable. On examination she is not orientated to time or place and is being aggressive, which her husband says is completely out of character. She has 3/5 weakness in her left leg. The rest of the examination is unremarkable. Her blood tests are: Hb 136 g/L Male: (135-180) Female: (115 - 160) Platelets 336 * 109/L (150 - 400) WBC 14.2 * 109/L (4.0 - 11.0) Na+ 140 mmol/L (135 - 145) K+ 4.6 mmol/L (3.5 - 5.0) Urea 5.2 mmol/L (2.0 - 7.0) Creatinine 106 µmol/L (55 - 120) CRP 78 mg/L (< 5) Which is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy
Natalizumab can cause reactivation of the JC virus causing progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML). Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) is associated with natalizumab treatment in multiple sclerosis (MS). It is caused by reactivation of the JC virus due to immunodeficiency secondary to natalizumab (it can also occur with a few other MS modifying drug treatments and HIV). The reactivation of the JC virus causes demyelination and the symptoms a patient has depends on the site and extent of the demyelination. The most common symptoms are confusion, behavioural change, ataxia, hemiparesis and visual deficits.

Bacterial meningitis
Bacterial meningitis can cause confusion and behavioural disturbance but is unlikely to cause left leg weakness. Additionally there is no mention of pyrexia and the inflammatory markers, while slightly up, are not significantly raised.

Autoimmune encephalitis
There is no preceding history of minor infection to suggest autoimmune encephalitis. The symptoms are not typical for autoimmune encephalitis which tends to develop subacutely (over days) rather than acutely.

Intracranial haemorrhage
There is no history of a headache to suggest intracranial haemorrhage and this is unlikely to cause unilateral weakness.

Toxoplasmosis
There are no risk factors for exposure to toxoplasmosis and there are no systemic symptoms to suggest this either.

stem: A 43-year-old woman with multiple sclerosis presents for review. She is having increasing problems with painful involuntary contractions of the leg muscles. What is the most appropriate first-line therapy?
explanation:
Baclofen
Baclofen is a GABA-B receptor agonist which acts as a muscle relaxant. It is considered first-line therapy for spasticity in multiple sclerosis according to the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guidelines. It works by inhibiting reflexes at the spinal level, thus reducing muscle tone and frequency of spasms.

Referral for relaxation therapy
Referral for relaxation therapy can be beneficial in managing symptoms of multiple sclerosis, including muscle spasms. However, it's not considered as a first-line treatment for painful involuntary contractions of leg muscles. It may be used in conjunction with pharmacological treatments but should not replace them.

Diazepam
Diazepam is a benzodiazepine that can be used to manage severe or disabling muscle spasticity when other treatments are ineffective. However, due to its potential side effects such as sedation and risk of dependency, it's not usually the first choice of treatment.

Dantrolene
Dantrolene acts peripherally to interfere with muscle contraction mechanism by inhibiting calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum in skeletal muscles. While it can be used in the management of spasticity, it's generally reserved for severe cases where other treatments have failed due to its potential hepatotoxicity.

Natalizumab
Natalizumab is a monoclonal antibody used in the treatment of relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis. It works by preventing potentially damaging immune cells from migrating from the bloodstream into the brain and spinal cord. While effective in managing overall disease progression, it does not directly treat muscle spasticity and hence would not be appropriate as a first-line therapy for this specific symptom.

stem: A 68-year-old man attends the neurology clinic with a worsening tremor in both hands, which now interferes with writing. He has a history of poorly controlled asthma. He notes that a small amount of alcohol provides temporary relief. On examination, a fine postural tremor is evident in both outstretched hands. There are no other neurological deficits. What is the most appropriate medication to commence?
explanation:
Primidone
Primidone is the correct answer. The clinical presentation of a longstanding, bilateral postural tremor that improves with alcohol is characteristic of essential tremor. While propranolol is the first-line treatment, this patient has poorly controlled asthma, which is a significant contraindication to non-selective beta-blockers due to the risk of inducing bronchospasm. Primidone, an anticonvulsant, is a well-established and effective alternative first-line agent for essential tremor and is the most appropriate choice in this scenario. Patients should be initiated on a low dose and titrated slowly to minimise side effects such as sedation, dizziness, and nausea.

Clonazepam
Clonazepam is a benzodiazepine that can be used to treat essential tremor, but it is typically reserved for refractory cases due to its side effect profile, including sedation, cognitive impairment, and the potential for dependence. It would not be considered a first-line alternative to propranolol in an older patient.

Gabapentin
Gabapentin is sometimes used as a third-line agent for essential tremor, but evidence for its efficacy is less robust compared to propranolol and primidone. It would not be the most appropriate initial medication in this case, as a more effective and established alternative is available.

Levodopa
Levodopa is the primary treatment for Parkinson's disease. This patient's clinical features are not suggestive of Parkinson's. He has a postural tremor, not the typical resting tremor of Parkinson's, and lacks other cardinal features such as bradykinesia, rigidity, or postural instability. The improvement with alcohol is also a classic feature of essential tremor.

Propranolol
Propranolol is the first-line pharmacological treatment for essential tremor. However, as a non-selective beta-blocker, it is contraindicated in patients with poorly controlled asthma. Its use could precipitate a severe exacerbation of his respiratory condition. Therefore, it is not an appropriate choice for this patient.

stem: A 35-year-old woman presents with a three-month history of progressive stiffness and weakness in her legs, associated with difficulty walking and urinary urgency. She recalls a transient episode of visual loss in her left eye three years ago, which resolved spontaneously. Neurological examination reveals bilateral spasticity, hyperreflexia, and upgoing plantar reflexes. MRI of the brain reveals multiple periventricular hyperintensities and spinal imaging shows a short-segment lesion in the thoracic spinal cord. Which is the strongest evidence to confirm the diagnosis?
options: Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) oligoclonal bands not present in serum
Gadolinium enhancement of the spinal lesion
T2 hyperintensities in the basal ganglia
explanation:
Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) oligoclonal bands not present in serum
Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) oligoclonal bands not present in serum is the correct answer because the detection of oligoclonal bands (OCBs) exclusively in cerebrospinal fluid, with their absence in serum, is a characteristic feature of multiple sclerosis (MS). This finding suggests local production of IgG within the central nervous system. OCBs are found in approximately 95% of individuals diagnosed with MS and serve as an important diagnostic marker when considered alongside clinical presentation and imaging results. The patient's clinical symptoms, such as spastic paraparesis and urinary issues, together with MRI findings indicative of MS, make the presence of OCBs a significant factor in confirming this diagnosis.

Antibodies to aquaporin-4 in serum
Antibodies to aquaporin-4 in serum is an incorrect option since these antibodies are indicative of neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (NMOSD), which can present with similarities to MS. NMOSD typically features severe optic neuritis that is often bilateral and extensive spinal cord lesions extending over three or more vertebral segments. In contrast, the MRI observations of periventricular lesions and a shorter spinal lesion align more closely with MS rather than NMOSD.

Gadolinium enhancement of the spinal lesion
Gadolinium enhancement of the spinal lesion is incorrect because although gadolinium uptake indicates active inflammation and supports the presence of an inflammatory demyelinating disease, it lacks specificity for MS. Gadolinium enhancement can be seen in various conditions including NMOSD, sarcoidosis, or other inflammatory diseases. While it signifies active disease pathology, it does not specifically confirm MS.

Longitudinally extensive spinal cord lesion
Longitudinally extensive spinal cord lesion is an incorrect choice as this refers to a lesion that extends across three or more vertebral segments, which is typical for NMOSD rather than MS. Given that this patient has a short-segment lesion on spinal imaging consistent with MS pathology, the presence of a longitudinally extensive lesion would not be expected and therefore does not aid in diagnosing MS.

T2 hyperintensities in the basal ganglia
T2 hyperintensities in the basal ganglia is also incorrect due to its nonspecific nature; such findings may be associated with various other conditions such as vascular diseases, toxic-metabolic disorders, or neurodegenerative processes. Basal ganglia hyperintensities are not commonly seen in MS and thus do not support its diagnosis.

stem: A 64-year-old female with a history of rheumatoid arthritis presents with increased difficulty in walking. On examination there is weakness of ankle dorsiflexion and of the extensor hallucis longus associated with loss of sensation on the lateral aspect of the lower leg. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Common peroneal nerve palsy
Common peroneal nerve lesion can cause weakness of foot dorsiflexion and foot eversion. The most likely diagnosis in this case is common peroneal nerve palsy. The common peroneal nerve, also known as the common fibular nerve, is a branch of the sciatic nerve that supplies the muscles responsible for ankle dorsiflexion and extension of the toes, specifically the extensor hallucis longus. Damage to this nerve can result in foot drop and sensory loss over the lateral aspect of the lower leg, which are both symptoms described in this scenario.

Tibial nerve palsy
Tibial nerve palsy is an incorrect answer because it primarily affects the plantar flexors of the ankle and flexors of the toes. Sensory loss would be expected on the sole of the foot rather than on the lateral aspect of the lower leg.

Obturator nerve palsy
Obturator nerve palsy is another incorrect answer. The obturator nerve supplies muscles in the medial compartment of the thigh, which are responsible for hip adduction. A lesion affecting this nerve would not cause weakness in ankle dorsiflexion or sensory changes in the lower leg.

Lateral cutaneous nerve palsy
Lateral cutaneous nerve palsy, also known as lateral femoral cutaneous nerve palsy or meralgia paraesthetica, is an incorrect answer because it only affects sensation over the anterolateral aspect of the thigh without any motor deficits. It does not cause weakness in ankle dorsiflexion or affect sensation on the lateral aspect of the lower leg.

Pudendal nerve palsy
Finally, pudendal nerve palsy is incorrect as well since it mainly affects muscles and sensation in genitalia and perineum area. It does not have any impact on muscles or sensations related to walking or movement of legs.

stem: A 28-year-old man presents with hearing loss which has progressively worsened over the past 6 months. On examination, air conduction is better compared to bone conduction in both ears, and Weber's test does not lateralise. You also note a bilateral loss of the corneal reflex. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Neurofibromatosis type 2 (NF2)
Neurofibromatosis type 2 (NF2) is correct. The clinical features are suggestive of bilateral acoustic neuromas. Weber's and Rinne's tests are consistent with bilateral sensorineural hearing loss. Bilateral vestibular schwannomas are frequently seen in NF2.

Li-Fraumeni syndrome
Li-Fraumeni syndrome is incorrect. Li-Fraumeni syndrome (LFS) is an inherited predisposition to a wide range of certain cancers caused by pathogenic TP53 germline variants. Both children and adults are susceptible to developing multiple cancers, most notably soft-tissue and bone sarcomas, breast cancer, brain tumours, adrenocortical carcinoma and leukaemia. Acoustic neuromas are not classically associated with this condition.

Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1)
Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) is incorrect. NF1 is a multisystem disorder characterized by multiple cafe au lait macules, intertriginous freckling, multiple cutaneous neurofibromas, and learning disability or behaviour problems. Acoustic neuromas are not classically associated with this condition.

Tuberous sclerosis
Tuberous sclerosis is incorrect. This condition can manifest in multiple organ systems with the cutaneous and renal systems being the most commonly affected. Renal angiomyolipoma, cysts, and carcinoma can also occur. Acoustic neuromas are not classically associated with this condition.

Von Hippel-Lindau syndrome
Von Hippel-Lindau syndrome is incorrect. Von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) syndrome is characterized by hemangioblastomas of the brain, spinal cord, and retina; renal cysts and clear cell renal cell carcinoma. Acoustic neuromas are not classically associated with this condition.

stem: A 19-year-old woman is referred to the neurology outpatient department with 2 years of progressive weakness. She notices that she finds it difficult to walk upstairs and lift heavy objects over her head. Her mother has commented that her smile doesn't seem quite as 'bright' as it was previously. She has no significant past medical history and is not on any regular medications. She does not smoke or drink alcohol. On examination, she has difficulty closing her eyes and smiling. Power is 4+/5 at the proximal muscles of the upper and lower limbs. There is no rash. What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Facioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy
Facioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy is correct. The onset of this disorder is typically prior to the age of 20. It is characterized by facial weakness (difficulty closing eyes and smiling) and weakness of the shoulder and hip girdle muscles (i.e. the proximal muscles). A winged scapula may also be a feature.

Bell's palsy
Bell's palsy is incorrect. This would be of an acute onset rather than an insidious progression. Additionally, it is characterized by facial weakness and does not cause limb weakness.

Dermatomyositis
Dermatomyositis is incorrect. There is no rash and therefore this is not dermatomyositis.

Duchenne muscular dystrophy
Duchenne muscular dystrophy is incorrect. This is an X-linked recessive disorder and therefore doesn't affect females.

Myasthenia gravis
Myasthenia gravis is incorrect. This disorder is characterized by 'fatigable weakness'. The examination findings, in this case, do not mention that there was no weakness initially and subsequent development of weakness on repeated examination.

stem: A 76-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department, this is his 5th attendance in 2 months. His past medical history includes hypertension, hypercholesterolaemia and chronic alcohol use. You have never seen him and prior to entering the cubicle the registrar tells you to give his usual treatment of fluids, Pabrinex and discharge back home. You manage to take a minimal history from the patient but he denies falling or a history of head trauma. You examine him as best you can. He has an ataxic gait, horizontal nystagmus and dysmetria. What is an important cause of his symptoms not to be missed?
explanation:
Cerebellar stroke
Cerebellar stroke patients can present like they are 'drunk'. Patients with cerebellar strokes can present like they are drunk, and those with alcohol misuse this diagnosis can be missed.

Alcohol withdrawal
Alcohol withdrawal can range from mild, moderate and severe/delirium tremens depending on the symptoms. Mild to moderate withdrawal may start as early as 4 to 6 hours after the last drink, and peak at 24 to 36 hours. Severe withdrawal symptoms occur after 24 hours and usually peak at day 2. Delirium tremens generally occurs after 3 days of abstinence or decreased drinking.

Extradural haemorrhage
Extradural haemorrhages usually present with a history of trauma, like a blow to the pterion impacting on the middle meningeal artery.

Subdural haemorrhage
Subdural haemorrhages are seen in patients with chronic alcohol intake and the elderly and may present with a reduced GCS or confusion, particularly if they are on anticoagulants.

Vestibular neuronitis
Vestibular neuronitis is characterised by acute, spontaneous, and prolonged vertigo, commonly after a viral infection. Hearing loss and tinnitus are not features but may be present in labyrinthitis.

stem: A 68-year-old man has been brought to the emergency department after his family noticed a progressive deterioration in his breathing. He has a past medical history of COPD and is managed with inhalers. On examination, he has no wheeze but is making minimal respiratory effort. He has wasting of the small muscles of his hands, fasciculations of the left bicep and calf muscles, increased tone of the upper limbs, hyporeflexia of the biceps and reduced power in upper and lower limbs. An arterial blood gas (ABG) on room air demonstrates a mild type 2 respiratory failure. A chest x-ray demonstrates bilateral diaphragmatic palsy. What is the best treatment for prolongation of life in this patient?
explanation:
Non-invasive ventilation (NIV)
NIV is the correct option as this patient has a classical presentation of motor neuron disease (MND) with a mixture of upper motor neuron signs: hypertonia and most likely a spastic paralysis of the muscles of respiration (seen by the raised diaphragm) and lower motor neuron signs: muscle wasting, fasciculations and hyporeflexia. The most likely subtype of MND, in this case, is amyotrophic lateral sclerosis due to the early presentation with respiratory failure and profound diaphragmatic weakness. NIV has shown a survival benefit of 7 months on average.

Long-term oxygen therapy (LTOT)
LTOT is incorrect as COPD is not the cause of the breathlessness, in this case, demonstrated by the minimal work of breathing (tachypnoea in COPD worsening), bilateral diaphragmatic palsy (hyper-expanded 'barrel' lungs in COPD) and the other neurological signs point towards MND as the most likely cause of the type 2 respiratory failure in this case.

Pulmonary rehabilitation
Pulmonary rehabilitation is incorrect even though it has the best evidence base for prolonging the life expectancy of COPD patients. This is not the case when muscle function is being lost at the rate of this patient due to MND.

Pyridostigmine
Pyridostigmine is incorrect because this is a drug used to reduce symptoms in myasthenia gravis. MND is a much more likely diagnosis, even though myasthenia gravis can present with respiratory weakness and type 2 respiratory failure, it typically presents with muscle fatigability, worse towards the end of the day and usually marked ptosis.

Riluzole
Riluzole is an incorrect option, as it prolongs life in MND by an average of 3 months.

stem: You are working on the neurology ward. A 32-year-old woman with two young children has just been diagnosed with a chronic neurological disease after presenting with acute double vision. Two years ago she had an episode of acute vertigo which she put down to labyrinthitis. She has had an MRI scan of her brain and spine. She wants to know what sort of disease course she should expect. Which of the following patterns is most likely for the first several years of the disease?
options: Symptoms affecting peripheral nervous system first, and central nervous system later
Occasional flares of new symptoms in different areas of the body with variable recovery in between
A slow and gradual accumulation of symptoms over the next 20 years
Symptoms gradually ascending up her body starting with foot drop
Rapid accumulation of new symptoms initially but slowing after around 10 years
explanation:
Occasional flares of new symptoms in different areas of the body with variable recovery in between
The most common pattern for progression of multiple sclerosis is relapsing-remitting. This woman is likely to have multiple sclerosis (MS). She has distinct lesions in different areas of her brain and spine, which have developed at different times. The most likely disease course is relapsing and remitting - the occasional onset of new symptoms with complete or partial recovery in between episodes and the gradual accumulation of disability.

stem: A 66-year-old man is reviewed in the Neurology clinic after reporting a one-month history of progressive weakness, primarily affecting his upper limbs. He also reports that his limbs feel very stiff in the mornings. On examination, his movements are 4+/5 bilaterally in his lower limbs, and 3/5 bilaterally in his upper limbs on the Medical Research Council (MRC) power scale. He is also noticed to have a nasal quality to his speech, and occasional calf fasciculations. Peripheral sensation is intact. Given the likely diagnosis, which of the following treatment options is most likely to extend this patient's survival?
explanation:
Non-invasive ventilation
Non-invasive ventilation (NIV) confers the longest survival benefit (on average, 7 months), helping to mitigate type 2 respiratory failure in more advanced disease.

Interferon alpha
Interferon alpha is used in the treatment of hepatitis C, and has no role in the management of motor neuron disease.

Interferon beta
Interferon beta is used in the management of multiple sclerosis relapses. The purely motor nature of the patient's symptoms, presence of lower motor neuron signs and older age of onset ensure that motor neuron disease is a more likely diagnosis than multiple sclerosis in this patient.

Riluzole
Riluzole offers a mild survival benefit in the context of motor neuron disease via down-regulation of GABAergic transmission. However, this benefit is less marked than that offered by NIV.

Chest wall physiotherapy
Chest wall physiotherapy is an important tool in the management of secretions in motor neuron disease. However, its use is not associated with a significant survival benefit, as is the case with NIV.

stem: A 42-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with a 6-hour history of progressive weakness in his right leg. He was involved in a road traffic accident 2 days ago, sustaining a penetrating injury to his back from a metal fragment. On examination, he has reduced power (3/5) in his right leg with normal power in his left leg. There is loss of pain and temperature sensation on the left side below the level of T10, with preserved light touch and proprioception. Vibration and joint position sense are absent in the right leg. Reflexes are brisk in the right leg with an upgoing plantar response. Anal tone is preserved. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Brown-Séquard syndrome
Brown-Séquard syndrome is a result of lateral hemisection of the spinal cord. The clinical presentation in this case is highly characteristic of Brown-Séquard syndrome, which results from a lateral hemisection of the spinal cord. The patient has sustained a penetrating injury to his back, which is a common mechanism for this syndrome. The key features supporting this diagnosis are the ipsilateral weakness (right-sided in this case) and loss of proprioception and vibration sense (also right-sided), combined with contralateral loss of pain and temperature sensation (left-sided) below the level of the lesion. This pattern occurs because the lateral corticospinal tract (motor) and dorsal columns (proprioception, vibration) are affected on the same side as the hemisection, while the spinothalamic tract fibres (pain and temperature) cross at the level of entry and thus are affected on the opposite side. The presence of hyperreflexia and an upgoing plantar response on the right side further supports an upper motor neuron lesion on that side.

Anterior spinal artery syndrome
Anterior spinal artery syndrome results from ischaemia to the anterior two-thirds of the spinal cord. This typically presents with bilateral motor weakness and bilateral loss of pain and temperature sensation below the level of the lesion, with preservation of proprioception and vibration sense (as the dorsal columns are supplied by the posterior spinal arteries). The unilateral nature of the motor deficit and the contralateral sensory loss for pain and temperature make this diagnosis unlikely.

Cauda equina syndrome
Cauda equina syndrome affects the lumbosacral nerve roots and typically presents with saddle anaesthesia, bladder and bowel dysfunction, and lower motor neuron signs in the lower limbs. The patient has preserved anal tone and upper motor neuron signs (hyperreflexia and upgoing plantar), which are inconsistent with cauda equina syndrome. Additionally, the dissociated sensory loss pattern is not a feature of cauda equina syndrome.

Central cord syndrome
Central cord syndrome typically occurs after hyperextension injuries to the cervical spine, particularly in older patients with cervical spondylosis. It classically presents with greater weakness in the upper limbs than the lower limbs, and variable sensory loss. The pattern of neurological deficit in this case, with unilateral weakness and contralateral sensory loss for pain and temperature, is not consistent with central cord syndrome.

Complete spinal cord transection
Complete spinal cord transection would result in complete loss of all motor and sensory function below the level of the lesion, including loss of voluntary bowel and bladder control. The patient has preserved function in the left leg and selective sensory loss, which rules out a complete transection.

stem: A 44-year-old man presents to his GP complaining of weakness in his hands and legs and numbness in his feet. He first noticed some problems with walking in his late teens and reports that he's always been 'clumsy' and will often trip over. He is otherwise well and takes no regular medications. On examination, he has a high-stepping gait with wasting of the lower legs and high arches. Power is reduced in all limbs and reflexes are difficult to elicit. There is a reduction in sensation which is more pronounced distally. Coordination is intact. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Subacute combined degeneration of the cord
explanation:
Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease
Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease can affect both motor and sensory peripheral nerves. Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease is a hereditary sensory and motor peripheral neuropathy. UMN signs are not present in these patients. Patients can present with lower motor neurone signs in all limbs and reduced sensation (more pronounced distally).

Duchenne muscular dystrophy
Duchenne muscular dystrophy is an inherited myopathy. It is caused by progressive degeneration and weakness of specific muscle groups. Most patients lose the ability to walk by 12 years of age and require ventilatory support by the age of 25. Sensation is intact in these patients.

Cervical spondylotic myelopathy
Cervical spondylosis is the term used for osteoarthritis of the spine and can result in compression of the spinal cord. This is more likely to result in LMN signs at the level of the compression (i.e., upper limb if the lesion is below C5) with UMN signs below (in the lower limb). Patients usually complain of neck pain and stiffness.

Guillain-Barre syndrome
Guillain-Barre syndrome (GBS) is an inflammatory peripheral sensory and motor neuropathy. It typically presents over the course of days to weeks, not years. There is often a recent bacterial or viral infection in the history.

Subacute combined degeneration of the cord
Patients with subacute combined degeneration of the cord (SCDC) classically have an ataxic gait (due to degeneration of the dorsal columns) and mixed UMN and LMN signs (due to degeneration of lateral motor tracts and peripheral nerves). The history will typically be subacute, occurring over months rather than decades. Patients with SCDC often notice sensory symptoms before weakness.

stem: A 56-year-old man presents to the Diabetes clinic for review. He has a history of poorly-controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus, which was first diagnosed fifteen years ago, and primary open angle glaucoma. He is taking latanoprost, metformin, sitagliptin and once-daily insulin glargine. His most recent HbA1c reading was 98mmol/mol. At his last clinic review three months previously, he had complained of a burning, painful sensation in both his feet. He had been started on gabapentin, which he had uptitrated gradually to the maximum licensed dose. In spite of this, he reports no discernible improvement in the burning sensation in his feet. What is the most appropriate management option with respect to his neuropathy?
explanation:
Stop gabapentin, start duloxetine
As such, stopping gabapentin and starting duloxetine is the best option here.

Continue gabapentin, start duloxetine
Continuing gabapentin whilst starting duloxetine is in contravention of the principle of using drugs for neuropathic pain as monotherapy.

Continue gabapentin, start codeine
Codeine is unlikely to be an effective additional analgesic for this patient's neuropathic pain.

Stop gabapentin, start amitriptyline
